practice.subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main characteristics of kleptomania.
parts.answer: Repeated failure to resist urges to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their money value; a rising sense of tension or arousal before the theft; and a feeling of pleasure, gratification or relief during or immediately after stealing. The stealing is not done out of anger or revenge, and the objects are often given away, hidden or thrown away.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: recurrent failure to control urge to steal; items not needed/of little value; tension before; relief/gratification during or after; not motivated by anger, revenge or delusion; items discarded/hoarded/returned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one difference between kleptomania and pyromania.
parts.answer: In kleptomania the impulse is to steal objects, whereas in pyromania the impulse is to set fires (with a fascination with fire).
parts.working: 1 mark: stealing vs deliberate fire-setting.

practice.subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal spends many hours a day on online betting apps, chasing his losses, and has borrowed money from his relatives without telling his wife. Suggest how operant conditioning could explain why Bilal continues to gamble.
parts.answer: Gambling is maintained by positive reinforcement – occasional wins give money and excitement (and a dopamine 'high'). Wins come on a variable-ratio schedule: they are unpredictable, so Bilal keeps betting in case the next bet pays out, and this schedule is very resistant to extinction. Near misses may also feel rewarding. Gambling may also be negatively reinforced if it lets him escape stress or worry about his debts, so 'chasing losses' continues.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive reinforcement from wins. 1 mark: variable-ratio / partial reinforcement schedule. 1 mark: resistance to extinction / near misses. 1 mark: negative reinforcement or application to Bilal's chasing losses.

practice.subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe imaginal desensitisation as a treatment for gambling disorder.
parts.answer: Based on classical conditioning and systematic desensitisation. The client is first taught progressive muscle relaxation. Then, while relaxed, they imagine scenes that would normally trigger the urge to gamble (e.g. walking past a betting shop, having money in their pocket, seeing a match on TV), imagining themselves feeling the urge but not gambling and leaving the situation. Over several short sessions (often guided by recordings for practice at home), the relaxation response is paired with the cues, so the arousal and tension that drive the urge are reduced. It aims to break the link between gambling cues and arousal so the person can resist the urge.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 of: based on conditioning/reciprocal inhibition; relaxation training; imagined gambling cues/scenes; imagining resisting the urge and leaving; repeated sessions/audio recordings; reduces arousal/tension linked to cues; aim to weaken cue–urge association; may be compared with aversion therapy.

practice.subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the feeling-state theory of behavioural addiction.
parts.answer: Miller's feeling-state theory proposes that an addictive behaviour (e.g. gambling or stealing) becomes linked with an intense positive feeling at a particular moment – such as a feeling of success, power or excitement – forming a 'feeling-state' (a memory combining the sensations, emotions, thoughts and the behaviour). Later, when the person experiences an unmet need or negative emotion, the feeling-state is triggered, producing an urge to repeat the behaviour to get that feeling again. Treatment (the feeling-state addiction protocol) aims to identify and break up these feeling-states, e.g. using eye-movement techniques.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive feeling linked to the behaviour. 1 mark: forms a feeling-state memory (sensations, emotions, cognitions). 1 mark: triggered later by negative emotions/unmet needs, producing the urge. 1 mark: treatment link (identify and process feeling-states).

practice.subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the K-SAS (Kleptomania Symptom Assessment Scale) is useful for measuring kleptomania, and give one weakness of using it.
parts.answer: It is a self-report rating scale that asks about the key features of kleptomania over the past week, e.g. how strong and frequent urges to steal were, how much time was spent thinking about stealing, and how much distress was felt, giving a total score. Because it gives quantitative scores, it can be used to compare patients and to measure change before and after treatment. Weakness: it relies on honest self-report; people may under-report stealing because it is illegal and embarrassing (social desirability), so scores may not be valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report rating scale of symptoms. 1 mark: example items (urges, thoughts, time, distress). 1 mark: strength – quantitative/compare/track change. 1 mark: weakness explained.

practice.subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a study to investigate whether covert sensitisation reduces the urge to steal in people with kleptomania. Your plan must use a self-report rating scale and an experiment with an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Sample: e.g. 40 adults diagnosed with kleptomania, recruited through psychiatric clinics (volunteer/opportunity), with consent. Design: independent measures; randomly allocated to covert sensitisation or a waiting-list/relaxation control. IV: type of treatment. Covert sensitisation: patients imagine the urge to steal, then immediately imagine aversive consequences (e.g. being caught by security, embarrassment in front of family, or nausea), over 8 weekly sessions with home practice. DV: urge to steal measured by a self-report scale, e.g. the K-SAS or an urge rating of 0 (no urge) to 10 (overwhelming urge), completed weekly and at a 3-month follow-up; plus number of thefts reported. Controls: same number and length of sessions, same therapist training, rating completed in private. Ethics: informed consent, confidentiality (thefts are illegal), right to withdraw, controls offered treatment afterwards. Analysis: compare mean change scores.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): plan fully meets the requirements – independent measures with allocation, self-report scale with example items/anchors, covert sensitisation described, sample, procedure, controls, ethics; replicable. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, some requirements missing. Level 1 (1–2): very limited.

practice.subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate explanations of impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction, including a discussion about reductionism.
parts.answer: Points may include: behavioural explanation (operant conditioning, variable-ratio reinforcement) is supported by the persistence of gambling and the design of gambling machines, and leads to treatments such as imaginal desensitisation; but it cannot explain why only some people who gamble develop a disorder. Biological explanations (dopamine reward pathways, possible genetic vulnerability) are supported by the use of opioid antagonists such as naltrexone reducing urges; but correlations between brain activity and gambling do not prove cause. Feeling-state theory explains individual differences in triggers but has limited research support and relies on subjective reports. Reductionism: biological and behavioural explanations reduce complex behaviour to single factors (neurotransmitters, reinforcement) – useful for treatment but ignore social, cultural and economic influences (e.g. availability of online betting); a more holistic, interactionist view combining biology, learning and cognition may be better. Also: nature/nurture, determinism, usefulness, cultural differences.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation of at least two explanations with evidence; reductionism explicitly and effectively discussed; well organised. Level 3 (6–8): reasonable evaluation; named issue discussed. Level 2 (3–5): limited, may be mostly descriptive; named issue brief. Level 1 (1–2): basic, anecdotal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Positive symptoms are experiences or behaviours added to normal functioning, e.g. hallucinations (hearing voices) or delusions (false beliefs such as being persecuted). Negative symptoms are a loss or reduction of normal functioning, e.g. avolition (lack of motivation), alogia (poverty of speech) or flat affect.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive = additions to normal experience. 1 mark: example. 1 mark: negative = loss/reduction of normal function. 1 mark: example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia.
parts.answer: The hypothesis states that schizophrenia is associated with abnormal dopamine activity. Excess dopamine activity, or over-sensitive/too many D2 receptors, in the mesolimbic pathway is linked to positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions. Later versions suggest low dopamine activity in the mesocortical pathway (prefrontal cortex) is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms. Evidence: drugs that increase dopamine (e.g. amphetamines) can produce psychotic-like symptoms; typical antipsychotics block D2 receptors and reduce positive symptoms; the dose of antipsychotics needed relates to how strongly they bind to D2 receptors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: excess dopamine; D2 receptors (sensitivity/number); mesolimbic → positive symptoms; low prefrontal dopamine → negative symptoms; amphetamine evidence; antipsychotics block D2; L-dopa evidence; revised hypothesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline Frith's cognitive explanation of schizophrenia.
parts.answer: Frith proposed that schizophrenia involves a deficit in metarepresentation – the ability to reflect on our own thoughts and intentions. A failure of self-monitoring means the person does not recognise their own inner speech or actions as self-generated, so they experience them as coming from an outside source (auditory hallucinations, delusions of control). A deficit in central control (willed action) means they cannot suppress automatic responses, producing disorganised speech and thought (e.g. derailment) and possibly negative symptoms.
parts.working: 1 mark: metarepresentation deficit. 1 mark: self-monitoring failure → hallucinations/delusions of control. 1 mark: central control deficit. 1 mark: link to disorganised speech/negative symptoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical twin study found that 28 of 60 identical (MZ) twin pairs were concordant for schizophrenia, compared with 5 of 55 non-identical (DZ) twin pairs. Calculate the concordance rate for each type of twin, as a percentage to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results suggest about the nature versus nurture debate in schizophrenia.
parts.answer: The much higher concordance for MZ twins, who share all their genes, than DZ twins, who share about half, suggests a genetic (nature) influence; but because MZ concordance is far below 100 %, environmental (nurture) factors must also play a part (diathesis–stress).
parts.working: 1 mark: higher MZ concordance supports genetic influence. 1 mark: concordance < 100 % shows environment also involved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare typical and atypical antipsychotic drugs as treatments for schizophrenia.
parts.answer: Typical antipsychotics (e.g. chlorpromazine) mainly block dopamine D2 receptors and reduce positive symptoms, but often cause extrapyramidal side effects such as tremors and, with long-term use, tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements). Atypical antipsychotics (e.g. clozapine, risperidone) act on dopamine and serotonin receptors, can help some negative symptoms and cause fewer movement side effects, but may cause weight gain, and clozapine needs regular blood tests because of the risk of agranulocytosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: typical – D2 blockade, positive symptoms. 1 mark: typical side effects. 1 mark: atypical – dopamine and serotonin, broader effect. 1 mark: atypical side effects/fewer motor effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) has 30 items, each rated by a clinician from 1 (absent) to 7 (extreme). Seven items form the positive scale. State the lowest and highest possible scores on the positive scale and on the whole PANSS.
parts.answer: Positive scale: 7 to 49. Whole PANSS: 30 to 210.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using a clinician-rated interview scale such as the PANSS rather than a self-report questionnaire to assess schizophrenia.
parts.answer: Strength: trained clinicians can rate symptoms that patients may lack insight into (e.g. they may not see their delusions as unusual), and a structured interview with defined anchors gives standardised, quantitative scores that can track change. Weakness: ratings depend on the clinician's judgement, so they can be subjective or biased (e.g. by expectations of a treatment), and the interview is time-consuming and requires training.
parts.working: Strength: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation (insight/standardised). Weakness: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation (subjectivity/inter-rater reliability/time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate treatment and management of schizophrenia, including a discussion about ethics.
parts.answer: Points may include: antipsychotics are effective in reducing positive symptoms and relapse, allowing many patients to live in the community; but side effects (tardive dyskinesia, weight gain) raise ethical concerns, and patients may lack capacity to consent or be treated compulsorily. Token economies (e.g. Paul and Lentz's social-learning programme) improved self-care and social behaviour in long-stay hospital patients, but behaviour may not generalise outside the institution and withholding privileges raises ethical issues about dignity and control. CBT helps patients challenge delusional beliefs and cope with voices; it respects autonomy and has fewer side effects, but needs insight and motivation and may not suit acute patients. Ethical discussion: informed consent and capacity, right to refuse, risk–benefit balance, coercion, stigma. Also: effectiveness, generalisability, reductionism, individual differences.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced evaluation of at least two treatments with evidence; ethics thoroughly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): reasonable evaluation; ethics included. Level 2 (3–5): limited/descriptive. Level 1 (1–2): basic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the characteristics of generalised anxiety disorder (GAD).
parts.answer: Persistent, excessive worry about many everyday events (e.g. family, health, work or money) rather than one specific trigger, lasting for months (several months, most days), and difficult to control; with symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension, sleep problems, difficulty concentrating, irritability and autonomic overactivity (racing heart, sweating), causing distress or impairment.
parts.working: 1 mark: general, excessive worry about many things. 1 mark: persistent (months, most days) / hard to control. 1 mark: physical or other symptoms (any two).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The GAD-7 questionnaire has 7 items, each scored 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day) for the past two weeks. A client's item scores are 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 1 and 3. Calculate the client's total score and state the severity band, given the bands: 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–21 severe.
parts.answer: 14 – moderate anxiety.
parts.working: B1: total = 14. B1: moderate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a clinician should not diagnose GAD from the GAD-7 score alone.
parts.answer: It is a short self-report screening tool; the client may over- or under-report symptoms (e.g. social desirability or misunderstanding), and the score does not check other diagnostic features such as duration, other causes or impairment, so a clinical interview is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report bias / screening only. 1 mark: explanation – need for interview to check diagnostic criteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zara faints whenever she sees blood or has an injection, so she has avoided going to the dentist for years. Suggest how applied tension could be used to treat her.
parts.answer: Applied tension targets the drop in blood pressure that causes fainting in blood-injection-injury phobia. Zara would be taught to tense the large muscles of her arms, legs and torso for about 10–15 seconds until she feels warmth in her face, then release (without fully relaxing), repeating this several times. Once she has learned the technique, she would practise it while being gradually exposed to blood-related stimuli – e.g. pictures of blood, a video of an injection, then a real finger prick – using tension at the first sign of a drop in blood pressure, so she can stay conscious and stop avoiding the dentist.
parts.working: 1 mark: aim – raise blood pressure / prevent fainting. 1 mark: tensing large muscle groups for a few seconds. 1 mark: practice with gradual exposure to blood/injury stimuli. 1 mark: application to Zara (dentist/injections).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how classical conditioning explains the development of phobias. Refer to Watson and Rayner's study in your answer.
parts.answer: A neutral stimulus becomes associated with an unconditioned stimulus that naturally causes fear, so the neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus producing a conditioned fear response. Watson and Rayner studied 'Little Albert', an 11-month-old boy who initially showed no fear of a white rat. Each time he reached for the rat, a steel bar was struck loudly with a hammer behind him (UCS), causing fear and crying (UCR). After several pairings, the rat alone (CS) caused crying and attempts to crawl away (CR). Albert's fear then generalised to similar furry objects such as a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat and a Santa Claus mask. Avoidance of the feared object is then negatively reinforced because it reduces anxiety, which maintains the phobia (two-process model).
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 of: NS paired with UCS; becomes CS producing CR (fear); Albert, 11 months, no initial fear of rat; loud noise (steel bar) as UCS; rat alone produced fear after pairings; stimulus generalisation with examples; avoidance maintained by negative reinforcement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe systematic desensitisation as a treatment for specific phobias.
parts.answer: Based on classical conditioning and reciprocal inhibition – a person cannot feel relaxed and anxious at the same time. Step 1: the client learns deep muscle relaxation (and breathing). Step 2: the client and therapist build an anxiety hierarchy of situations involving the feared object, ranked from least to most frightening (e.g. for spiders: the word 'spider', a cartoon, a photo, a spider in a closed jar, holding a spider). Step 3: the client works up the hierarchy while relaxed, either in imagination (in vitro) or with real stimuli (in vivo), moving to the next step only when they can stay relaxed. The fear response is replaced (counter-conditioned) by relaxation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 of: classical conditioning/counter-conditioning; reciprocal inhibition; relaxation training; hierarchy built with client; example items; gradual progression only when relaxed; in vivo/in vitro; several sessions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical trial for GAD in a clinic in Karachi, 35 patients received CBT and 40 patients received medication. After 12 weeks, 14 CBT patients and 6 medication patients were classed as 'recovered'. Calculate the percentage recovered in each group.
parts.answer: CBT: 40 %; medication: 15 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why it would be wrong to conclude from these results alone that CBT is more effective than medication for GAD.
parts.answer: 1. Patients may not have been randomly allocated – e.g. those with milder anxiety or more motivation may have chosen CBT, so participant variables could explain the difference. 2. The measure of 'recovered' may have been made by clinicians who knew which treatment each patient received (no blinding), introducing bias; also the follow-up was short (12 weeks) and the groups were small, so long-term effectiveness is unknown.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the trial.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nature versus nurture debate, and explain one reason why explanations of anxiety and fear-related disorders can be seen as supporting nurture.
parts.answer: The nature–nurture debate concerns whether behaviour is mainly caused by inherited, biological factors (nature) or by experiences and the environment (nurture). Explanations of phobias such as classical conditioning support nurture because fear is learned through experiences: Little Albert's fear of the rat was created by pairing it with a loud noise, and fears can be learned by observing others (social learning). However, some fears (e.g. of snakes) may be easier to acquire because of evolved preparedness, which supports nature.
parts.working: 2 marks: outline of the debate (nature = genes/biology; nurture = environment/experience). 2 marks: reason supporting nurture explained with example (conditioning/modelling).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between obsessions and compulsions, giving an example of each.
parts.answer: Obsessions are persistent, intrusive and unwanted thoughts, images or urges that cause anxiety, e.g. a recurring thought that one's hands are contaminated with germs. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts that a person feels driven to perform to reduce the anxiety caused by obsessions, e.g. washing hands many times in a particular way, or checking the door is locked again and again.
parts.working: 1 mark: obsessions defined. 1 mark: example. 1 mark: compulsions defined (reduce anxiety). 1 mark: example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) has 10 items: 5 about obsessions and 5 about compulsions, each scored 0 to 4. A patient's obsession item scores are 3, 3, 2, 4 and 3, and the compulsion item scores are 3, 4, 2, 3 and 3. Calculate the obsession subtotal, the compulsion subtotal and the total score, and state the severity band (0–7 subclinical, 8–15 mild, 16–23 moderate, 24–31 severe, 32–40 extreme).
parts.answer: Obsessions 15, compulsions 15, total 30 – severe.
parts.working: B1: 15 and 15. B1: total 30. B1: severe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using the Y-BOCS to measure OCD.
parts.answer: It is administered by a trained clinician in a semi-structured interview, so ratings are standardised and give a quantitative score; this allows the severity of different patients to be compared and changes during treatment to be measured.
parts.working: 1 mark: standardised/quantitative/clinician-administered. 1 mark: allows comparison or measurement of progress.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ahmed checks the gas stove up to 30 times before leaving home, because he fears that if the house burns down it will be his fault. Suggest how exposure and response prevention (ERP) could be used to treat Ahmed.
parts.answer: The therapist and Ahmed build a hierarchy of situations that make him anxious about the stove, from leaving after checking 10 times up to leaving the house after not checking at all. He is exposed to each situation (e.g. turning the stove off once and walking away) and prevented from carrying out the compulsion (checking again). He stays with the anxiety until it falls (habituation), learning that the feared disaster does not happen. He moves up the hierarchy over sessions and practises as homework.
parts.working: 1 mark: hierarchy. 1 mark: exposure to anxiety-provoking situation. 1 mark: response prevention – not checking. 1 mark: habituation/learning feared outcome does not occur, linked to Ahmed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lovell et al. compared CBT (exposure and response prevention) for OCD delivered by telephone with the same treatment delivered face to face. Explain one strength and one weakness of delivering therapy by telephone, using evidence from this study.
parts.answer: Strength: Lovell et al. found telephone-delivered ERP was about as effective as face-to-face treatment in reducing OCD symptoms (measured with the Y-BOCS), while saving travel time and costs and making treatment accessible to people who live far away or find it hard to leave home. Weakness: the therapist cannot see the patient's body language or carry out exposure exercises together in person, and some patients may feel less supported, so it may not suit everyone (e.g. those with severe symptoms).
parts.working: Strength: 1 mark identification, 1 mark linked to Lovell's finding of equivalence/accessibility. Weakness: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate explanations of obsessive-compulsive disorder, including a discussion about determinism.
parts.answer: Biological: low serotonin activity is supported by the effectiveness of SSRIs in reducing symptoms; family and twin evidence suggests a genetic component; but SSRIs do not help everyone and correlation does not show cause. Cognitive (e.g. Salkovskis's inflated responsibility): intrusive thoughts are normal, but people with OCD interpret them as meaningful and feel responsible for preventing harm, leading to neutralising compulsions; supported by the success of CBT/ERP, but it is unclear whether faulty thinking causes OCD or results from it. Behavioural: compulsions maintained by negative reinforcement (anxiety reduction). Determinism: biological explanations are hard-determinist (genes/neurotransmitters cause OCD), which may reduce blame but suggests the patient has little control; cognitive explanations are softer – patients can learn to change their thoughts – which supports therapy and personal responsibility. Also: reductionism, nature/nurture, usefulness.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): detailed, balanced evaluation of at least two explanations with evidence; determinism explicitly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): reasonable evaluation; determinism included. Level 2 (3–5): limited/descriptive. Level 1 (1–2): basic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between a depressive disorder and bipolar disorder.
parts.answer: Depressive disorder involves episodes of low mood and/or loss of interest only. Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mania or hypomania (elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, reduced need for sleep), usually alternating with depressive episodes.
parts.working: 1 mark: depression – low mood/loss of interest only. 1 mark: bipolar – manic/hypomanic episodes (often with depression).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe Beck's cognitive triad.
parts.answer: Beck proposed that depressed people have three types of negative automatic thoughts: a negative view of the self (e.g. 'I am worthless'), a negative view of the world/experiences (e.g. 'everyone is against me') and a negative view of the future (e.g. 'things will never get better').
parts.working: 1 mark each for self, world and future (with example or explanation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) has 21 items, each scored 0 to 3. State the maximum possible score.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient's item scores add up to 22. Using the bands 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate and 29–63 severe, state the patient's level of depression.
parts.answer: Moderate depression.
parts.working: B1: moderate (22 lies in 20–28).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the BDI as a measure of depression.
parts.answer: It is a self-report questionnaire, so patients may exaggerate or minimise symptoms (e.g. social desirability, or stigma about mental illness), and it only covers the last two weeks, so scores may not be valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report bias / snapshot of two weeks. 1 mark: explanation of effect on validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mehreen has felt low for months since failing her university entrance exam. She now believes she is a failure at everything and refuses to apply for any course. Suggest how cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) could help her.
parts.answer: The therapist would help Mehreen identify her negative automatic thoughts (e.g. 'I fail at everything') and challenge them by looking for evidence against them, such as subjects she has done well in (reality testing). She would learn to replace them with more balanced thoughts ('I failed one exam, but I can prepare differently'). Behavioural tasks such as scheduling enjoyable activities and taking small steps towards applying to a course would provide evidence of success and improve mood. Homework such as a thought diary would help her practise between sessions.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify negative thoughts. 1 mark: challenge/dispute with evidence. 1 mark: behavioural activation/homework. 1 mark: application to Mehreen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the biological (biochemical) treatment of mood disorders, including a discussion about individual differences.
parts.answer: Antidepressants such as SSRIs increase the availability of serotonin in the synapse; many patients improve, they are relatively cheap and easy to take, and they can be combined with therapy. Weaknesses: they take several weeks to work; side effects (e.g. nausea, sleep problems) can lead to stopping treatment; relapse is common when they are stopped; some trials suggest only small advantages over placebo for mild depression; they treat symptoms rather than causes such as negative thinking or life events. Mood stabilisers (e.g. lithium) are used for bipolar disorder but need blood monitoring. Individual differences: patients respond very differently – some need several drugs before one works, genetics and severity affect response, and some prefer psychological therapy; a nomothetic, one-size approach may not suit everyone, so combining medication with CBT tailored to the person may be best. Also: reductionism, ethics, comparison with CBT.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with evidence; individual differences explicitly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): reasonable evaluation; named issue included. Level 2 (3–5): limited/descriptive. Level 1 (1–2): basic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two types of retail store layout.
parts.answer: Grid layout: shelves arranged in long parallel aisles at right angles, as in most supermarkets; shoppers move up and down aisles, and it is efficient for finding everyday items. Freeform layout: displays and racks are placed in irregular, flowing patterns, as in fashion boutiques; it encourages browsing and relaxed movement around the store. (Accept racetrack/loop layout: one main path leads shoppers past all departments, as in large furniture stores.)
parts.working: 2 marks per layout: 1 for naming/identifying it with a key feature, 1 for a further detail or example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a freeform layout might suit a small clothing boutique better than a grid layout.
parts.answer: Customers in a boutique want to browse and try items rather than find things quickly; a freeform layout encourages them to wander, look at more displays and stay longer, which can increase unplanned purchases.
parts.working: 1 mark: browsing/exploration/longer time in store; 1 mark: link to more purchases or customer enjoyment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the findings of research by Milliman on music tempo in a supermarket.
parts.answer: When slow-tempo music was played, shoppers moved through the store more slowly and sales were higher than when fast-tempo music was played.
parts.working: 1 mark: slow music slowed shoppers' pace; 1 mark: higher sales with slow music.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how a Karachi supermarket manager could apply these findings, and give one reason why this might not work.
parts.answer: Play slow music during quiet weekday hours to encourage longer browsing; however, at busy times slow movement may cause crowding and annoy shoppers, so faster music might be better then (or local shoppers may prefer different music).
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable application; 1 mark: limitation (crowding, cultural differences, customer purpose such as quick top-up shopping).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nadia is opening a clothing store for young adults in a Lahore shopping mall. Suggest how she could use music to influence customers' behaviour in her store.
parts.answer: She could play music that fits the store's image and her young customers, such as current pop music, because music congruent with the store and audience creates a positive mood and approach behaviour. She could use slower-tempo music at quiet times so customers move more slowly and browse longer (research found slow music in a supermarket slowed shoppers and increased sales). She should keep the volume moderate so customers can talk and are not driven away.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant, justified suggestion, up to 4; suggestions must be linked to psychological evidence (tempo, congruence/fit, volume, mood) and applied to Nadia's store; max 2 if no link to evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the procedure of North et al.'s study of music in a restaurant.
parts.answer: The study took place in a real restaurant over a number of evenings. On different evenings either classical music, pop music or no music was played in the background. The bills of diners were used to record how much was spent per head on starters, main courses, desserts, coffee, drinks and in total, and this was compared across the three music conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: field setting (a real restaurant); three conditions – classical, pop, no music; conditions varied between evenings; spending per person measured from bills, including different courses/items.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the main finding of this study.
parts.answer: Customers spent more in total when classical music was played than when pop music or no music was played.
parts.working: 1 mark: classical music led to the highest spending.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the way the conditions were organised in this study.
parts.answer: Different evenings had different customers, so differences in spending may be due to the kind of diners on each evening (e.g. people celebrating special occasions) rather than the music; customers could not be randomly allocated to conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (participant variables / independent measures / no random allocation / other changes between evenings); 1 mark: explained in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the conditions in North, Hargreaves and McKendrick's study of in-store music and wine choice.
parts.answer: On alternate days, French accordion music or German Bierkeller (beer-hall) music was played beside a display of French and German wines in a supermarket.
parts.working: 1 mark: French vs German music; 1 mark: alternated between days, at a wine display in a supermarket.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline the results of the study.
parts.answer: More French wine than German wine was sold when French music was played, and more German wine than French wine when German music was played.
parts.working: 1 mark for each direction of the result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some shoppers were asked whether the music had influenced their choice. Explain what their answers suggested.
parts.answer: Very few shoppers said the music had influenced their choice, suggesting that the music affected their decisions without conscious awareness (it primed thoughts of the country).
parts.working: 1 mark: few shoppers aware/mentioned music; 1 mark: influence was unconscious/priming.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the determinism versus free will debate.
parts.answer: Determinism is the view that behaviour is caused by factors outside a person's control (internal or external), whereas free will is the view that people can choose how to behave.
parts.working: 1 mark: determinism; 1 mark: free will.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why research into store atmospherics (such as music and scent) can be seen as deterministic.
parts.answer: It suggests customers' choices – what they buy and how much they spend – are caused by environmental cues like music tempo or scent that they are not aware of, rather than by free, conscious choices.
parts.working: 1 mark: environmental cues cause behaviour; 1 mark: example from research (e.g. French music → French wine) and lack of awareness/control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'congruence' between scent and other features of a store, using research to support your answer.
parts.answer: Congruence is when the scent fits the store, its products or other atmospheric cues such as music. Spangenberg et al. found that a Christmas scent produced more favourable evaluations of a store when Christmas music was also played, but less favourable evaluations with non-Christmas music.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of congruence; 1 mark: supporting research evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ali owns a perfume and attar shop in Rawalpindi. Suggest two ways he could use the physical environment to increase sales during Eid.
parts.answer: 1) Use a light, festive scent congruent with his products (e.g. a mild rose or oud attar) diffused in the shop, as congruent scents improve evaluations and approach behaviour. 2) Use warm lighting and an uncluttered layout with testers displayed at the front, so customers can browse comfortably; play quiet traditional music congruent with Eid, as music that fits the setting creates a positive mood.
parts.working: 2 marks per suggestion: 1 for a suitable suggestion, 1 for justification from psychology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe research into the effects of sound (music) on consumer behaviour.
parts.answer: North et al. found that restaurant diners spent more when classical music was played than with pop music or no music, possibly because classical music creates an upmarket image (a 'sophisticated' priming effect). North, Hargreaves and McKendrick played French or German music on alternate days next to a supermarket wine display: French wine outsold German wine when French music played, and German wine outsold French when German music played; few shoppers said the music had influenced them. Milliman found that slow-tempo music in a supermarket slowed shoppers' movement and increased sales compared with fast-tempo music.
parts.working: Credit named studies with procedure and findings; theory such as priming/congruence/arousal. Marks: 1 mark per accurate point, or 2 for a well-detailed point, up to 6; the answer should name the research and its findings in detail for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate research into the effects of sound on consumer behaviour, including a discussion of ecological validity.
parts.answer: Strengths: field studies in real restaurants and supermarkets have high ecological validity – real customers spending their own money; useful applications for retailers. Weaknesses: lack of control in field settings – other variables (weather, day of the week, special offers) may affect spending; customers cannot be randomly allocated; ethical concerns – shoppers are influenced without awareness or consent (unconscious manipulation); cultural differences – musical associations (e.g. classical = expensive) may not hold in other cultures such as Pakistan; results are often small and may depend on the type of product; reductionism – music is only one part of the atmosphere; determinism vs free will – suggests consumers are passive.
parts.working: Must include ecological validity (named issue); credit other issues and debates (application, ethics, control, generalisability, culture, determinism). Level 4 (9–10): a range of well-developed evaluative points, including the named issue, with effective use of examples from research; clear structure. Level 3 (6–8): several evaluative points, mostly developed; the named issue covered. Level 2 (3–5): limited evaluation, mostly undeveloped; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field experiment to investigate whether a pleasant scent in a bakery increases the amount customers spend. Your plan must include an independent measures design and a way of measuring the dependent variable from sales records.
parts.answer: A possible plan: field experiment in a bakery in Islamabad; IV – a vanilla/fresh-bread scent released from a diffuser near the entrance vs no added scent; conditions alternate on matched days (e.g. Mondays and Wednesdays scent, Tuesdays and Thursdays no scent) over four weeks; independent measures – different customers in each condition; DV – mean spending per customer from till receipts (total sales ÷ number of transactions), plus the number of items per receipt; controls – same opening hours, prices, staff, displays and music, no promotions during the study, scent intensity kept the same; ethics – scent safe and mild, no personal data recorded, public setting.
parts.working: Mark points: IV operationalised; independent measures with how conditions are allocated; DV from sales records operationalised; controls; sample/setting; duration; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): detailed, coherent plan covering all the required features with clear operationalisation. Level 3 (6–8): clear plan with most features. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, several features missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief/muddled. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the psychological knowledge on which your plan is based.
parts.answer: Research on scent in retail: pleasant ambient scent can improve mood and evaluations of a store, increasing approach behaviour such as browsing longer and spending more. Spangenberg et al. found that a Christmas scent improved evaluations of a store when combined with Christmas music, but not with non-Christmas music – showing the importance of congruence between scent and setting; a bread or vanilla scent is congruent with a bakery. Mehrabian–Russell model: environmental stimuli produce pleasure and arousal, leading to approach or avoidance behaviour.
parts.working: Credit relevant theories and studies on scent/atmospherics and their link to the plan. Level 4 (7–8): accurate, detailed psychology (named theory/studies) clearly linked to the plan. Level 3 (5–6): mostly accurate and linked. Level 2 (3–4): basic or partly relevant. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons for choosing the features of your plan.
parts.answer: Independent measures: customers each visit only once, so a repeated measures design is not practical and order effects are avoided; alternating days balances out weekday differences. Sales records: objective, quantitative and already collected by the bakery, so customers are unaware they are being studied (no demand characteristics) and the measure is reliable.
parts.working: 3 marks for each of two choices: 1 identifies the choice, 1 explains why it is appropriate, 1 links to the plan or psychological evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which packaging can influence consumer choice.
parts.answer: Colour: colours carry associations, e.g. green packaging suggests a natural or healthy product, so consumers may judge the product as healthier. Shape and size: a tall, slim bottle may look as if it holds more, or an attractive shape stands out on a crowded shelf and attracts attention, increasing the chance of purchase.
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 for the feature (colour, shape, size, labels/information, material), 1 for how it influences perception or choice.

practice.stem: A researcher at a university in Faisalabad asked 30 students to taste three mango juices from unlabelled cups and to rank them in order of preference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the taste test was carried out 'blind'.
parts.answer: So that participants rated the juices on taste alone; if they could see the brands, their existing brand loyalty and expectations would affect their ratings.
parts.working: 1 mark: brand not visible; 1 mark: removes the effect of expectations/brand image.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the order in which the three juices were tasted was varied between participants.
parts.answer: To counterbalance order effects – e.g. the first juice might seem better because the participant was thirsty, or later juices worse because of aftertaste – so these effects are spread equally across the juices.
parts.working: 1 mark: counterbalancing/order effects; 1 mark: example of an order effect in tasting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of measuring participants' preferences, other than asking them to rank the juices.
parts.answer: Ask them to rate each juice from 1 (very unpleasant) to 9 (very pleasant), or measure how much of each juice they drink when offered freely.
parts.working: 1 mark: a different, operationalised measure (rating scale, amount consumed, choice of a free bottle).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how McClure et al. investigated the effect of brand knowledge on preferences for cola drinks.
parts.answer: Participants tasted cola drinks in a brain scanner (fMRI). In some trials they did not know which brand they were drinking (blind tasting); in others they were told or shown the brand (e.g. a Coke label) before tasting. Their preferences and brain activity were compared across these conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: blind tasting vs brand-labelled tasting; drinks delivered while in an fMRI scanner; preferences/stated choices recorded; brain activity compared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one finding of this study.
parts.answer: Knowing that the drink was Coke increased people's preference for it, compared with blind tasting.
parts.working: 1 mark: brand knowledge (Coke) biased preferences; accept activation of brain areas linked to memory and higher thinking (e.g. hippocampus, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) when the brand was known.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the blind-tasting condition was needed.
parts.answer: It showed preference based on taste alone, so any change when the brand was known could be attributed to brand knowledge rather than the taste of the drink.
parts.working: 1 mark: baseline/control based on taste only; 1 mark: allows effect of brand to be isolated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal is launching a new brand of packaged chai for busy young professionals in Pakistan. Suggest how he could use psychology to design the product's name and packaging.
parts.answer: Name: choose a short, easy-to-pronounce name that is easy to remember and conveys the benefit (e.g. a word suggesting energy or speed), because easy-to-process names are liked more and remembered better. Packaging: use colours associated with warmth and energy (e.g. deep red or gold) and a modern, simple design that stands out on the shelf and matches the young professional image; include clear information about preparation time to show convenience.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant suggestion with justification, up to 4; suggestions must apply to Bilal's product and use psychology (memorability, colour associations, brand image, attention).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the individual versus situational explanations debate.
parts.answer: Individual explanations say behaviour is caused by characteristics of the person (e.g. personality, preferences, biology); situational explanations say behaviour is caused by features of the environment (e.g. packaging, price, store setting).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how research on the product supports a situational explanation of consumer choice.
parts.answer: Blind taste tests show that preferences change when the brand label is visible, so the choice is driven by information in the situation (the packaging/brand) rather than only by the person's own taste.
parts.working: 1 mark: situational feature of the product influences choice; 1 mark: example from research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe research into how product information, such as brand or price, affects how consumers experience a product.
parts.answer: McClure et al. used fMRI while participants tasted colas: when they knew a drink was Coke, their preference for it increased compared with blind tasting, and brain areas linked to memory and higher thinking were more active – brand associations changed the experience. Plassmann et al. found that when the same wine was presented with a higher price, participants rated it as more pleasant and activity in an area of the brain linked to pleasure (medial orbitofrontal cortex) increased – a price–quality heuristic. Blind taste tests in general show that people often cannot identify their 'favourite' brand without the label.
parts.working: Credit named studies, procedure, findings and explanations (brand associations, price–quality heuristic, expectation). Marks: 1 mark per accurate point, or 2 for a well-detailed point, up to 6; the answer should name the research and its findings in detail for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate research into how product information affects how consumers experience a product, including a discussion of the use of physiological measures.
parts.answer: Physiological measures (fMRI): objective evidence that brand/price information changes brain responses, not just what people say – avoids social desirability; but scanners are artificial (lying still, drinks via tubes), samples are small and costly, and brain activity is correlational and open to interpretation (reverse inference). Other points: laboratory control allows causal conclusions about the label; low ecological validity – tasting tiny amounts is unlike real consumption; generalisability across cultures and brands (Coke is unusually familiar); application – explains why branding and pricing are effective; ethics – raises concerns about 'neuromarketing'; reductionism – reduces preference to brain areas.
parts.working: Must include physiological measures (named issue). Level 4 (9–10): a range of well-developed evaluative points, including the named issue, with effective use of examples from research; clear structure. Level 3 (6–8): several evaluative points, mostly developed; the named issue covered. Level 2 (3–5): limited evaluation, mostly undeveloped; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe utility theory and satisficing as explanations of consumer decision-making.
parts.answer: Utility theory: consumers are rational; they consider all available options and their features, and choose the one that gives the greatest overall value (utility). Satisficing (Simon): consumers do not have the time or ability to compare every option, so they choose the first option that meets their minimum requirements – 'good enough' rather than the best.
parts.working: 2 marks per theory: 1 for the basic idea, 1 for elaboration or example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of satisficing in an everyday purchase.
parts.answer: When buying a pen at a stationery shop, a student picks the first one that writes well and costs under Rs 100 rather than comparing every brand.
parts.working: 1 mark: everyday example; 1 mark: shows a minimum standard accepted without full comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Farah visits an electronics market in Karachi to buy a mobile phone. The shop shows her more than 40 models, and she leaves without buying anything. Suggest how psychology could explain her behaviour and how the shop could make a sale more likely.
parts.answer: Choice overload: when there are too many options, comparing them is difficult and people worry about making the wrong choice, so they may delay or avoid deciding (Iyengar and Lepper found more people bought jam when 6 rather than 24 varieties were offered). The shop could ask Farah about her needs and budget and then show only three or four suitable phones, or group phones into clear categories (e.g. 'best for camera', 'best battery'), making comparison easier.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies choice overload; 1 mark: explains why (difficult comparison/anticipated regret); 1 mark: evidence; 1 mark: practical suggestion for the shop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the procedure of Iyengar and Lepper's jam study.
parts.answer: A tasting booth was set up in an upmarket grocery store. On some occasions it offered 24 varieties of jam (extensive choice) and on others 6 (limited choice). Researchers recorded how many passing shoppers stopped at the booth and how many later used the discount coupon they were given to buy a jar of jam.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: field setting in a grocery store; 24 vs 6 jams; conditions alternated over time; number stopping recorded; purchases measured by use of discount coupons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline the findings of the study.
parts.answer: More shoppers stopped at the booth with 24 jams, but a much higher proportion of those who saw only 6 jams went on to buy one.
parts.working: 1 mark: extensive choice attracted more shoppers; 1 mark: limited choice led to more purchases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one strength of this study.
parts.answer: It was a field experiment with real shoppers making real purchases, so it has high ecological validity and they were unaware of being studied, so demand characteristics were low.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify (ecological validity, realistic behaviour, no demand characteristics, objective measure via coupons); 1 mark: explain in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shoe shop in Lahore labels a pair of shoes 'Was Rs 9,000 – now Rs 5,499'. Explain how the anchoring heuristic could influence customers.
parts.answer: The original price (Rs 9,000) acts as an anchor; customers judge the new price relative to it, so Rs 5,499 seems like a bargain even if it is the normal market price.
parts.working: 1 mark: anchor = first number seen; 1 mark: later judgement made relative to it → perceived bargain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The shop also displays a sign: 'Only 3 pairs left in your size!' Explain why this might increase sales.
parts.answer: Scarcity heuristic: people assume items that are scarce are more valuable and fear missing out (a potential loss), so they decide quickly without comparing alternatives.
parts.working: 1 mark: scarcity heuristic/value; 1 mark: urgency/fear of loss → faster decision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue with using these techniques.
parts.answer: If the 'was' price was never really charged or the stock is not actually low, customers are being deceived and pushed into decisions they might regret, which exploits cognitive biases.
parts.working: 1 mark: deception/manipulation; 1 mark: consequence for consumers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe prospect theory as an explanation of consumer decision-making.
parts.answer: Kahneman and Tversky proposed that people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not in terms of final wealth. Losses are felt more strongly than equal gains (loss aversion), e.g. losing Rs 1,000 feels worse than gaining Rs 1,000 feels good. People are risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking to avoid losses. This explains framing effects: '20 % off' or 'save Rs 500' (a gain) and 'avoid paying Rs 500 extra' (a loss) can lead to different choices though the outcome is the same; and why 'free trial' offers work – once owned, giving up a product feels like a loss.
parts.working: Credit: reference point; gains vs losses; loss aversion; risk attitudes; framing with examples; application to consumers. Marks: 1 mark per accurate point, or 2 for a well-detailed point, up to 6; the answer should name the research and its findings in detail for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate prospect theory as an explanation of consumer decision-making, including a discussion of the usefulness of the theory.
parts.answer: Usefulness: explains and predicts real behaviour such as framing of discounts, free trials, money-back guarantees; marketers and policymakers use it (e.g. framing health messages). Strengths: supported by many experiments showing loss aversion and framing; more realistic than utility theory, which assumes rational choice. Weaknesses: much evidence comes from hypothetical choices in laboratory experiments with students, so low ecological validity; does not explain individual differences (experts, wealthy people may be less loss averse) – individual vs situational; cultural differences in risk attitude; describes rather than fully explains why losses loom larger; reductionist about emotion and social influences; ethics of using framing to manipulate consumers.
parts.working: Must include usefulness (named issue). Level 4 (9–10): a range of well-developed evaluative points, including the named issue, with effective use of examples from research; clear structure. Level 3 (6–8): several evaluative points, mostly developed; the named issue covered. Level 2 (3–5): limited evaluation, mostly undeveloped; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a study to investigate whether the number of options displayed affects the likelihood of customers buying a product in a Pakistani supermarket. Your plan must include a field experiment and quantitative data.
parts.answer: A possible plan: field experiment in a large Lahore supermarket; IV – a promotional stand displaying either 5 or 20 varieties of a new brand of biscuits (all equally priced); conditions alternate in four-hour blocks over two weeks, balanced across days and times; DV – (i) the percentage of passing shoppers who stop at the stand (counted by two covert observers) and (ii) the percentage of stoppers who buy, measured by a numbered discount voucher redeemed at the till; independent measures; controls – same location, same staff member with a standard script, same price and discount, no other promotions; ethics – public place, no personal data, store manager's permission.
parts.working: Mark points: IV with two operationalised levels; DV quantitative and operationalised; field setting; design and allocation; controls; data recording; sample; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): detailed, coherent plan covering all the required features with clear operationalisation. Level 3 (6–8): clear plan with most features. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, several features missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief/muddled. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the psychological knowledge on which your plan is based.
parts.answer: Choice overload: Iyengar and Lepper found more shoppers stopped at a 24-jam display but a higher proportion bought when only 6 jams were offered; too many options make comparison hard and increase fear of choosing wrongly, leading to decision avoidance. Satisficing (Simon) suggests consumers accept a 'good enough' option when options are limited; utility theory would predict more choice is always better, which the study tests. Bounded rationality – limited cognitive capacity for comparing many attributes.
parts.working: Credit relevant theory and evidence linked to the plan. Level 4 (7–8): accurate, detailed psychology (named theory/studies) clearly linked to the plan. Level 3 (5–6): mostly accurate and linked. Level 2 (3–4): basic or partly relevant. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons for choosing the features of your plan.
parts.answer: Field experiment: shoppers make real decisions with their own money, giving high ecological validity, and are unaware of being studied, reducing demand characteristics. Discount voucher: provides objective, quantitative evidence of purchase that can be linked to the condition, rather than relying on shoppers saying what they intend to buy.
parts.working: 3 marks for each of two choices: 1 identifies the choice, 1 explains why it is appropriate, 1 links to the plan or psychological evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the AIDA model of advertising.
parts.answer: AIDA describes the stages an advert should take a consumer through: Attention – the advert must first be noticed (e.g. bright colours, a celebrity); Interest – it must keep the consumer engaged with information about the product; Desire – it must make the consumer want the product by showing its benefits; Action – it must prompt the consumer to buy (e.g. 'order today').
parts.working: 1 mark for each stage correctly described; naming the four stages without description earns 1 mark at most.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one weakness of the AIDA model.
parts.answer: It assumes consumers move through the stages in a fixed order, but many purchases (e.g. cheap snacks) are made on impulse without passing through interest and desire.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (linear, ignores impulse buying, emotional responses, post-purchase stage); 1 mark: explanation/example.

practice.stem: A company in Pakistan has launched a television advert for a new washing powder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two ways the company could measure the effectiveness of its television advert.
parts.answer: 1) A recall test: a day after the advert is broadcast, telephone a random sample of viewers and ask which washing powder adverts they remember (unaided recall), giving a percentage who recall the brand. 2) Compare weekly sales of the washing powder in shops in the region for four weeks before and four weeks after the campaign starts.
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 for the method, 1 for an operationalised detail (who, when, how measured).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using sales figures to measure the effectiveness of an advert.
parts.answer: Sales may change for other reasons, such as a price cut, a competitor's product being unavailable or seasonal changes, so an increase cannot definitely be attributed to the advert.
parts.working: 1 mark: confounding factors; 1 mark: example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'high self-monitor' and a 'low self-monitor' in Snyder and DeBono's research.
parts.answer: High self-monitors pay close attention to social situations and change their behaviour to create the right image; low self-monitors act according to their own inner values and attitudes regardless of the situation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the two types of advertisement used in Snyder and DeBono's research.
parts.answer: Image-oriented adverts, which linked the product with a desirable image or lifestyle; and quality-oriented adverts, which made claims about the quality, taste or performance of the product itself.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline the main findings of this research.
parts.answer: High self-monitors responded more favourably to image-oriented adverts (and were willing to pay more for products advertised that way), whereas low self-monitors responded more favourably to quality-oriented adverts.
parts.working: 1 mark: high self-monitors – image; 1 mark: low self-monitors – quality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sara works for an agency planning an advertising campaign for a new running shoe aimed at young people in Karachi. Suggest how she could use psychology to make the campaign effective.
parts.answer: She could use product placement in popular local web dramas or music videos watched by young people, because repeated exposure in an entertaining context builds familiarity and positive attitudes. She could use a well-liked young athlete or influencer, as an attractive, credible source increases persuasion and links the shoe with a desirable image (appealing to high self-monitors), while also stating quality features such as grip and comfort (appealing to low self-monitors, as Snyder and DeBono found).
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant, justified suggestion, up to 4; must apply to Sara's campaign and use psychology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nomothetic versus idiographic debate.
parts.answer: The nomothetic approach looks for general laws that apply to all or most people, usually using large samples and quantitative data; the idiographic approach focuses on the unique individual and their detailed experiences, often using qualitative methods.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Snyder and DeBono's research on advertising combines nomothetic and idiographic ideas.
parts.answer: It is nomothetic because it seeks general rules about how types of people respond to types of advert, using a standard self-monitoring scale; but it recognises that individuals differ in personality, so it moves away from a single rule for everyone towards matching adverts to individual differences.
parts.working: 1 mark: nomothetic elements (general rules, scale scores, groups); 1 mark: recognition of individual differences (closer to idiographic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe research into product placement in films and television.
parts.answer: Product placement is when a brand appears in a film or programme as part of the content rather than as an advert. Auty and Lewis showed children a film clip in which a well-known cola brand appeared, while a control group saw a clip without it; children who had seen the brand were more likely to choose that cola when later offered a drink, suggesting placement influences choice even without explicit advertising. Explanations include mere exposure (familiarity increases liking) and priming – the brand is more accessible in memory at the point of choice. Placements that are central to the plot are remembered better than background ones.
parts.working: Credit definition, named research with procedure and findings, explanations (mere exposure, priming). Marks: 1 mark per accurate point, or 2 for a well-detailed point, up to 6; the answer should name the research and its findings in detail for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate research into product placement, including a discussion of the use of children in research.
parts.answer: Children: they are an important target audience, so research with them has high usefulness for regulating advertising aimed at children; but they cannot give fully informed consent (parental consent needed), may be more easily influenced, and may give answers to please adults (demand characteristics). Other points: experimental control shows cause and effect; low ecological validity – short clips and immediate choice differ from watching a whole film at home; effects may be short-lived; cultural differences in brands; ethics of influencing children without awareness; application to policy (e.g. limiting placement in children's programmes).
parts.working: Must include use of children (named issue). Level 4 (9–10): a range of well-developed evaluative points, including the named issue, with effective use of examples from research; clear structure. Level 3 (6–8): several evaluative points, mostly developed; the named issue covered. Level 2 (3–5): limited evaluation, mostly undeveloped; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Customers at a bank in Lahore complain about long waits. Suggest how the bank could use psychology to make waiting feel shorter.
parts.answer: Occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time, so the bank could provide a television, reading material or forms to fill in while customers wait. Uncertain waits feel longer, so a token system with a display showing how many people are ahead and the expected waiting time would help. Unfair waits feel longer, so a single queue with numbered tokens (first come, first served) prevents people pushing in.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant, justified suggestion, up to 4 (occupy time, reduce uncertainty, explain delays, ensure fairness, start the service process early).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Research on menu design found that diners spent more when prices were shown as plain numbers (for example '12') than when they included a currency sign or were written in words. Suggest one explanation for this finding.
parts.answer: The currency sign reminds diners that they are spending money, which may make them feel the 'pain of paying' and choose cheaper items; plain numbers make prices less noticeable.
parts.working: 1 mark: currency sign makes spending/cost salient; 1 mark: leads to more cautious choices (pain of paying).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a restaurant in Islamabad could design its menu to increase spending, using psychological principles.
parts.answer: Place high-profit dishes where diners look first or at the top of a section (primacy), or box/highlight them to attract attention; use descriptive names (e.g. 'slow-cooked Peshawari lamb karahi') to make dishes seem more appealing; include a very expensive 'decoy' dish so the next most expensive item seems reasonable (anchoring); list prices without currency signs and without lining them up in a column, so diners do not compare on price alone.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant suggestion with justification, up to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how personal space and crowding can affect customers' behaviour in a restaurant.
parts.answer: When tables are placed close together, diners' personal space is invaded; they may feel uncomfortable, unable to have a private conversation and less satisfied, and may leave sooner or not return. Perceived crowding (a psychological feeling, not just density) increases stress and reduces enjoyment, especially when people feel they lack control; however, some lively, low-cost restaurants may benefit from a busy atmosphere, which signals popularity.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: invasion of personal space; discomfort/privacy concerns; behavioural effects (shorter stay, lower satisfaction, avoidance); perceived crowding vs density / perceived control; context-dependent effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why it may be difficult to generalise research on personal space in restaurants to different cultures.
parts.answer: Norms about comfortable distances differ between cultures; for example, in some cultures people sit close together and see closeness as friendly, while in others greater distance is expected, so findings from one country may not apply in Pakistan or elsewhere.
parts.working: 1 mark: cultural differences in personal space norms; 1 mark: consequence for generalisation with example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by 'unrealistic optimism' in health psychology.
parts.answer: A belief that you are less likely than other people to experience negative health events (and more likely to experience positive ones), so you may ignore health warnings.
parts.working: 1 mark: less likely than others; 1 mark: effect on health behaviour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way unrealistic optimism could make a health promotion campaign about road safety less effective.
parts.answer: Young drivers may accept that speeding causes accidents but believe 'it won't happen to me' because they think they are better drivers than average, so they do not change their behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark: 'not me' thinking; 1 mark: applied to the campaign.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dr Farah runs a dental clinic in Multan and wants to persuade teenagers to stop chewing gutka. Using psychological research on fear appeals, suggest how she could design her health promotion message.
parts.answer: Use a low-to-moderate level of fear rather than very frightening images, because research on fear arousal (Janis and Feshbach) found the minimal-fear message produced the most change in dental behaviour while strong fear produced least (people may avoid or deny a very frightening message). Combine the warning with clear, specific, achievable advice (e.g. where to get help to quit, what to chew instead), so teenagers feel able to act.
parts.working: 1 mark: moderate/low fear; 1 mark: research evidence; 1 mark: give clear specific actions; 1 mark: explanation (defensive avoidance / self-efficacy) applied to Dr Farah's clinic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the study by Janis and Feshbach on fear arousal in health promotion.
parts.answer: Aim: to see whether the amount of fear in a health message affects behaviour change. High-school students were randomly given one of three versions of a 15-minute illustrated lecture on dental hygiene: strong fear (vivid images and warnings of pain, infection and decay), moderate fear, or minimal fear; a control group heard a lecture on a different topic. Dental hygiene practices were measured by questionnaire before and one week after. The minimal-fear group showed the greatest change towards the recommended practices and the strong-fear group the least. Conclusion: too much fear may make people avoid or dismiss the message.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: aim; sample (high-school students in the USA); three fear levels; control group; self-report questionnaire before and after; result (minimal most change, strong least); conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the determinism versus free will debate.
parts.answer: Determinism is the view that behaviour is caused by forces outside our control (e.g. reinforcement, biology); free will is the view that people choose their own behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark each side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why using a token economy to improve worksite safety (Fox et al.) is deterministic.
parts.answer: It assumes miners' safe behaviour is controlled by rewards: giving trading stamps for accident-free periods reinforced safety, so behaviour is seen as shaped by consequences rather than chosen freely.
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour caused by reinforcement; 1 mark: link to Fox et al. (stamps / mines / fewer days lost).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the 'Food Dudes' health promotion programme (Tapper et al.) for increasing children's fruit and vegetable consumption, including a discussion about generalisability.
parts.answer: Strengths: high ecological validity – carried out in real schools during normal lunchtimes; objective measures of food eaten (weighing what is left) give reliable quantitative data; clear practical application – combines modelling by admired peers (the Food Dudes videos) with rewards, using social learning and operant principles; effects were maintained at follow-up. Weaknesses / issues: generalisability – UK primary schools may not represent other cultures or older children, and food preferences and school meal systems differ (e.g. in Pakistan); rewards may produce extrinsic motivation that fades once rewards stop; ethical issues are minor but involve children; difficult to separate the effect of the videos from the rewards.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced evaluation with at least four developed points, generalisability discussed in depth, linked to Food Dudes throughout. Level 3 (6–8): mostly developed points, generalisability included. Level 2 (3–5): basic points, little elaboration. Level 1 (1–2): vague or descriptive. Max 6 without generalisability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field experiment to investigate whether a health promotion programme increases handwashing before lunch in primary schools in Lahore. Your plan must include a named sampling technique and a way of measuring handwashing.
parts.answer: Example: IV – schools receiving a 4-week programme (cartoon video of child 'hygiene heroes', posters and sticker rewards for washing) vs schools continuing as normal. DV – percentage of pupils who wash hands with soap before lunch, recorded by trained observers using a checklist (washes with soap for at least 20 seconds), plus soap used (grams) per week. Sample: stratified sample of 8 government and private schools, randomly assigned to conditions; pupils aged 7–9. Procedure: baseline observation for a week, programme, observation immediately after and 3 months later. Controls: same observation times, observers blind to condition. Ethics: permission from head teachers and parents, children's assent, anonymity. Data: compare mean percentages; bar chart.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): clear, detailed, replicable plan with IV/DV, named and justified sampling technique, operationalised measure, procedure, controls and ethics. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan. Level 1 (1–2): little relevant content.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the psychological knowledge on which your plan is based.
parts.answer: Health promotion strategies: modelling (social learning) as in the Food Dudes programme, where children copied admired peer models and received small rewards, increasing fruit and vegetable consumption; positive reinforcement and token economies (Fox et al.) increasing safe behaviour; fear appeals (Janis and Feshbach) showing that strong fear is not the most effective, so a positive, low-fear message is used; health promotion in schools reaching many children at an age when habits form.
parts.working: Level 4 (7–8): accurate, detailed description of relevant theory/studies clearly linked to the plan. Level 3 (5–6): accurate with some detail. Level 2 (3–4): limited. Level 1 (1–2): vague.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason for your choice of sampling technique.
parts.answer: Stratified sampling ensures both government and private schools are represented in proportion, because hygiene facilities (soap, water) and family background differ between them; this increases generalisability to Lahore's schools. It also reduces bias compared with an opportunity sample of schools that volunteer, which may already be more health-conscious. Weakness acknowledged: it needs a full list of schools and takes time.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): reason well explained, linked to the plan and to the psychology, with evaluation. Level 2 (3–4): reason explained with some link. Level 1 (1–2): reason stated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate health promotion in worksites and communities, including a discussion about individual and situational explanations.
parts.answer: Strengths: worksite token economies (Fox et al.) produced large, lasting reductions in days lost through accidents – real-world, objective data, high ecological validity; community campaigns reach many people and can change norms.
