Issues: situational – these programmes assume behaviour can be changed by altering the environment (rewards, information, social norms), which ignores individual differences such as unrealistic optimism, personality or motivation, so some people will not respond; individual approaches (e.g. tailored advice) may be needed alongside. Other weaknesses: extrinsic rewards may stop working when removed; difficult to control extraneous variables in field settings, so cause and effect is uncertain; cultural generalisability.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, at least four developed points, individual/situational debate discussed thoroughly with examples. Level 3 (6–8). Level 2 (3–5). Level 1 (1–2). Max 6 without the debate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the General Adaptation Syndrome (Selye).
parts.answer: Selye proposed that the body responds to any prolonged stressor in the same three stages. Alarm reaction: the stressor is detected, the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal glands release adrenaline, heart rate and blood pressure rise – 'fight or flight'. Resistance: if the stressor continues, the body adapts, with stress hormones such as cortisol staying high; the person seems to cope but resources are being used up. Exhaustion: after long-term stress, the body's resources are depleted, the immune system is weakened and stress-related illnesses (e.g. ulcers, high blood pressure) can develop. Based on experiments in which rats were exposed to different stressors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: same response to all stressors; alarm stage with detail; resistance stage with detail; exhaustion stage with detail; link to illness/immune suppression; based on animal research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal is a bank manager in Karachi. He has frequent headaches, sleeps badly and feels tense all day. Suggest how stress inoculation training could be used to help him.
parts.answer: Phase 1 (conceptualisation): a therapist helps Bilal identify his stressors (e.g. targets, difficult customers) and how he thinks about them. Phase 2 (skills acquisition and rehearsal): he learns coping skills such as relaxation, positive self-statements and time management and practises them in role-plays. Phase 3 (application and follow-through): he uses the skills in real situations at the bank, starting with milder stressors, with booster sessions.
parts.working: 1 mark per phase correctly applied (max 3); 1 mark for clear application to Bilal throughout.

practice.stem: Usman, a university student in Peshawar, completes the Social Readjustment Rating Scale. In the past year he experienced: death of a close family member (63), change in living conditions (25), begin or end school (26), change in residence (20), change in sleeping habits (16) and a vacation (13). Holmes and Rahe suggested that 150–299 LCU indicates moderate risk of stress-related illness, and 300 or more indicates high risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Usman's total life change units (LCU).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the guideline given, state Usman's level of risk.
parts.answer: Moderate risk (150–299).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using the Social Readjustment Rating Scale to measure Usman's stress.
parts.answer: Each event is given a fixed value, but the same event affects people differently (e.g. moving house may be exciting for Usman, not stressful), so the score may not validly measure his stress; it also ignores daily hassles.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explanation applied to Usman.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of measuring stress using physiological measures such as heart rate or cortisol in saliva.
parts.answer: Strength: objective and quantitative – the reading cannot be faked or affected by social desirability, so it is reliable and easy to compare. Weakness: physiological arousal can be caused by things other than stress (e.g. caffeine, exercise, excitement), and the equipment/setting may itself cause anxiety, so the measure may lack validity.
parts.working: 2 marks each: point + explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one self-report measure that could be used alongside it.
parts.answer: A daily hassles diary/scale on which participants tick which minor everyday stressors (e.g. traffic, losing things) they experienced and rate how severe each was.
parts.working: 1 mark named/clear measure; 1 mark detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nomothetic versus idiographic debate.
parts.answer: The nomothetic approach studies large groups to find general laws that apply to everyone; the idiographic approach studies individuals in depth to understand their unique experience.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the study of work stress in civil servants (Chandola et al.) is nomothetic.
parts.answer: It used a very large sample of London civil servants and statistical analysis to find a general relationship between work stress and coronary heart disease, rather than studying any one person's experience in depth.
parts.working: 1 mark large sample/general law; 1 mark link to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why daily hassles may be a better predictor of psychological health than major life events, referring to research by Kanner et al.
parts.answer: Kanner et al. found that scores on a hassles scale (minor everyday irritations such as misplacing things, traffic, concerns about weight) were a better predictor of psychological symptoms than life-events scores. Hassles happen often and accumulate, so they produce continuous low-level stress; major life events are rare and their effect may operate partly through the hassles they create (e.g. divorce leads to cooking, money worries). Uplifts may also buffer the effect of hassles.
parts.working: 1 mark Kanner finding; 1 mark frequency/accumulation; 1 mark life events act via hassles; 1 mark further point (uplifts / individual appraisal).

practice.stem: Ms Mehwish, a teacher in Hyderabad, has tension headaches caused by stress.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how biofeedback could be used to help Ms Mehwish manage her tension headaches.
parts.answer: Electrodes on her forehead measure muscle tension (EMG) and turn it into a tone or a display; she learns relaxation techniques and watches/hears the signal fall as she relaxes the muscles; the feedback rewards successful relaxation (operant conditioning); with practice she can relax without the machine and use the skill at work when she feels tension starting.
parts.working: 1 mark each: physiological measure; feedback signal; learning to control it by relaxation/reinforcement; transfer to everyday life.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of biofeedback compared with stress inoculation training.
parts.answer: Biofeedback deals only with the physical symptoms and does not address the thoughts or situations causing her stress, so the headaches may return; SIT also teaches cognitive coping skills.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between acute pain and chronic pain.
parts.answer: Acute pain is short-term (usually less than about 3 months) and linked to a specific injury that heals; chronic pain lasts longer than about 3 months and may continue after the tissue has healed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why chronic pain may need psychological as well as medical treatment.
parts.answer: Chronic pain is often linked to anxiety, depression and changed behaviour (e.g. avoiding activity), which can make the pain feel worse; psychological methods such as CBT address these thoughts and behaviours where painkillers alone do not.
parts.working: 1 mark psychological factors; 1 mark how treatment helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the gate control theory of pain (Melzack and Wall).
parts.answer: Pain is not simply a direct signal from injury to brain. A 'gate' in the spinal cord (dorsal horn, substantia gelatinosa) controls whether pain signals reach the brain. Small fibres (A-delta and C) carrying pain signals open the gate. Large fibres (A-beta) carrying touch/pressure, e.g. rubbing a bump, close it. Messages descending from the brain can also open or close the gate: anxiety and attention to pain open it; distraction, relaxation and positive emotion close it. This explains why the same injury causes different pain in different situations and why phantom limb pain and episodic analgesia occur.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: gate in spinal cord; small fibres open; large fibres close (example); descending control from brain; psychological factors that open/close; explains individual/situational differences or examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nurse Rabia works in a children's hospital in Peshawar. Five-year-old Ali has just had an operation and cannot describe his pain in words. Suggest two ways Nurse Rabia could measure Ali's pain.
parts.answer: 1) Paediatric self-report scale: show Ali the Wong-Baker FACES scale, six cartoon faces from 'no hurt' (0) to 'hurts worst' (10), and ask him to point to the face that shows how he feels. 2) Behavioural observation: use an observational pain scale designed for young children (e.g. the FLACC scale: face, legs, activity, cry, consolability), or a pain behaviour checklist like the UAB scale, to rate observed behaviours such as crying, guarding the wound, grimacing and reluctance to move.
parts.working: 2 marks each: method + application to Ali. Accept other paediatric self-report scales (e.g. a pain thermometer or colour scale) and any named or clearly described observational checklist.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two strengths of the McGill Pain Questionnaire as a measure of pain.
parts.answer: 1) It measures the quality of pain, not just its intensity, using many descriptive words in sensory, affective and evaluative categories, so it gives a detailed picture that helps diagnosis. 2) It is standardised and produces scores (pain rating index), so pain can be compared over time or between patients, giving reliable quantitative data.
parts.working: 2 marks each: strength + explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the McGill Pain Questionnaire.
parts.answer: It relies on a good vocabulary and understanding of the descriptor words, so it is unsuitable for children or people with a different first language, which could reduce validity.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem:
In a hypothetical study, five patients with chronic back pain at a clinic in Islamabad marked their pain on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (0 = no pain, 100 = worst pain imaginable) before and after a 6-week programme of non-pain imagery and attention diversion.
Before (mm): 72, 65, 80, 58, 70
After (mm): 45, 50, 52, 40, 48

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean pain rating before and after the programme, in mm.
parts.answer: Before: 69 mm; after: 47 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the mean pain rating. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the researcher cannot be sure the programme caused the reduction.
parts.answer: There was no control group: pain may have reduced naturally over 6 weeks or because patients expected to improve (placebo effect / demand characteristics).
parts.working: 1 mark no control group; 1 mark alternative explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate psychological techniques for managing pain (such as attention diversion, non-pain imagery and cognitive redefinition), including a discussion about individual differences.
parts.answer: Strengths: supported by gate control theory – attention and emotion close the gate; no side effects or addiction risk compared with painkillers; give patients a sense of control and can be used anywhere; useful for chronic pain alongside medical treatment. Weaknesses: individual differences – people vary in imagination, concentration and willingness to engage, and children or very anxious patients may find imagery hard, so effectiveness differs; less effective for severe acute pain; evidence often uses self-report measures, open to demand characteristics; hard to separate which component of a combined programme works.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, four developed points, individual differences discussed thoroughly with examples. Level 3 (6–8). Level 2 (3–5). Level 1 (1–2). Max 6 without individual differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one subjective and one objective way of measuring adherence.
parts.answer: Subjective: asking patients by questionnaire or interview how often they took their medicine. Objective: counting remaining pills / electronic pill-bottle caps / blood or urine tests.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why subjective measures of adherence may lack validity.
parts.answer: Patients may overstate adherence to please the doctor or avoid criticism (social desirability), or may simply forget missed doses.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation.

practice.stem: Mr Javed, who lives in Lahore, is prescribed 2 tablets a day for 28 days for high blood pressure. When he returns to the clinic after 28 days, 18 tablets are left in the bottle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of tablets Mr Javed should have taken.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of prescribed tablets that Mr Javed appears to have taken. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why a pill count may not be a valid measure of adherence.
parts.answer: Removed tablets may not have been swallowed – a patient could throw them away or share them – or may have been taken at the wrong times, so the count can overestimate adherence.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mrs Nasreen has been prescribed tablets for high blood pressure. They make her feel tired and dizzy, and she feels perfectly well without them, so she has stopped taking them. Using the idea of rational non-adherence and the health belief model, explain her behaviour.
parts.answer: Rational non-adherence: she has made a reasoned decision that the costs (side effects such as tiredness and dizziness) outweigh the benefits, because high blood pressure has no symptoms she can feel. Health belief model: her perceived susceptibility and severity are low (she feels well), perceived barriers (side effects) are high and perceived benefits are low, so the likelihood of taking action is low.
parts.working: 2 marks for rational non-adherence applied; 2 marks for HBM components applied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the study by Watt et al. on using a 'Funhaler' to improve adherence in children with asthma.
parts.answer: Aim: to see whether a novel spacer device that was fun to use would improve young children's adherence to asthma medication. Sample: children aged about 1.5–6 years with asthma in Australia, and their parents. The Funhaler had a spinning toy and a whistle activated by the child's breathing. Children used their normal spacer and then the Funhaler, each for a period of about two weeks. Parents answered questions (including by telephone) about whether the child had been medicated and about problems using the device. Results: adherence was higher and parents reported fewer difficulties with the Funhaler. Conclusion: making medication fun can improve adherence in young children.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 accurate points: aim; sample; description of Funhaler; repeated measures design/procedure; self-report from parents; result; conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dr Kamran runs a tuberculosis (TB) clinic in Faisalabad. Patients must take antibiotics every day for six months, but many stop early. Suggest two ways of improving adherence, based on psychological research, and explain why each should work.
parts.answer: 1) Behavioural reinforcement and reminders: send daily SMS reminders and give small rewards (e.g. travel vouchers) for attending clinic checks, because reminders and incentives have been shown to increase health behaviours such as attending immunisations (positive reinforcement). 2) Use the health belief model: explain clearly the seriousness of TB and that stopping early can cause drug-resistant TB (increase perceived severity and benefits), and reduce barriers by giving medicines for side effects or supervised dosing near home.
parts.working: 2 marks each: suggestion + psychological explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue with using rewards to improve adherence.
parts.answer: Rewards may put pressure on poorer patients so their choice is not entirely free; patients who cannot attend could feel unfairly excluded, so rewards must be fair and not coercive.
parts.working: 1 mark issue; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dr Imran tells patients what is wrong and what to do without asking for their views. Dr Saba asks patients about their concerns and decides treatment together with them. Identify the style each doctor uses.
parts.answer: Dr Imran: doctor-centred (directive) style; Dr Saba: patient-centred (sharing) style.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline the findings of Savage and Armstrong on patients' satisfaction with these styles.
parts.answer: In a study at a general practice in London, patients randomly given a directive (doctor-centred) consultation were more satisfied than patients given a sharing (patient-centred) consultation, particularly those who were ill and expected a clear diagnosis.
parts.working: 1 mark directive preferred / more satisfied; 1 mark detail (random allocation / questionnaire / patients wanted clear diagnosis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the study by McKinstry and Wang on doctors' dress.
parts.answer: Aim: to find out patients' attitudes to the way doctors dress. Patients attending general practices in Scotland were shown photographs of a male and a female doctor wearing different styles of clothing, e.g. a formal suit, a white coat, smart informal dress and casual clothes such as jeans. They completed a questionnaire rating how happy they would be to see each doctor and how much confidence they would have in them. Overall, patients preferred more formal dress (suit, white coat) and casual clothes were least preferred. Older patients were especially likely to prefer formal dress. Conclusion: dress is part of a doctor's non-verbal communication and affects patients' confidence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: aim; sample; photographs of male and female doctors; range of dress styles; rating questionnaire; results (formal preferred, older patients especially); conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the individual versus situational explanations debate.
parts.answer: Individual explanations say behaviour is caused by personal characteristics (e.g. beliefs, personality); situational explanations say it is caused by external circumstances (e.g. cost, other people, the environment).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using research on delay in seeking treatment (Safer et al.), explain one example of an individual explanation and one of a situational explanation.
parts.answer: Individual: a person's own appraisal of symptoms – e.g. believing that a lump is not serious (appraisal delay), or fear of what the doctor will find. Situational: practical barriers such as cost of treatment or difficulty getting time off work, which lengthen utilisation delay.
parts.working: 1 mark each, linked to stages of delay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by Munchausen syndrome as a misuse of health services.
parts.answer: A disorder in which a person repeatedly feigns, exaggerates or deliberately causes symptoms of illness in order to receive medical attention and treatment, often visiting many hospitals.
parts.working: 1 mark feigning/causing symptoms; 1 mark to gain medical attention (not money).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Munchausen syndrome is usually studied using case studies.
parts.answer: It is rare and patients hide their behaviour, so it is not possible to gather a large sample; a case study gives detailed (idiographic) information about one patient's history over time.
parts.working: 1 mark rare/hidden; 1 mark depth of information.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one problem for doctors in diagnosing Munchausen syndrome.
parts.answer: Doctors may make a type I error – diagnosing a healthy person as ill – because the feigned or self-induced symptoms appear real, leading to unnecessary tests, operations and treatments that can harm the patient.
parts.working: 1 mark problem; 1 mark consequence.

practice.stem: In a hypothetical screening clinic in Karachi, 200 people were checked for diabetes. Later tests showed that 40 of them really had diabetes. The clinic's doctor diagnosed 50 people as having diabetes, of whom 34 really had it. (A type I error = diagnosing a healthy person as ill; a type II error = diagnosing an ill person as healthy.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of type I errors made.
parts.working: 50 diagnosed ill − 34 truly ill = 16 healthy people diagnosed as ill.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of type II errors made.
parts.working: 40 ill − 34 detected = 6 ill people diagnosed as healthy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of healthy people who were wrongly diagnosed as ill.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why practitioners might make more type I errors than type II errors.
parts.answer: Doctors usually think it is safer to diagnose a healthy person as ill than to miss a real illness, because missing an illness could have serious consequences for the patient (and for the doctor). So when unsure they tend to diagnose illness and order further tests, which increases type I errors. The cost is unnecessary anxiety, tests and treatment for healthy patients.
parts.working: 1 mark: missing illness seen as worse; 1 mark: so err on the side of diagnosing; 1 mark: consequence for patients.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between rapid rotation and slow rotation shift systems.
parts.answer: In rapid rotation workers change shifts every few days (e.g. 2 mornings, 2 evenings, 2 nights); in slow rotation they stay on the same shift for longer, e.g. one to three weeks, before changing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct description of each system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a forward-rotating (morning → evening → night) shift system is thought to be better than a backward-rotating one.
parts.answer: The body clock naturally finds it easier to delay (stay up later) than to advance (go to sleep earlier), so moving shifts forward (phase delay) causes less disruption to circadian rhythms and sleep.
parts.working: 1 mark: link to circadian rhythms/body clock. 1 mark: phase delay is easier than phase advance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three types of human error that can lead to accidents at work.
parts.answer: Any three of: slips (doing the wrong action, e.g. pressing the wrong button); lapses (forgetting a step); mistakes (wrong plan or decision, e.g. misjudging a situation); violations (deliberately breaking a rule).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three; credit an example in place of a definition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: A psychologist wants to measure how noise in an open-plan call centre in Karachi affects workers' concentration. Suggest one objective way and one self-report way to measure concentration.
parts.answer: Objective: number of errors made when entering customer details per hour, taken from the call-centre computer system. Self-report: a rating scale at the end of each shift, e.g. 'How easy was it to concentrate today?' 1 = very difficult to 7 = very easy.
parts.working: 2 marks per measure: 1 for the method, 1 for operationalised detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Saima is the manager of a textile factory in Faisalabad where several minor accidents have happened on the night shift. Suggest how she could use a token economy to reduce accidents.
parts.answer: Workers (or teams) earn tokens/stamps for every week (or month) without an accident or safety violation, and for safety suggestions; tokens are lost if an accident happens. Tokens can be exchanged for goods or vouchers (e.g. groceries, phone credit). The scheme should be explained clearly to all workers, with tokens given promptly so safe behaviour is reinforced (operant conditioning).
parts.working: 1 mark: tokens earned for accident-free periods/safe behaviour. 1 mark: exchanged for rewards (named). 1 mark: practical detail (team tokens, lost after accident, prompt delivery). 1 mark: link to operant conditioning/positive reinforcement or to Fox et al.'s mining study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the debate about determinism versus free will.
parts.answer: Determinism is the view that behaviour is caused by factors outside the person's control (biological or environmental); free will is the view that people can choose how they behave.
parts.working: 1 mark for each side defined.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the Swiss cheese model of accidents can be seen as deterministic.
parts.answer: It explains accidents as the result of weaknesses ('holes') in organisational layers – management decisions, supervision, conditions – lining up, so an individual worker's error is caused by the system rather than freely chosen.
parts.working: 1 mark: model attributes accidents to system/organisational factors. 1 mark: so the worker's behaviour is determined by forces outside their control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the findings of research into the effects of open-plan offices on workers.
parts.answer: Oldham and Brass studied newspaper employees who moved from a conventional office to an open-plan office (a natural experiment), measuring them before and after the move. Employee satisfaction with work and internal motivation decreased after the move; workers reported fewer boundaries, more interruptions and less privacy, and found it harder to concentrate. Friendship opportunities did not increase as expected. Other research suggests open-plan offices increase noise and distraction but can make communication with supervisors easier, and that more private 'quiet zones' improve satisfaction.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): accurate, detailed description using psychological terms. Level 2 (3–4): mostly accurate, some detail. Level 1 (1–2): brief or partly inaccurate. Creditworthy: Oldham and Brass (natural/quasi-experiment, newspaper employees, measures before and after); decrease in satisfaction and motivation; reasons (lack of privacy, interruptions, no boundaries, distractions); other findings on noise/communication.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical data: A company introduced a token economy for safety. In the 12 months before, there were 48 lost-time accidents; in the 12 months after, there were 30. Calculate the percentage reduction in accidents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this reduction might not be caused by the token economy.
parts.answer: Other changes happened at the same time (e.g. new machinery, safety training, fewer hours worked or fewer workers), or workers may under-report accidents to keep their tokens, so the fall might not be due to the scheme itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: alternative explanation identified. 1 mark: explained (no control group / confounding variable / under-reporting).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a token economy to improve safety.
parts.answer: It gives immediate, concrete rewards for safe behaviour, which reinforces it, and the tokens can be exchanged for rewards each worker values, so it can motivate a large workforce cheaply compared with the cost of accidents.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength identified. 1 mark: explained in a workplace context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate what psychologists have found about the effects of temporal conditions of work (shift work), including a discussion about the usefulness of research.
parts.answer: Usefulness: findings (e.g. Czeisler et al. – moving workers to forward-rotating, slower schedules improved satisfaction, health and productivity at an industrial plant) are directly applied to design better rotas; research on nurses (e.g. Gold et al.) showing more sleep problems and errors in rotating shifts helps hospitals reduce risks. Methodology: many studies are field studies with real workers (high ecological validity) but have many uncontrolled variables (family life, second jobs); self-report sleep diaries may be inaccurate. Generalisability: samples are often one factory or one profession. Individual differences: 'larks' and 'owls' adapt differently, so one rota may not suit everyone. Determinism: biological explanation (circadian rhythms) vs individual choice. Ethics: experimental changes to rotas affect workers' health and livelihoods. Conclusion: research is useful but recommendations should be tailored.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named issue: usefulness (applications to rota design, health, safety; limits).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between hygiene factors and motivators in Herzberg's two-factor theory.
parts.answer: Hygiene factors (e.g. pay, company policy, supervision, working conditions) prevent dissatisfaction when they are adequate but do not create satisfaction; motivators (e.g. achievement, recognition, responsibility, the work itself, advancement) create job satisfaction and motivation.
parts.working: 1 mark for each with an example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the method Herzberg used to develop the two-factor theory.
parts.answer: He interviewed engineers and accountants (about 200) in Pittsburgh using the critical incident technique, asking them to describe times when they felt exceptionally good and exceptionally bad about their jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: interviews / critical incident technique. 1 mark: detail – engineers and accountants; times they felt very good or very bad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the five facets of job satisfaction measured by the Job Descriptive Index (JDI).
parts.answer: The work itself, pay, opportunities for promotion, supervision and co-workers.
parts.working: 3 marks for all five; 2 marks for four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of measuring job satisfaction using the JDI.
parts.answer: Workers may give socially desirable answers (e.g. not criticise their supervisor) if they fear the employer will see their responses, so the scores may not reflect their true satisfaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (social desirability, fixed Yes/No/? answers lack detail, may not cover all aspects). 1 mark: explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal works on a mobile-phone assembly line in Lahore, fitting the same screen into each phone all day. His manager wants to improve his job satisfaction. Suggest how the manager could use job enrichment and job rotation.
parts.answer: Job enrichment: give Bilal more responsibility and control, e.g. assembling and testing the whole phone, checking quality of his own work, deciding the order of tasks, so the job becomes more meaningful (vertical loading). Job rotation: move Bilal between different stations (screen fitting, battery fitting, packing) every few days so he has more variety and less boredom.
parts.working: 2 marks for enrichment (idea + applied to Bilal). 2 marks for rotation (idea + applied to Bilal).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what psychologists have found about measuring job satisfaction, including the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ) and the Quality of Work Life (QWL) approach.
parts.answer: MSQ: a self-report questionnaire measuring satisfaction with many specific aspects (facets) of a job, such as ability utilisation, pay, co-workers, independence and working conditions; long form has 100 items, short form 20 items, each rated on a 5-point scale from very dissatisfied to very satisfied. QWL (Walton): judges a job against broad categories such as adequate and fair compensation, safe and healthy working conditions, opportunity to use and develop capacities, opportunity for growth and security, social integration, constitutionalism (rights), work and total life space, and social relevance. Other measures include the JDI (five facets, Yes/No/?).
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): accurate, detailed description using psychological terms. Level 2 (3–4): mostly accurate, some detail. Level 1 (1–2): brief or partly inaccurate. Credit accurate details of MSQ (facets, long/short form, 5-point scale) and QWL categories.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to find out whether nurses in a large hospital in Islamabad are more satisfied with their jobs on day shifts or night shifts. Plan a study to investigate this using a questionnaire.
Your plan must include: the sampling technique; at least one rating-scale question; the type of data collected.
parts.answer: Example: Sample – stratified sample of 80 nurses: 40 who work mainly day shifts and 40 mainly night shifts, chosen randomly from staff rosters within each group, including different wards. Questionnaire – adapted from the JDI/MSQ facets: work itself, pay, supervision, co-workers, promotion; e.g. 'How satisfied are you with the support from your supervisor?' 1 = very dissatisfied to 5 = very satisfied (10 items, total 10–50); plus open questions such as 'What would improve your job satisfaction?'. Procedure – anonymous, distributed with sealed return boxes; same instructions for all. Data – quantitative (rating totals, compared using means and a bar chart) and qualitative (themes from open answers). Ethics – consent, confidentiality from hospital management, right to withdraw.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): detailed, coherent plan with all required features and justification. Level 3 (5–7): mostly clear plan, most features. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan with gaps. Level 1 (1–2): brief or confused.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the psychological knowledge on which your plan is based.
parts.answer: Herzberg's two-factor theory (hygiene factors such as working conditions vs motivators); job satisfaction measures (JDI five facets, MSQ, QWL); research on temporal conditions – shift work disrupts circadian rhythms and sleep and is linked to lower satisfaction and more errors (e.g. studies of nurses on rotating shifts); questionnaire design (rating scales, open/closed questions, social desirability).
parts.working: Level 3 (6–8): accurate, detailed and relevant knowledge clearly linked to the plan. Level 2 (3–5): some relevant knowledge, partly linked. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason for your choice of sampling technique.
parts.answer: Stratified sampling ensures equal numbers of day and night nurses (and nurses from different wards) are included, so that the comparison is fair and the sample represents each group of the hospital's staff; random selection within strata reduces researcher bias. Because night-shift nurses are fewer and harder to reach, an opportunity sample would probably over-represent day staff and distort the comparison. A weakness is that full staff lists are needed and it takes longer.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): well-justified reason linked to the aim, with comparison to an alternative or acknowledgement of a weakness. Level 2 (3–4): reason explained with some link to the plan. Level 1 (1–2): reason stated with little justification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate what psychologists have found about job design and job satisfaction, including a discussion about reductionism and holism.
parts.answer: Reductionism/holism: Herzberg reduces satisfaction to two sets of factors, which is easy to test and apply, but ignores how factors interact (e.g. pay can also be a form of recognition); job enrichment approaches (e.g. job characteristics model) look at several features together, which is more holistic. Methodology: Herzberg's critical incident interviews may be biased because people attribute good events to themselves and bad events to the company (self-serving bias); samples of engineers/accountants limit generalisability. Usefulness: job rotation, enlargement and enrichment are widely applied and practical. Individual differences: not everyone wants enriched jobs – some prefer routine. Cultural differences: research mainly Western. Conclusion.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named issue: reductionism vs holism, explained not just labelled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the three needs in Alderfer's ERG theory.
parts.answer: Existence – basic material and physical needs (food, pay, safe conditions); Relatedness – the need for relationships with others (colleagues, family, friends); Growth – the need for personal development and fulfilling one's potential.
parts.working: 1 mark for each need correctly named and described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way ERG theory differs from Maslow's hierarchy of needs.
parts.answer: ERG allows more than one need to be active at once and includes frustration–regression (if a higher need is blocked, a person focuses more on a lower need), whereas Maslow says needs are satisfied in a fixed order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'intrinsic' and 'extrinsic' motivation.
parts.answer: Intrinsic motivation comes from within – doing the work because it is interesting or satisfying in itself. Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards or pressures – e.g. pay, bonuses, praise or avoiding punishment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a non-monetary reward an employer could use.
parts.answer: Any one: praise/recognition (e.g. employee of the month), extra holiday, flexible hours, a better job title, training opportunities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hina manages a team of sales staff in a bank in Karachi. Using goal-setting theory, suggest how she could increase their motivation.
parts.answer: She should set specific goals (e.g. open 15 new accounts per month) rather than 'do your best'; goals should be difficult but achievable; she should involve staff in setting goals to increase commitment; and give regular feedback (e.g. weekly progress charts) so they can see how close they are to the goal.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four applied points: specific; challenging but achievable; commitment/participation in goal setting; feedback; deadline; rewards for reaching goals. Must be applied to Hina's team for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In Vroom's expectancy (VIE) theory, motivational force = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. An employee believes there is a 0.8 probability that extra effort will lead to high performance (expectancy), a 0.5 probability that high performance will lead to a bonus (instrumentality), and values the bonus at 0.9 (valence, scale 0–1). Calculate the motivational force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the motivational force would be zero if the employee believed the bonus would never be paid.
parts.answer: Instrumentality would be 0; because the terms are multiplied, a zero for any one of them makes the whole motivational force zero, however high expectancy and valence are.
parts.working: 1 mark: instrumentality = 0. 1 mark: multiplication means the product is zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nomothetic versus idiographic debate.
parts.answer: The nomothetic approach looks for general laws that apply to everyone, often using large samples and quantitative data; the idiographic approach focuses on understanding the unique individual in depth, often using qualitative methods such as case studies.
parts.working: 1 mark for each side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why McClelland's theory of needs (achievement, affiliation and power) could be seen as idiographic.
parts.answer: It recognises that individuals differ in the strength of each need – one employee may be driven mainly by achievement, another by affiliation – and needs are assessed for each person (e.g. through their stories on the Thematic Apperception Test), so motivation is understood at the individual level.
parts.working: 1 mark: emphasis on individual differences in need strength. 1 mark: elaboration, e.g. individual assessment with TAT, tailoring jobs to the person.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate need theories of motivation to work (such as Maslow, Alderfer and McClelland), including a discussion about cultural differences.
parts.answer: Cultural differences: Maslow's hierarchy reflects individualistic Western values (self-actualisation at the top); in collectivist cultures such as Pakistan, belonging/family or group needs may be ranked higher, so the order may not be universal. Evidence: little empirical support for a fixed order of needs; ERG is more flexible and better supported (frustration–regression). McClelland's needs are measurable (TAT) and useful for selection, but TAT scoring is subjective and has low reliability. Usefulness: managers can match rewards to needs (security, social events, development). Reductionism: need theories reduce complex motivation to a few needs and ignore cognitive factors such as goals and expectations (goal-setting, VIE). Individual differences: people vary in which needs dominate. Conclusion.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named issue: cultural differences, developed with examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the two dimensions of leadership behaviour identified in the Ohio State studies.
parts.answer: Initiating structure – how far the leader defines and organises tasks, roles and goals for the group; consideration – how far the leader shows concern, trust and respect for followers' feelings and wellbeing.
parts.working: 1 mark for each dimension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem with the 'great person' theory of leadership.
parts.answer: It assumes leaders are born with special traits, but research has not found a consistent set of traits shared by all effective leaders, and it ignores the situation and followers, so it cannot explain why a leader succeeds in one setting but fails in another.
parts.working: 1 mark: problem identified (no consistent traits, ignores situation, gender/cultural bias, retrospective). 1 mark: explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Muczyk and Reimann's four styles of leadership.
parts.answer: Directive autocrat – makes decisions alone and closely supervises how work is done. Permissive autocrat – makes decisions alone but lets subordinates decide how to carry them out. Directive democrat – involves subordinates in decisions but closely supervises how work is done. Permissive democrat – involves subordinates in decisions and gives them freedom in carrying out the work.
parts.working: 1 mark for each style correctly described (decision-making: autocratic/democratic; execution: directive/permissive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mr Farooq has just been promoted to supervise a team of experienced software engineers in Islamabad who are working on a creative new app. Using Fiedler's contingency theory, suggest how he could decide on the most effective leadership style.
parts.answer: He could complete the Least Preferred Co-worker (LPC) scale to see whether he is task-oriented (low LPC) or relationship-oriented (high LPC). He should then judge how favourable the situation is: leader–member relations (new to the team, so may be moderate), task structure (a creative project is low in structure) and position power (as supervisor, moderate–high). In moderately favourable situations Fiedler predicts relationship-oriented leaders do best, so if he is task-oriented he might change the situation (e.g. build relations) since Fiedler sees style as fixed.
parts.working: 1 mark: LPC scale to identify style. 1 mark: three situational factors named. 1 mark: applied to Mr Farooq's situation. 1 mark: correct prediction/advice (relationship-oriented best in moderate; task-oriented in very favourable/unfavourable; change the situation not the leader).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: A researcher uses a questionnaire to measure whether employees in a Lahore factory see their supervisor as a transformational leader. Write two items the questionnaire could include, each linked to a different feature of transformational leadership.
parts.answer: Inspirational motivation: 'My supervisor talks enthusiastically about what our team can achieve' (1 = never to 5 = always). Individualised consideration: 'My supervisor spends time helping me develop my own skills' (1 = never to 5 = always). (Others: idealised influence – 'I am proud to work with my supervisor'; intellectual stimulation – 'My supervisor encourages me to find new ways of solving problems'.)
parts.working: 2 marks per item: 1 for a suitable item with a response scale, 1 for correctly linking it to a feature of transformational leadership (idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what psychologists have found about leadership and the situation, including Fiedler's contingency theory.
parts.answer: Fiedler argued that a leader's effectiveness depends on the match between their style and the situation. Style is measured with the Least Preferred Co-worker (LPC) scale: low-LPC leaders are task-oriented, high-LPC leaders relationship-oriented. Situational favourableness depends on leader–member relations (good/poor), task structure (high/low) and position power (strong/weak). Task-oriented leaders are most effective when the situation is very favourable or very unfavourable; relationship-oriented leaders are best in moderately favourable situations. Style is seen as fixed, so the situation should be changed to fit the leader. Other situational approaches suggest leaders should adapt their style to followers' readiness/maturity.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): accurate, detailed description using psychological terms. Level 2 (3–4): mostly accurate, some detail. Level 1 (1–2): brief or partly inaccurate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate universalist and behavioural theories of leadership, including a discussion about individual and situational explanations.
parts.answer: Individual vs situational: great person and charismatic theories are individual explanations (leadership comes from traits), but they ignore the situation – the same leader may fail in a different context; behavioural theories (Ohio State) focus on what leaders do, which can be learned, and situational/contingency theories (Fiedler) show the interaction. Evidence: Ohio State used large questionnaire studies (LBDQ) – quantitative and reliable, but self-report/followers' ratings may be biased; transformational leadership is linked to follower satisfaction and performance. Usefulness: behavioural theories can be used to train leaders (consideration and structure); great person theory cannot. Cultural/gender bias: great person theory based on historical male leaders. Conclusion: a combination of individual and situational factors explains leadership best.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named debate: individual vs situational explanations, with examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the stages of group development described by Tuckman.
parts.answer: Forming – members meet, are polite and uncertain, and depend on the leader. Storming – conflict over roles, power and ideas. Norming – agreement on rules, roles and ways of working; cohesion grows. Performing – the group works effectively towards its goals. (Adjourning – the group breaks up once the task is finished.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each of four stages correctly named and described; adjourning can replace one stage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A management committee at a cricket equipment company in Sialkot quickly agreed to launch a new bat without any member raising concerns, and the product failed. Suggest how groupthink might explain this and how it could be avoided in future.
parts.answer: Groupthink: in a cohesive group, members want agreement so much that they do not criticise ideas – e.g. self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, pressure on anyone who disagreed, and an illusion of invulnerability. To avoid it, the leader could hold back their own opinion at first, appoint a 'devil's advocate' to challenge the plan, invite outside experts, or use anonymous voting.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition/explanation of groupthink. 1 mark: named symptom applied to the committee. 1 mark: one way to avoid it. 1 mark: explanation of how it helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the five conflict-handling styles described by Thomas.
parts.answer: Competing – assertive and uncooperative, pursuing one's own concerns at the other's expense. Collaborating – assertive and cooperative, working together to find a solution that satisfies both. Compromising – moderate on both, each side gives up something. Avoiding – unassertive and uncooperative, sidestepping the conflict. Accommodating – unassertive and cooperative, giving in to the other side.
parts.working: 1 mark for each style named and described (may refer to the dimensions of assertiveness and cooperativeness).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate what psychologists have found about group development and team roles (e.g. Tuckman, Belbin), including a discussion about the usefulness of research.
parts.answer: Usefulness: Tuckman's stages help managers anticipate conflict and support new teams; Belbin's team roles (e.g. plant, shaper, coordinator, monitor evaluator, teamworker, completer finisher) are used to build balanced teams and in training. Limitations: Tuckman's model was based on reviews of small, often therapy and laboratory groups, so may not apply to work teams; groups may not move through stages in order and may return to storming. Belbin's self-perception inventory is self-report and has been criticised for low reliability/validity; roles may change with the task. Reductionism: reducing team behaviour to set stages or nine roles ignores organisational context and culture. Cultural differences in how conflict is expressed. Conclusion: useful frameworks but should be applied flexibly.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named issue: usefulness, discussed with examples of application and its limits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one similarity between the samples used by Milgram (obedience) and Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans).
parts.answer: Both samples were drawn from the USA (Americans living in or near a city), so both studied American adults.
parts.working: 1 mark for the similarity (e.g. both American / both adults); 1 mark for linking it to both studies (Milgram: men from the New Haven area; Piliavin: passengers on the New York subway).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one difference between the samples used in these two studies.
parts.answer: Milgram's 40 participants were all male volunteers who answered an advertisement; Piliavin's participants were thousands of male and female passengers who did not volunteer and did not know they were in a study.
parts.working: 1 mark for the difference identified (gender mix / volunteer vs unaware / sample size); 1 mark for detail from both studies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one feature that the studies by Pozzulo et al. (line-ups) and Andrade (doodling) have in common.
parts.answer: Both measured memory performance (recognition/identification accuracy in Pozzulo et al.; recall of names and places in Andrade).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid shared feature: both cognitive; both measured memory; both laboratory-based; both quantitative data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between the participants in the two studies.
parts.answer: Pozzulo et al. tested both children and adults, so age was the independent variable and was not manipulated; Andrade tested only adults (aged 18–55), and the IV (doodling or not) was manipulated by the researcher.
parts.working: 1 mark for the difference identified; 1 mark for Pozzulo detail; 1 mark for Andrade detail / effect on the type of experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the procedure of the study by Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans).
parts.answer: Participants who joined an 8-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) course were given MRI brain scans before and after the course; a waiting-list control group was scanned at the same times without doing the course. Participants recorded their home meditation practice and completed a mindfulness questionnaire. Grey matter concentration in chosen brain areas (e.g. the hippocampus) was compared before and after.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to four points: 8-week MBSR course (weekly group sessions plus daily home practice); MRI scans before and after; waiting-list control group; home practice recorded / mindfulness questionnaire; comparison of grey matter concentration in regions of interest such as the left hippocampus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one similarity and one difference between the study by Hölzel et al. and the study by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams).
parts.answer: Similarity: both used objective physiological measuring equipment (MRI scans in Hölzel; EEG recordings of brain waves and eye movements in Dement and Kleitman), giving quantitative data less open to bias. Difference: Hölzel et al. compared an MBSR group with a separate control group (independent measures), whereas Dement and Kleitman had no separate control group – each of the nine participants was woken in different sleep stages (repeated measures).
parts.working: Similarity (4): identified 1; explained 1; example from Hölzel 1; example from Dement and Kleitman 1. Difference (4): identified 1; explained 1; example from each study 1 + 1. Other creditworthy points: both biological approach; both small samples; difference in setting (sleep laboratory overnight vs scans at a hospital/medical centre plus normal daily life).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sample used in the study by Baron-Cohen et al. (eyes test).
parts.answer: Several groups of adults were tested: a group of adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism, a large group of adults from the general population, a group of university students, and a small group of adults with Tourette syndrome. Most participants were from the UK.
parts.working: 1 mark for each group correctly described (AS/HFA adults; general population adults; UK university students; adults with Tourette syndrome as a comparison group); credit sample sizes if correct (15, 122, 103, 14).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one similarity and one difference between the study by Baron-Cohen et al. and the study by Andrade (doodling).
parts.answer: Similarity: both collected quantitative data from a test (number of correct answers on the 36-item Eyes Test; number of names and places recalled in Andrade), which makes comparison between groups straightforward. Difference: Andrade randomly allocated participants to a doodling or non-doodling condition (a laboratory experiment with a manipulated IV), whereas Baron-Cohen et al. compared pre-existing groups such as adults with and without Asperger syndrome (a quasi-experiment; the IV was not manipulated).
parts.working: Similarity (4) and difference (4): 1 identify, 1 explain, 1 + 1 examples from each study. Accept other valid points, e.g. both cognitive approach; both done in controlled conditions; Andrade used deception (surprise memory test) whereas the Eyes Test aim was clear.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one similarity between the study by Milgram (obedience) and the study by Perry et al. (personal space) in terms of the research method.
parts.answer: Both were controlled laboratory studies with a standardised procedure, so all participants experienced the same conditions (e.g. the same prods in Milgram; the same nasal spray procedure and distance task in Perry et al.).
parts.working: 1 mark for the similarity; 1 mark for an example from both studies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between these two studies in terms of the type of explanation they support.
parts.answer: Milgram's results support a situational explanation (obedience produced by the authority of the experimenter and the setting), whereas Perry et al. looked at a biological factor (oxytocin) and how its effect depended on an individual difference (the participant's level of empathy).
parts.working: 1 mark for each study's explanation, clearly contrasted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the studies by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams) and Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans) in terms of ecological validity.
parts.answer: Piliavin et al. has higher ecological validity: it was a field experiment on a real New York subway train and passengers behaved naturally because they did not know they were being studied. Dement and Kleitman has lower ecological validity: participants slept in an unfamiliar laboratory, attached to electrodes, and were woken by a doorbell during the night, which is unlike normal sleep at home.
parts.working: 1 mark for the comparison (Piliavin higher); 1 mark Piliavin explanation; 1 mark Dement and Kleitman explanation; 1 mark for linked detail (doorbell / electrodes / avoided caffeine and alcohol vs real commuters).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one similarity and one difference between the study by Bandura et al. (aggression) and the study by Saavedra and Silverman (button phobia).
parts.answer: Similarity: both studied children and both explain behaviour as learned rather than innate – Bandura showed aggression is imitated from a model; Saavedra and Silverman showed a phobia (and its disgust response) can be learned and changed through conditioning-based therapy. Difference: Bandura et al. used a large sample (72 children) in a controlled laboratory experiment with groups, whereas Saavedra and Silverman was a case study of one 9-year-old boy, so it gave detailed, idiographic data that cannot be generalised in the same way.
parts.working: Similarity: identified 1, explained 1, example from Bandura 1, example from Saavedra and Silverman 1. Difference: identified 1, explained 1, examples 1 + 1. Credit: method (experiment vs case study), type of learning (social learning vs classical/evaluative conditioning), data (observation counts vs self-rated distress such as a fear thermometer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the results of the study by Hassett et al. (monkey toy preferences).
parts.answer: Male rhesus monkeys showed a consistent and strong preference for wheeled (masculine) toys over plush (feminine) toys. Female monkeys showed more varied preferences, interacting with both types of toy, with some preferring plush toys. The pattern was similar to the toy preferences found in human children.
parts.working: 1 mark per point: males preferred wheeled toys; females' preferences more variable / interacted with both; some females preferred plush; similarity to human children; conclusion credited only if linked to results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one similarity and one difference between the study by Hassett et al. and the study by Fagen et al. (elephant learning).
parts.answer: Similarity: both studied non-human animals living in a social/managed setting (rhesus monkeys at a field station; juvenile elephants in Nepal), which raises the question of how far findings generalise to humans. Difference: Hassett et al. supports a nature explanation – the monkeys showed gender-typed toy preferences without human socialisation – whereas Fagen et al. shows nurture: the elephants' new behaviours were trained using positive reinforcement with food rewards and a bridging stimulus.
parts.working: Similarity 4 marks (identify, explain, two examples); difference 4 marks (identify, explain, two examples). Accept: observation of free choice (Hassett) vs training procedure (Fagen); both raise animal welfare issues handled carefully.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ms Sana teaches at a school in Lahore. Her pupils must listen to long, dull morning announcements and forget most of them. Suggest one piece of advice Ms Sana could take from the study by Andrade (doodling).
parts.answer: Allow pupils to doodle (e.g. shade shapes on a sheet) while listening, because in Andrade's study doodlers recalled more information from a boring message than non-doodlers.
parts.working: 1 mark for advice; 1 mark for the link to Andrade's finding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this advice might not work for Ms Sana's pupils.
parts.answer: Andrade's participants were adults (18–55) listening to a monotonous telephone message in a quiet room; school children may find doodling distracting or turn it into drawing, so the effect may not generalise.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason; 1 mark for explanation linked to Andrade's sample or task.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mr and Mrs Qureshi let their six-year-old son watch cartoons in which characters hit each other. Using the study by Bandura et al. (aggression), explain one piece of advice you could give the parents.
parts.answer: Limit the aggressive cartoons and choose programmes with non-aggressive role models, because Bandura et al. found that children who watched an adult model hitting a Bobo doll imitated specific aggressive acts, especially when the model was the same sex as the child.
parts.working: 1 mark advice; 1 mark Bandura result; 1 mark explanation of observational learning / imitation of same-sex model.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The manager of a shopping mall in Karachi is worried that shoppers do not help people who collapse. Using the study by Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans), suggest two ethical ways the manager could increase helping.
parts.answer: 1) Lower the 'costs' of helping: clear signs and a help button / trained staff so shoppers know helping is quick and safe. 2) Make the person in need seem deserving and not responsible for their state (e.g. publicity showing that people who collapse are often ill, not drunk), because in Piliavin's study the ill victim with a cane was helped far more often than the drunk victim. The campaign must not deceive or frighten shoppers.
parts.working: For each suggestion: 1 mark practical idea, 1 mark link to Piliavin (cost–reward model; ill victim helped more than drunk victim; helping was quicker for the cane victim). Max 2 if not ethical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The keepers at a wildlife park in Islamabad need their elephants to keep still while blood samples are taken. Using the study by Fagen et al. (elephant learning), suggest how the keepers could train the elephants.
parts.answer: Use positive reinforcement: reward each small step towards the target behaviour (e.g. presenting an ear or leg) with a preferred food. Pair the food with a bridging stimulus (a sound such as a whistle) so the elephant knows exactly which action earned the reward, and shape the full behaviour gradually over short daily sessions.
parts.working: 1 mark each: positive reinforcement with food; bridging stimulus / secondary reinforcer; shaping in small steps; link to Fagen (juvenile elephants in Nepal trained for a trunk-wash procedure using positive reinforcement instead of negative methods).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A software company in Bengaluru wants to reduce stress among its staff. Using the study by Hölzel et al., suggest how the company could do this.
parts.answer: Offer an 8-week mindfulness course (like MBSR) with weekly group sessions and short daily home practice, because Hölzel et al. found increases in grey matter concentration in areas such as the hippocampus, linked to learning, memory and emotion regulation, after such a course.
parts.working: 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark detail of programme; 1 mark link to findings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why taking part in the course must be voluntary.
parts.answer: Staff must give informed consent and have the right to withdraw; forcing them would break ethical guidelines and could itself cause stress.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A police officer in Faisalabad plans to ask a seven-year-old girl, who saw a theft, to pick the thief from a line-up. Using the study by Pozzulo et al. (line-ups), explain two pieces of advice you would give the officer.
parts.answer: 1) Tell the child clearly that the thief may not be in the line-up and that it is fine to say 'not there', because Pozzulo et al. found children were more likely than adults to choose someone when the culprit was absent (more false identifications). 2) Treat a child's identification with caution and look for other evidence, because children's identification accuracy in target-absent line-ups was poorer than adults'. The child should be supported and not pressured.
parts.working: Each advice: 1 mark for the advice, 1 mark for link to Pozzulo's finding that children made more errors than adults in target-absent line-ups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one way in which Hassett et al. (monkey toy preferences) protected the welfare of their animals.
parts.answer: The monkeys lived in their normal social groups in a large outdoor enclosure at a field station and were simply offered toys to play with, so they were not isolated, deprived or harmed.
parts.working: 1 mark point; 1 mark detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the study by Andrade (doodling) involved deception.
parts.answer: Participants were not told that their memory would be tested; the recall test was a surprise so that they would not deliberately rehearse the names, which would have made the results invalid.
parts.working: 1 mark: memory test was a surprise / true aim hidden; 1 mark: reason (avoid rehearsal / demand characteristics).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way this deception could be justified.
parts.answer: The deception was mild and unlikely to cause distress, and participants could be debriefed afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether Milgram (obedience) followed the ethical guideline of the right to withdraw.
parts.answer: It was not fully followed: participants were told they could keep the money whatever happened, but when they tried to stop, the experimenter used verbal prods (e.g. 'You have no other choice, you must go on'), making it hard to withdraw.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark evidence from the study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether Milgram followed the ethical guideline of debriefing.
parts.answer: It was followed: after the session participants met the unharmed learner and were told the shocks were not real; they were later sent a report and a follow-up questionnaire.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two students disagree. Ayesha says the study by Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans) was unethical. Hamza says it was ethical. Explain one point that supports Ayesha and one point that supports Hamza.
parts.answer: Ayesha: passengers did not give informed consent and were deceived – they believed a real person had collapsed, which may have caused distress, and they were not debriefed. Hamza: the situation was one that could happen in everyday life, the ride lasted only a few minutes, the 'victim' was helped by the model if no one else did, and consent would have destroyed the natural behaviour being studied.
parts.working: 2 marks for each side: 1 for the point, 1 for linking to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one way in which the study by Bandura et al. (aggression) may have broken the ethical guideline of protection from harm.
parts.answer: Children were exposed to an adult hitting a Bobo doll and were then deliberately frustrated (attractive toys taken away), which may have upset them or encouraged aggressive behaviour that lasted after the study.
parts.working: 1 mark point; 1 mark detail.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researchers could have reduced this risk.
parts.answer: Return the children to play with the attractive toys and a friendly adult afterwards, and explain to parents/teachers what happened so they could watch for and correct any copied aggression.
parts.working: 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the study by Milgram (obedience) in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about ethics.
parts.answer: Strengths could include: high internal validity through a standardised procedure (same prods, same 15 V steps, scripted learner responses); quantitative data (65% went to 450 V) allowing clear comparison; usefulness in explaining real obedience; debriefing and follow-up questionnaire showed most participants were glad to have taken part. Weaknesses could include: ethical problems – deception about the shocks, psychological distress (sweating, nervous laughter) and pressure from prods against the right to withdraw; a sample of 40 American men only, limiting generalisability; low ecological validity of giving shocks to a stranger.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): four developed points, each well linked to Milgram, ethics point detailed and two-sided; balanced. Level 3 (6–8): four points, mostly developed, or three well developed. Level 2 (3–5): points identified with limited development or link. Level 1 (1–2): vague or one point. Max 6 if no ethics point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by the individual versus situational explanations debate.
parts.answer: Whether behaviour is caused by factors within the person (personality, attitudes, biology, e.g. empathy) or by factors in the environment around them (e.g. setting, other people, rewards).
parts.working: 1 mark individual side; 1 mark situational side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a situational explanation and one example of an individual explanation from the study by Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans).
parts.answer: Situational: the type of victim – the ill victim with a cane was helped more often than the drunk victim. Individual: the passenger's own race / gender – helpers were more often male, and same-race helping tended to be higher for the drunk victim.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the study by Fagen et al. (elephant learning) can be used to support both sides of the individual versus situational debate.
parts.answer: Situational: the elephants learned the new behaviours because of the training environment – positive reinforcement with food and a bridging stimulus changed their behaviour. Individual: the elephants did not all learn at the same speed or reach the same level, showing that differences between individual animals (e.g. temperament, motivation) also affected learning.
parts.working: 2 marks each side: 1 point, 1 link to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether the results of Milgram's study (obedience) support a situational explanation more than an individual explanation.
parts.answer: Mostly situational: 65% of ordinary men gave the maximum 450 V when ordered by an experimenter in a lab-coat at Yale, and all went to at least 300 V, suggesting the authority and setting rather than personality produced obedience. But 35% defied the experimenter and participants varied in the point at which they stopped and in their tension, so individual differences also mattered; the conclusion is that the situation had a strong effect but did not fully determine behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark situational evidence; 1 mark explanation; 1 mark individual evidence; 1 mark reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one feature of the study by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams) that increased its reliability.
parts.answer: A standardised procedure: every participant was attached to the same EEG equipment, woken by the same doorbell and asked to speak into a recording device, so the study could be repeated in the same way.
parts.working: 1 mark feature; 1 mark explanation of why that improves reliability (consistency / replicability).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two psychologists disagree about the validity of the Revised Eyes Test used by Baron-Cohen et al. One says it validly measures theory of mind; the other says it does not. Explain one point for each view.
parts.answer: Valid: adults with Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism scored lower than the comparison groups, as theory predicts, and scores correlated negatively with the Autism Spectrum Quotient. Not valid: the test uses still, black-and-white photographs of the eye region only, whereas in real life people read emotions from whole moving faces, tone of voice and context, so it may lack ecological validity.
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 point, 1 link to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the study by Andrade (doodling) in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about generalisability.
parts.answer: Strengths: controlled procedure (same recorded monotonous message, same shading task, same recall test) gives high reliability and internal validity; quantitative recall scores allow objective comparison of doodlers and non-doodlers; useful application to classrooms and meetings. Weaknesses: generalisability – a small sample of 40 adults from one participant panel in the UK, recruited after another study, may not represent children or other cultures; the task (a boring phone message about a party) lacks ecological validity; the surprise memory test involved deception, which raises ethical issues.
parts.working: Levels as for 10-mark evaluation: L4 9–10 four detailed, linked points, generalisability discussed in depth; L3 6–8; L2 3–5; L1 1–2. Max 6 without a generalisability point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using children as participants in the study by Bandura et al. (aggression).
parts.answer: Strength: young children (aged about 3–5) have had less exposure to social norms, so researchers could see whether aggression is learned by observation without much prior learning getting in the way. Weakness: children cannot give fully informed consent and are more vulnerable to harm, e.g. being frustrated and possibly learning aggressive acts.
parts.working: 2 marks each: point + link to Bandura.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the study by Pozzulo et al. (line-ups) needed to use children as participants, and describe one ethical issue this raised.
parts.answer: The aim was to compare children's and adults' eyewitness identification, so child participants were essential – children do act as real witnesses and their accuracy must be understood. Ethical issue: consent – children cannot give fully informed consent, so parental consent is needed as well as the child's agreement, and the procedure (seeing a staged event and a line-up) must not frighten them; they must be able to stop at any time.
parts.working: 2 marks reason linked to aim; 2 marks ethical issue explained with link to study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the study by Hassett et al. (monkey toy preferences) supports the nature side of the nature versus nurture debate.
parts.answer: Male rhesus monkeys preferred wheeled toys, like human boys, even though the monkeys had not been taught gender roles by human society; this suggests a biological (possibly hormonal) basis for gender-typed preferences.
parts.working: 1 mark result; 1 mark link to nature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the study by Bandura et al. (aggression) supports the nurture side.
parts.answer: Children who watched an aggressive model copied specific aggressive acts they had not shown before, so aggression was learned from the environment through observation.
parts.working: 1 mark result; 1 mark link to nurture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one way in which the study by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams) relates to the nature versus nurture debate.
parts.answer: It supports nature: all participants showed the same regular cycles of REM and NREM sleep through the night, and dream recall was linked to REM sleep, suggesting that sleep stages and dreaming are biologically determined. However, dream content (what the person dreams about) is likely to be influenced by experience, which is nurture.
parts.working: 1 mark position; 1 mark evidence; 1 mark further explanation or counterpoint.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A student plans an experiment to see whether people remember more words in a quiet room than in a noisy room. She tests 10 friends in the quiet room in the morning and 10 different friends in the noisy room in the evening. Identify one weakness of this plan.
parts.answer: Time of day is a confounding variable (morning vs evening), or the sample of friends is small/biased.
parts.working: B1 for any valid weakness.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the weakness you identified could be overcome.
parts.answer: Test both conditions at the same time of day (e.g. all in the morning), allocating participants to rooms randomly, so time of day cannot explain any difference in recall.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable change. 1 mark: explanation of why it improves the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A researcher plans to measure aggression in teenagers using a single question: 'Are you an aggressive person? Yes/No'. Explain one weakness of this measure.
