parts.answer: It is likely to produce socially desirable answers (few will admit aggression) and gives only a yes/no answer, so it cannot show different levels of aggression – low validity and sensitivity.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness identified (social desirability, limited detail, closed yes/no). 1 mark: explained in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improved measure of aggression.
parts.answer: A questionnaire of several items rated on a 1–5 scale (e.g. 'I lose my temper easily'), or an observation of aggressive acts (hitting, shouting) during a sports game, with clear behavioural categories.
parts.working: 1 mark: improved measure. 1 mark: detail showing it measures levels/behaviour objectively.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: Dr Ahmed plans an observation of students in a university library to see how often they check their phones. He will sit at a table with a clipboard and tell students he is observing them. Explain one strength and one weakness of this plan.
parts.answer: Strength: it is overt, so students know they are being studied, which is more ethical – consent can be obtained and privacy respected. Weakness: because students know they are being watched, they may check their phones less often than normal (participant reactivity), so the data would be less valid.
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (identified + explained in context). 2 marks for weakness (identified + explained in context).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A researcher wants to investigate whether a mindfulness app reduces stress in workers at a call centre in Lahore. She uses volunteers who respond to an email, asks them to use the app for 4 weeks, and then asks, 'Do you feel less stressed now?' Explain two weaknesses of this plan.
parts.answer: No control group or baseline: without a comparison group (e.g. workers who do not use the app) or a stress measure before the 4 weeks, any change could be due to other factors (e.g. a quieter month at work). Volunteer sample and leading question: volunteers may be keen on mindfulness and the question suggests the answer, so demand characteristics may produce biased results.
parts.working: 2 marks per weakness: identified (1) + explained in context (1). Accept: no baseline, no control group, volunteer bias, leading/closed question, self-report bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A psychologist plans a repeated measures experiment in which participants solve anagrams first after drinking water and then, 15 minutes later, after drinking a caffeinated drink. Explain one problem with this plan and how it could be overcome.
parts.answer: Order effects: all participants do the caffeine condition second, so they may do better because of practice with anagrams (or worse because of fatigue), not because of caffeine. It could be overcome by counterbalancing – half do water first, half caffeine first – on separate days, so caffeine from the first session cannot affect the second, with different but equally difficult anagram sets.
parts.working: 1 mark: order effects identified. 1 mark: explained in context (practice/fatigue/carry-over of caffeine). 1 mark: counterbalancing / separate days. 1 mark: explanation of how this solves the problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A researcher plans a correlational study of the relationship between time spent reading for pleasure and vocabulary in 11-year-olds. She uses a 30-item vocabulary test and asks parents to estimate their child's weekly reading time. Explain one strength and one weakness of using parents' estimates as a measure of reading time.
parts.answer: Strength: parents see their child's daily routine at home and can report on reading that the child might forget, and it is quick and cheap to collect from many families. Weakness: estimates may be inaccurate – parents may not know about reading done in the child's room, or may exaggerate to appear good parents (social desirability), reducing validity. A reading diary could be more accurate.
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (identified + explained). 2 marks for weakness (identified + explained).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A researcher plans to study whether people help a stranger more in a small town than in a big city. She will have a confederate drop a bag of oranges in the main market of a small town in Punjab and in a busy market in Karachi, and record whether passers-by help. Evaluate this plan in terms of its validity.
parts.answer: Strength: it is a field setting with real passers-by who do not know they are being studied, so behaviour is natural and has high ecological validity. Weakness: other differences between the two markets (crowd size, time of day, the local language, how busy people are) are uncontrolled and could explain any difference in helping, so it is not certain that town/city size caused the difference; the confederate's behaviour should be standardised and the times of day matched.
parts.working: 2 marks for a point supporting validity (identified + explained). 2 marks for a point against validity (identified + explained), e.g. extraneous variables, sample bias, confederate inconsistency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A psychologist plans to interview 6 employees about their experience of working night shifts, using an unstructured interview. Explain one strength and one weakness of using an unstructured interview, and suggest one improvement to the plan.
parts.answer: Strength: the interviewer can follow up whatever the employee says with new questions, gathering rich qualitative detail about their experience of night shifts that was not anticipated. Weakness: each interview is different, so answers are hard to compare and the data are harder to analyse and replicate (low reliability); the interviewer's own views may also influence the questions. Improvement: use a semi-structured interview with a fixed set of core questions plus follow-ups, and increase the sample to 20 employees from different shifts and companies.
parts.working: 2 marks strength, 2 marks weakness (each identified + explained in context). 2 marks improvement (suggestion + why it helps).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher tests whether chewing gum improves concentration during a 20-minute proofreading task. Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: Participants who chew gum during a 20-minute proofreading task will detect more spelling errors than participants who do not chew gum.
parts.working: 1 mark: both conditions of the IV stated (gum vs no gum). 1 mark: operationalised DV with a direction (more errors detected).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one control the researcher should use in this study.
parts.answer: All participants proofread the same passage containing the same number of errors (e.g. 30), in the same quiet room.
parts.working: B1 for any relevant control (same passage, same time limit, same flavour of gum, same room/time of day).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: an experiment tests whether students in Karachi solve more puzzles when working with background traffic noise or in silence. Explain one reason for using an independent measures design in this study.
parts.answer: Each student only does the puzzles once, so they cannot improve with practice or become bored between conditions (no order effects), and they are less likely to guess the aim of the study.
parts.working: 1 mark: avoids order effects (practice/fatigue) or demand characteristics. 1 mark: linked to the puzzles/noise scenario.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using an independent measures design in this study.
parts.answer: Differences in puzzle-solving ability between the two groups (participant variables) could cause the difference in scores rather than the noise.
parts.working: 1 mark: participant variables. 1 mark: in context (puzzle ability, intelligence, motivation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher wants to test whether a 'growth mindset' video increases how long 12-year-olds persist at a difficult maths task. Explain how she could use a matched pairs design in this study.
parts.answer: Give all children a pre-test of maths ability (and/or a measure of initial persistence). Rank them by score and pair children with the closest scores; then randomly allocate one child of each pair to watch the growth-mindset video and the other to watch a neutral video, before both attempt the maths task.
parts.working: 1 mark: pre-test on a relevant variable. 1 mark: pairing children with similar scores. 1 mark: one of each pair randomly allocated to each condition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how persistence could be operationalised.
parts.answer: The number of seconds a child keeps working on an impossible maths problem before choosing to stop (up to a maximum of 10 minutes).
parts.working: 1 mark: measurable unit (time in seconds/number of attempts). 1 mark: clear definition of start/stop or a maximum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher wants to compare the memory of people who sleep 8 hours with those who sleep 4 hours. Explain why this would be difficult to carry out as a laboratory experiment, and suggest one alternative way to study the question.
parts.answer: Restricting sleep to 4 hours in a lab may harm participants (tiredness, accidents travelling home) and is costly, as they must stay overnight under supervision; also sleeping in a lab is unnatural. Alternative: a natural/quasi-experiment comparing people who already sleep about 4 or 8 hours (measured with a sleep diary or wrist actigraph) on the same memory test.
parts.working: 1 mark: ethical problem (harm). 1 mark: practical problem (overnight, cost) or validity problem. 1 mark: alternative method named. 1 mark: alternative explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to test whether listening to Qur'an recitation or calm instrumental music before an exam reduces anxiety more than sitting in silence. Describe how she could conduct a laboratory experiment to investigate this.
Your plan must include details about:
• the experimental design
• how anxiety would be measured
• controls.
parts.answer: Example plan: IV = 10 minutes of recitation, 10 minutes of instrumental music, or 10 minutes of silence before a timed 15-minute mental arithmetic test (an exam-like task). Independent measures design with random allocation (e.g. names drawn from a box), 30 university students per group, to avoid order effects and practice effects on the test. DV = anxiety, measured by a 10-item self-report rating scale (1 = not at all anxious, 5 = extremely anxious; total 10–50) completed just before the test, plus heart rate measured with a finger pulse monitor. Controls: same room, lighting and temperature; same headphones and volume (e.g. 60 dB); standardised instructions read from a script; same test paper; all tested at the same time of day; participants who are already on anxiety medication excluded. Procedure: consent, baseline heart rate, listening phase, rating scale + heart rate, test, debrief.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: design named and justified (independent measures with random allocation, or repeated measures with counterbalancing); IV conditions operationalised (duration, what is played); DV operationalised (rating scale with anchors and/or heart rate); controls (setting, volume, instructions, time of day); sample and procedure; ethics (consent, right to withdraw, debrief).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A researcher wants to find out whether the colour of the paper on which a test is printed (white or yellow) affects how many words students recall. Describe how she could conduct an experiment to investigate this using a repeated measures design.
Your plan must include details about:
• the materials
• how order effects will be controlled
• the sample.
parts.answer: Example plan: Materials – two lists of 20 concrete, two-syllable nouns of similar frequency (list A and list B), each printed in black 14-point font on either white or yellow A4 paper; a stopwatch; blank answer sheets. Procedure – each participant studies a list for 2 minutes, does a 1-minute distractor task (counting backwards in 3s), then writes down as many words as they remember in 2 minutes. They do this twice, once with each paper colour. Order effects – counterbalancing: half do white then yellow, half yellow then white; different but matched word lists in each condition, with list–colour pairing also counterbalanced; a 10-minute break between conditions to reduce fatigue. Sample – 40 Grade 12 students from two colleges in Lahore, chosen by random sampling from class lists (each name given a number, numbers drawn by computer), with parental consent for under-18s. DV – number of words correctly recalled out of 20.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: materials described (word lists matched for length/frequency, paper colour, font); counterbalancing explained (half each order) and matched lists; sample with technique and size; DV operationalised; standardised procedure; ethics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher finds a correlation between the number of fruit portions students eat each day and their exam scores. Explain why she cannot conclude that eating fruit causes higher exam scores.
parts.answer: A correlation only shows that two variables are related; neither variable was manipulated, so a third variable (e.g. family income or a healthier lifestyle) could cause both.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation does not show cause/no IV manipulated. 1 mark: possible third variable or reverse direction in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a non-directional hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be a correlation between the number of fruit portions eaten per day and percentage exam score.
parts.working: 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised. 1 mark: non-directional (correlation/relationship, no direction stated).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher measures 'confidence' using a 1–10 rating and 'public speaking performance' using judges' ratings. Suggest how the judges' ratings could be made reliable.
parts.answer: Use two or more judges who are trained with the same clear criteria (e.g. eye contact, fluency, clarity each rated 1–5) and practise on sample videos; each judge rates every speaker independently; then the judges' ratings are correlated to check inter-rater reliability (e.g. agreement of +0.8 or above).
parts.working: 1 mark: clear operationalised criteria/rating scale. 1 mark: training/practice. 1 mark: independent ratings compared to check inter-rater reliability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a correlational design for this study.
parts.answer: Confidence cannot ethically or easily be manipulated, so a correlation lets the researcher study the relationship between naturally occurring levels of confidence and performance.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength (variables cannot be manipulated / shows strength and direction / quick to collect). 1 mark: in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher collected data from 8 participants on hours of revision (x) and test score out of 50 (y): (2, 20), (4, 26), (5, 25), (6, 31), (7, 35), (9, 38), (10, 41), (12, 44). Describe how she should present these data in a graph.
parts.answer: A scatter graph with hours of revision on the x-axis (labelled, 0–12) and test score on the y-axis (labelled, 0–50); each participant plotted as a single point; a title such as 'Scatter graph showing the relationship between hours of revision and test score'.
parts.working: 1 mark: scatter graph. 1 mark: correctly labelled axes with units/scales. 1 mark: points not joined / suitable title.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the correlation shown by these data and give a reason.
parts.answer: Positive: as hours of revision increase, test scores increase (e.g. 2 hours → 20, 12 hours → 44).
parts.working: 1 mark: positive. 1 mark: reason with reference to the data.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to investigate whether there is a correlation between the number of hours that teenagers spend gaming each week and their sleep quality. Describe how she could conduct this correlational study.
Your plan must include details about:
• how both co-variables will be measured
• the sampling technique
• how the data will be analysed.
parts.answer: Example plan: Co-variable 1 – hours gaming per week, measured by a 7-day diary in which teenagers record minutes spent gaming each day (total converted to hours). Co-variable 2 – sleep quality, measured by a 10-item questionnaire with 1–5 rating scales (1 = very poor, 5 = very good), total 10–50, completed at the end of the week. Sample – 100 students aged 14–16 from four schools in Islamabad, using stratified sampling so that boys and girls and each school are represented in proportion; parental consent. Procedure – standardised instructions, diaries returned in sealed envelopes with code numbers. Analysis – plot a scatter graph (hours gaming on the x-axis, sleep quality score on the y-axis) to see direction and strength; calculate a correlation coefficient; a negative correlation is predicted. Note that no causal conclusion can be drawn.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: both co-variables operationalised; named sampling technique explained with size and population; data analysis (scatter graph with labelled axes, correlation coefficient, direction expected); ethics; recognises correlation ≠ causation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A researcher wants to investigate whether there is a relationship between how often older people in a care home in Lahore receive visitors and their level of happiness. Describe how this correlational study could be carried out using observation and self-report data.
Your plan must include details about:
• how visits would be recorded
• the self-report measure
• ethical issues.
parts.answer: Example plan: Visits – care staff keep a visitor log for 4 weeks, recording each resident's visitors (date, time, length); co-variable = total number of visits per resident. Happiness – a structured interview with a short rating scale read aloud: 5 questions such as 'How happy have you felt this week?' rated 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely), total 5–35, asked at the end of the 4 weeks by the same trained interviewer. Sample – all 40 residents who are able to consent (opportunity sample). Ethics – informed consent from residents (and family if capacity is doubtful), right to withdraw explained simply and repeated, confidentiality by code numbers, privacy (log records only counts, not conversation content), protection from distress for lonely residents, debrief. Analysis – scatter graph and correlation coefficient; positive correlation predicted.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: visits operationalised (log, count); self-report measure with example question and scale; ethics specific to elderly/vulnerable participants; sample; analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: an observer watches customers in a shopping mall in Lahore. Explain the difference between a participant and a non-participant observation in this setting.
parts.answer: In a participant observation the observer joins in the activity being studied, e.g. acts as a shopper or works as a shop assistant; in a non-participant observation the observer watches from outside the activity, e.g. sitting at a café table without interacting with the shoppers.
parts.working: 1 mark for each type explained with reference to the mall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of a non-participant observation in this study.
parts.answer: The observer can record behaviour more objectively/continuously because they are not distracted by taking part and are less likely to influence shoppers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: two observers rate aggression in a video of children playing. Their tallies for six 1-minute intervals were: Observer 1 – 4, 2, 5, 3, 6, 1; Observer 2 – 4, 3, 5, 3, 5, 1. Calculate the percentage of intervals in which the two observers gave exactly the same tally. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: M1: matches in intervals 1, 3, 4 and 6 = 4 of 6. A1: 4 ÷ 6 × 100 = 66.7 → 67%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the observers could improve their agreement.
parts.answer: Agree and write clear operational definitions of 'aggression' (e.g. hitting, pushing, kicking, grabbing a toy), then practise together on a pilot video and discuss differences before the real observation.
parts.working: 1 mark: clearer operationalised categories / training. 1 mark: explanation of how it reduces subjective judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between time sampling and event sampling, using an example of an observation of shoppers queuing at a supermarket checkout.
parts.answer: Time sampling: the observer records behaviour only at set time intervals, e.g. every 2 minutes records how many people are in the queue and whether anyone is using their phone. Event sampling: the observer records every time a particular behaviour occurs, e.g. every time someone leaves the queue or pushes in, whenever it happens during the session.
parts.working: 2 marks for each: 1 for explanation, 1 for a relevant example in the queue setting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to study helping behaviour among children aged 5–7 during break time in a school playground in Hyderabad. Describe how she could conduct a naturalistic observation to investigate this.
Your plan must include details about:
• behavioural categories
• the sampling of behaviour (e.g. time or event sampling)
• whether the observation is overt or covert.
parts.answer: Example plan: Behavioural categories – helping a child who has fallen (helps them up, touches them), sharing (offers food/toy), comforting (puts an arm round a crying child), giving physical assistance (carries something with another child); each recorded on a tally chart. Sampling – time sampling: two observers each watch one target child for 30 seconds and record any category shown, then move to the next child, across 20-minute break times for 10 days; or event sampling – record every helping act seen in a defined zone. Observers – two trained observers, positioned at the edge of the playground (e.g. near the staff room window) so as not to interfere, recording independently to check inter-rater reliability. Overt/covert – overt with teachers' and parents' consent, but observers present for a week beforehand so children become used to them (habituation), reducing reactivity. Ethics – parental consent, confidentiality (no names), intervene if a child is at risk.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: at least three operationalised behavioural categories; time or event sampling explained with timings; overt/covert decision justified; observer position and inter-rater reliability; ethics for children.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A researcher wants to investigate how drivers in Karachi behave at a busy junction when the traffic light turns amber. Describe how this could be investigated using a structured covert observation.
Your plan must include details about:
• the location and timing
• how data would be recorded
• how reliability would be checked.
parts.answer: Example plan: Location – one busy four-way junction with traffic lights; observers seated in a parked car or a café overlooking the junction so drivers cannot tell they are being watched. Timing – 30-minute sessions at morning rush (8–8:30 a.m.), midday and evening rush, over five weekdays, so that different traffic conditions are sampled. Recording – event sampling: each time the light turns amber, record the behaviour of the first car in the lane facing it, using categories: stops before line; speeds up and crosses; crosses at normal speed; stops after the line; and record vehicle type (car, motorbike, rickshaw, bus). Tally chart/coded checklist. Reliability – two observers watch the same light changes independently, then compare their tallies; calculate percentage agreement or correlate their records; categories refined and observers trained in a pilot observation if agreement is low. Ethics – public place, no number plates recorded, so privacy is respected.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: covert position explained; timings and location; behavioural categories and sampling method; data recording sheet; inter-rater reliability method; ethics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a questionnaire about phone use is given to 200 office workers. Write one closed question and one open question that could be included.
parts.answer: Closed: 'On average, how many hours per day do you use your phone for non-work purposes? (less than 1 / 1–2 / 2–3 / more than 3)'. Open: 'Describe how using your phone affects your concentration at work.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a closed question with fixed responses. 1 mark for a genuinely open question allowing free answers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why participants may not answer questionnaires about phone use honestly.
parts.answer: Social desirability bias – they may under-report non-work phone use to appear hard-working to their employer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher designs a rating scale to measure job stress among nurses in Quetta. Write one rating-scale item, including the anchors, and explain how it would be scored.
parts.answer: Item: 'I feel exhausted at the end of my shift.' 1 = strongly disagree, 2 = disagree, 3 = neutral, 4 = agree, 5 = strongly agree. Scoring: the number chosen is the score for the item (higher = more stress); scores across all items are added to give a total stress score.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable item statement. 1 mark: labelled anchors at both ends (and/or each point). 1 mark: scoring explained (higher = more stress, items totalled; reverse-scored items if any).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some items on the scale should be reverse-scored.
parts.answer: If all items are worded in the same direction, participants may tick the same answer down the page without reading (response set/acquiescence); mixing positively and negatively worded items, which are reverse-scored, reduces this bias.
parts.working: 1 mark: avoids response bias/acquiescence. 1 mark: explanation of how reverse-scoring works or why it matters.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to investigate the reasons why university students in Pakistan choose to study abroad. Describe how she could conduct an interview study to investigate this.
Your plan must include details about:
• the type of interview
• example questions
• how the data would be analysed.
parts.answer: Example plan: Type – semi-structured interview, so that every student is asked the same core questions but the interviewer can follow up interesting answers. Sample – 20 final-year students from three universities in Lahore and Islamabad who have applied to study abroad, recruited by volunteer sampling through a notice on student portals. Questions – closed: 'Have you applied to study in another country? Yes/No'; 'How important is the reputation of the university to you? 1 (not important) to 5 (very important)'; open: 'What are the main reasons you want to study abroad?'; 'How did your family influence your decision?'; follow-up probes: 'Can you tell me more about that?'. Procedure – 30-minute interviews in a quiet room, audio-recorded with consent; same trained interviewer for all to reduce interviewer effects. Analysis – closed and rating answers summarised as percentages/means; open answers transcribed and analysed by thematic analysis, coding recurring themes (career prospects, quality of education, family expectations, finance), with two researchers coding independently to check reliability. Ethics – consent, confidentiality (codes), right to withdraw.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: interview type named and justified; at least one open and one closed example question; sample; procedure (recording, setting, interviewer); analysis of quantitative and qualitative data; ethics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'longitudinal study'.
parts.answer: A study in which the same participants are tested or observed repeatedly over a long period of time (months or years).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of a longitudinal study compared with testing different age groups at one time.
parts.answer: Because the same people are followed, changes over time are not caused by differences between groups (participant variables / cohort effects), so the development of each person can be tracked.
parts.working: 1 mark: same participants compared with themselves. 1 mark: removes participant variables/cohort effects or shows individual development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a 5-year study follows 400 teenagers' mental health. In year 1, 400 took part; by year 5, 292 remained. Calculate the percentage of the original sample lost by year 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this attrition could affect the validity of the findings.
parts.answer: If those who dropped out differ systematically from those who stayed (e.g. teenagers with worse mental health are more likely to drop out), the remaining sample is biased and may make mental health appear better than it really is.
parts.working: 1 mark: drop-outs may differ from those who stay. 1 mark: biased sample / distorted conclusions in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to investigate how children's friendships change between the ages of 6 and 10. Describe how she could conduct a longitudinal study to investigate this.
Your plan must include details about:
• the sample and how attrition would be reduced
• how friendships would be measured
• how often data would be collected.
parts.answer: Example plan: Sample – 120 six-year-olds from six primary schools in Lahore (both girls and boys), selected by stratified sampling from school registers, with parental consent. Attrition – collect several contact details, send newsletters about the study, give small gifts or certificates to children each year, and recruit extra participants at the start to allow for drop-out. Measures – each year, a short structured interview with the child ('Who are your best friends?', 'What do you like doing together?'), a sociometric nomination task (children name up to three classmates they like to play with), and a 15-minute playground observation of each child using time sampling (who they play with, in what kind of activity). Teachers complete a 5-point rating scale of each child's friendship quality. Frequency – once a year in the same month (e.g. October) from age 6 to 10, giving 5 data points, using the same measures and trained researchers each time. Analysis – compare number and type of friends across years (means, line graphs), and themes in interview answers.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: sample with technique and size; specific attrition strategies; measures operationalised (interviews, nominations, observation, rating); intervals and duration; consistency of measures; ethics with children.

practice.stem: A researcher plans a questionnaire to investigate mobile phone use among college students in Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write one closed question the researcher could include in the questionnaire.
parts.answer: 'Do you use your phone during meals with your family? Yes / No'
parts.working: 1 mark: a question with fixed response options relevant to phone use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write one open question the researcher could include in the questionnaire.
parts.answer: 'Describe how using your phone affects the time you spend with your family.'
parts.working: 1 mark: a question that allows participants to answer in their own words; must not be answerable with yes/no.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using closed questions in this study.
parts.answer: Students must choose from fixed answers that may not fit their real experience (e.g. they use the phone only sometimes), so the data may lack validity and detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: forced choice / lack of detail; 1 mark: linked to phone use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a rating-scale question that could be used to measure how stressed teachers feel at work. Your scale must have labelled anchor points.
parts.answer: 'How stressed do you feel at work most days?' 1 = not at all stressed, 2, 3, 4, 5 = extremely stressed.
parts.working: 1 mark: question about stress with a numerical scale; 1 mark: both ends (anchor points) labelled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a rating scale rather than an open question.
parts.answer: It gives numerical (quantitative) data, so the mean stress of teachers in different schools can be compared easily and objectively.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantitative / easy comparison; 1 mark: linked to teachers.

practice.stem: Dr Malik asks recently widowed women in Multan to talk about their experiences. She has no list of questions and simply follows what each woman wants to talk about.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which type of interview Dr Malik is using.
parts.answer: An unstructured interview.
parts.working: 1 mark: unstructured (no fixed questions, follows the conversation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this type of interview is suitable for this topic.
parts.answer: Grief is a sensitive and individual experience; an unstructured interview allows each widow to talk freely about what matters to her, building rapport and giving detailed, valid data.
parts.working: 1 mark: flexibility / rapport / depth; 1 mark: linked to the sensitive topic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe structured interviews and unstructured interviews, using any examples.
parts.answer: A structured interview uses a fixed list of questions asked in the same order to every participant, e.g. asking every patient the same ten questions about symptoms; it is easy to compare and replicate but the interviewer cannot follow up interesting answers. An unstructured interview has no fixed questions beyond a topic: the interviewer follows the conversation, e.g. a therapist asking a client to talk about childhood; it gives rich, detailed data but answers cannot easily be compared, and interviewer bias is more likely.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for each type: 1 for a description, 1 for an example, 1 for an elaboration (strength/weakness or feature such as standardisation, replicability, rapport, depth).

practice.stem: A researcher interviews parents in Karachi face to face about how they discipline their children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'social desirability' in self-report research.
parts.answer: When participants give answers that make them look good or match social norms, rather than the truth.
parts.working: 1 mark: answers to appear favourable/acceptable; 1 mark: rather than truthful, so data are invalid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why social desirability is a particular problem in this study.
parts.answer: Asking parents face to face how often they shout at or smack their children is sensitive; parents may underreport harsh discipline to avoid being judged by the interviewer.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the sensitive behaviour; 1 mark: direction of bias (under-reporting) linked to face-to-face interview.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Use an anonymous postal or online questionnaire instead of a face-to-face interview, so parents feel their answers cannot be traced back to them.
parts.working: 1 mark: anonymity/confidentiality/online questionnaire/filler questions; 1 mark: explanation of why it reduces the bias.

practice.stem: A hypothetical study interviews patients at a diabetes clinic in Islamabad about why they do or do not follow their doctor's advice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a semi-structured interview in this study.
parts.answer: The interviewer can ask set questions to all patients, giving some comparable data, but also follow up interesting answers (e.g. why a patient stopped taking medication), giving more detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: combination of fixed questions and flexibility; 1 mark: linked to patients.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using a semi-structured interview in this study.
parts.answer: Different follow-up questions are asked to different patients, so answers are harder to compare, and the interviewer's own views may influence which points are explored (interviewer bias).
parts.working: 1 mark: less standardised / interviewer bias / time-consuming; 1 mark: linked to the study.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one ethical issue the researcher must consider and how to deal with it.
parts.answer: Confidentiality: patients may disclose personal health information, so their names must not be recorded and data stored securely.
parts.working: 1 mark: issue (confidentiality, privacy, right to withdraw, protection from distress); 1 mark: how to deal with it.

practice.stem:
Hamza is writing a questionnaire about public transport in Karachi. Three of his questions are:
1 Don't you agree that the new bus service is excellent?
2 Are the buses cheap and clean? Yes / No
3 Do you often use public transport? Yes / No

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two problems with the questions written by Hamza.
parts.answer: Question 1 is a leading question ('Don't you agree…'), pushing respondents towards 'yes'. Question 2 is a double-barrelled question asking about two things at once (price and cleanliness).
parts.working: 1 mark each: leading question (Q1); double-barrelled (Q2). Accept: Q3 uses ambiguous terms ('often').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite question 3 so that it produces clearer data.
parts.answer: 'How many times did you use public transport in the last 7 days? 0 / 1–3 / 4–6 / 7 or more'
parts.working: 1 mark: removes the vague word 'often'; 1 mark: gives specific, mutually exclusive response options.

practice.stem: A researcher in Jeddah has written a questionnaire to measure attitudes to healthy eating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher could test the reliability of her questionnaire using the test–retest method.
parts.answer: Give the same questionnaire to the same participants twice, with a gap of a few weeks (long enough that they don't remember their answers but not so long that their real attitudes change). Correlate the two sets of scores; a strong positive correlation (e.g. above +0.8) shows the questionnaire is reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: same participants, same questionnaire, twice; 1 mark: suitable time gap with justification; 1 mark: compare/correlate scores – a strong positive correlation indicates reliability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a reliable questionnaire may still not be valid.
parts.answer: It may consistently measure something other than intended – e.g. items about 'healthy eating' may really measure knowledge of nutrition rather than what people actually eat, so answers are consistent but not accurate.
parts.working: 1 mark: consistency ≠ accuracy; 1 mark: example in context (e.g. social desirability gives the same false answers each time).

practice.stem: A psychologist wants to investigate the relationship between sleep habits and concentration in university students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this study could be conducted as a self-report using a questionnaire. Include details of the sampling technique, the types of questions with examples, and how the data would be analysed.
parts.answer: A possible plan: opportunity or stratified sample of 100 university students (e.g. equal numbers of first- and final-year students) from different faculties of a university in Lahore; online anonymous questionnaire with standardised instructions and consent page; closed questions (e.g. 'How many hours a night do you usually sleep on weekdays? less than 5 / 5–6 / 7–8 / more than 8'), rating scales (e.g. 'Rate your ability to concentrate in lectures: 1 = very poor to 7 = excellent'), and open questions (e.g. 'Describe what stops you sleeping before exams'); filler questions to reduce demand characteristics; pilot study to check clarity; quantitative data analysed as means/medians and bar charts by year group; qualitative answers coded into themes; ethics – informed consent, right to withdraw, confidentiality, debrief with sleep advice.
parts.working: Mark points: sampling technique and sample detail; recruitment; questionnaire format (online/paper, anonymous); at least two question types with examples; rating scale with anchors; filler questions/pilot; standardised instructions; analysis (descriptive statistics, graphs, thematic coding); ethics. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan and suggest how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Weakness: self-reported sleep hours may be inaccurate because students guess or overestimate, reducing validity. Improvement: ask students to keep a sleep diary for a week, or wear an activity tracker that records sleep, and compare the measures (triangulation).
parts.working: 1 mark: identify a weakness of the plan; 1 mark: explain it in context; 1 mark: suggest an improvement; 1 mark: explain how the improvement helps.

practice.stem: A hypothetical telecommunications company with 2,000 employees in branches across Pakistan wants to find out how employees feel about their managers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of collecting data with questionnaires rather than interviews in this study.
parts.answer: Strength: questionnaires can be sent to all 2,000 employees across the country quickly and cheaply, and anonymity may make employees more honest about their managers. Weakness: there is no chance to clarify unclear questions or follow up answers, and response rates may be low, so those who reply (e.g. very unhappy staff) may not be representative.
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (identify + link to the large company / anonymity); 2 marks for weakness (identify + link).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The response rate was 18 %. Calculate how many questionnaires were returned.

practice.stem: A neuropsychologist in Lahore studies a man who lost the ability to recognise faces after a stroke.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'case study'.
parts.answer: An in-depth investigation of a single individual, or a small group, usually using several methods.
parts.working: 1 mark: detailed study of one person/small group (or one event/organisation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of the case study method for studying this patient.
parts.answer: It gives detailed, rich information about a rare condition that could not be studied with a large sample, and can be followed over time to see changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: depth / rare cases / longitudinal; 1 mark: linked to the patient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the case study method for studying this patient.
parts.answer: The findings come from one unique person whose brain damage and life history are different from others, so they cannot be generalised to other people.
parts.working: 1 mark: generalisability / researcher bias / hard to replicate; 1 mark: linked to the patient.

practice.stem: A researcher studied a survivor who was trapped for three days after a building collapsed, to understand how she coped.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the case study method was used rather than an experiment.
parts.answer: The situation (surviving a building collapse) is rare and could not ethically be created by a researcher, so the only way to study it is to investigate the few people it has happened to in depth.
parts.working: 1 mark: rare / naturally occurring event; 1 mark: cannot be manipulated ethically in an experiment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one type of data, qualitative or quantitative, the researcher is likely to collect most and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Qualitative, because the researcher wants a detailed account of the survivor's thoughts, feelings and experiences, which are best captured in words.
parts.working: 1 mark: qualitative (accept quantitative with justification, e.g. symptom scores); 1 mark: justification.

practice.stem: A school psychologist in Islamabad carries out a case study of a 12-year-old boy who refuses to attend school.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'triangulation' in a case study.
parts.answer: Using several different methods or sources of data (e.g. interviews, observations, tests, records) to study the same case, and checking whether they agree.
parts.working: 1 mark: several methods/sources; 1 mark: comparing them to check consistency/validity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three different sources of data the researcher could use to triangulate in this case study.
parts.answer: An interview with the boy about how he feels in class; an observation of his behaviour in lessons; school records of attendance and grades (or a questionnaire for his parents/teachers, or a psychometric test).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three different, appropriate sources linked to the boy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why triangulation increases the validity of the case study.
parts.answer: If different sources give the same picture, the conclusion does not rely on one possibly biased source.
parts.working: 1 mark: agreement between sources makes conclusions more accurate/less dependent on one method's bias.

practice.stem: A researcher spent eighteen months visiting one family of refugees settling in Peshawar, interviewing them and observing their daily life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researcher's close relationship with the family could be a problem in this case study.
parts.answer: After months of contact she may become less objective and interpret the family's behaviour in a way that supports her own expectations (researcher bias), reducing validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of objectivity / bias; 1 mark: effect on interpretation in this case.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue that is particularly important in this case study.
parts.answer: Confidentiality: a detailed account of one family could easily identify them in a small community, so names and identifying details must be changed.
parts.working: 1 mark: issue (confidentiality/privacy/right to withdraw); 1 mark: why it is especially important in a case study.

practice.stem: A psychologist wants to carry out a case study of a child who is gifted at mathematics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this case study could be conducted. Include at least two methods of data collection, how long it would last, and one ethical consideration.
parts.answer: A possible plan: one gifted 9-year-old girl in a Lahore school; volunteer/parental consent; longitudinal over one school year; methods: semi-structured interviews with the child (e.g. 'Tell me what you enjoy doing in maths lessons'), interviews or questionnaires with parents and teachers; structured observations in class (event sampling for categories such as 'asks a question', 'helps a classmate'), standardised tests of ability at the start and end; school records; triangulation of findings; qualitative data analysed into themes, quantitative test and observation data summarised; ethics – informed consent from parents and assent from child, right to withdraw, confidentiality (pseudonym), protection from stress from being labelled.
parts.working: Mark points: participant and how chosen; duration/longitudinal; at least two methods described in detail with examples; triangulation; types of data and analysis; ethics specific to a child. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of your plan.
parts.answer: Strength: using interviews, observations and test scores (triangulation) means that conclusions about the girl's abilities are supported by several sources, reducing the effect of bias from any one method (e.g. a teacher's opinion), so the case study has higher validity. The year-long duration also shows how her behaviour changes over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify; 1–2 marks: explain with reference to the plan; 1 mark: why it improves the study.

practice.stem: A researcher wants to observe how waiting staff in a busy Karachi restaurant deal with rude customers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a participant and a non-participant observation, using this study as an example.
parts.answer: In a participant observation the researcher joins the group, e.g. works as a waiter alongside the staff; in a non-participant observation the researcher watches without joining in, e.g. sits as a customer and records the staff's behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark for each type with a link to the restaurant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of an overt observation in this study.
parts.answer: The staff know they are being observed and have agreed, so the study is ethical (informed consent and no invasion of privacy).
parts.working: 1 mark: ethical/informed consent; 1 mark: linked to the restaurant staff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one difference between a naturalistic and a controlled observation.
parts.answer: A naturalistic observation watches behaviour in its usual setting without changing anything (e.g. children in their own classroom); a controlled observation takes place in a setting arranged by the researcher, often a laboratory, where variables are standardised.
parts.working: 1 mark for each type; must show the contrast (normal setting vs researcher-controlled).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The researcher used a one-way mirror to observe children in a playroom set up at a university. State one advantage of this.
parts.answer: The children cannot see the observer, so their behaviour is less likely to change because they know they are being watched.
parts.working: 1 mark: reduces reactivity/demand characteristics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe event sampling and time sampling, using any examples.
parts.answer: Event sampling: the observer records every time a particular behaviour occurs, e.g. tallying each time a child hits another in the playground; useful for infrequent behaviours but may be hard if many events happen at once. Time sampling: the observer records behaviour only at set intervals, e.g. noting what a shopper is doing every 30 seconds; reduces the amount of data, but behaviour between intervals is missed.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for each: description, example, elaboration (strength/weakness).

practice.stem: In a hypothetical study, observers stood near the checkout in a Lahore hypermarket and secretly recorded how shoppers behaved while waiting in queues.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why the observation was covert.
parts.answer: If shoppers knew they were being watched they might change how they behave in the queue (e.g. queue more politely), so a covert observation reduces demand characteristics and gives more valid data.
parts.working: 1 mark: avoids participant reactivity/demand characteristics; 1 mark: linked to queue behaviour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical problem with this covert observation and suggest whether it is acceptable.
parts.answer: Shoppers did not give informed consent; however, the observation took place in a public place where people would expect to be seen by strangers, so it is usually considered acceptable as long as individuals are not identified.
parts.working: 1 mark: no consent/deception; 1 mark: justification about public place and anonymity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two behavioural categories the observers could use. Each must be operationalised.
parts.answer: 'Pushing in' – joining the queue in front of someone who arrived earlier. 'Complaining' – making a verbal comment about waiting time to another person.
parts.working: 1 mark each for operationalised observable categories.

practice.stem: A researcher wants to investigate road rage in drivers waiting at traffic signals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this study could be conducted as a structured observation. Include the setting, the type of observation, behavioural categories, the sampling of behaviour and how reliability would be checked.
parts.answer: A possible plan: naturalistic, non-participant, covert observation of drivers at a busy signal-controlled junction in Islamabad during rush hour (e.g. 5–7 p.m., weekdays over two weeks); two observers positioned on the pavement (or video recording from a public place, number plates not recorded); event sampling of each car arriving at a red light; operationalised categories: 'hooting' (horn used while stopped at red light), 'aggressive gesture' (hand gesture towards another driver), 'jumping the light' (crossing stop line after light turns red), 'calm waiting' (no hooting or movement until green); tally chart; quantitative data as frequencies compared between drivers of different vehicle types or sexes if visible; inter-rater reliability – both observers code the same cars and correlate tallies, training beforehand with practice video; ethics – public place, no identification of drivers.
parts.working: Mark points: setting and time; naturalistic/controlled; participant/non-participant; overt/covert with justification; behavioural categories operationalised; event or time sampling; recording method (tally/video); inter-rater reliability; data type and analysis; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan.
parts.answer: Weakness: observers can see behaviour but not the reasons for it – a driver who hoots may be warning another driver rather than being aggressive, so the category may be misinterpreted, reducing validity. This could be improved by stopping a sample of drivers at a nearby petrol station to interview them, or by refining the category definitions.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify weakness; 1–2 marks: explain with reference to the plan; 1 mark: consequence for validity/reliability or improvement.

practice.stem: A researcher in Singapore asks teenagers how many hours they spend playing violent video games each week and gives them a questionnaire measuring aggression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a non-directional hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be a correlation between the number of hours spent playing violent video games per week and the score on an aggression questionnaire.
parts.working: 1 mark: states a relationship/correlation without direction; 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised (e.g. hours per week, questionnaire score).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this study is a correlation and not an experiment.
parts.answer: Neither variable is manipulated by the researcher: both violent video game hours and aggression are measured as they already are, so we are looking for a relationship between two co-variables rather than the effect of an IV on a DV.
parts.working: 1 mark: no manipulation of an IV; 1 mark: two measured co-variables.

practice.stem: A head teacher in Hyderabad found a correlation coefficient of −0.72 between the number of days students were absent and their final exam scores (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a correlation coefficient of −0.72 shows about the relationship between the two variables.
parts.answer: A fairly strong negative correlation: as the number of days absent increases, exam scores tend to decrease.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength (fairly strong/strong); 1 mark: negative direction described in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a correlation coefficient of +0.05 would have shown instead.
parts.answer: There is almost no relationship between absence and exam scores.
parts.working: 1 mark: no (or extremely weak) correlation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the head teacher cannot conclude that absence causes lower exam scores.
parts.answer: A third variable such as illness, family problems or poor motivation may cause both absence and low scores.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation cannot show cause/effect; 1 mark: suitable third variable or reverse direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the type of correlation in each statement:
(i) The more coffee a student drinks, the fewer hours they sleep.
(ii) The more hours a nurse works overtime, the higher her stress score.
parts.answer: (i) Negative correlation; (ii) positive correlation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a correlation to study the link between overtime and stress in nurses.
parts.answer: It would be unethical to make nurses work extra hours to see if they become stressed; a correlation allows the relationship to be studied using the hours they already work.
parts.working: 1 mark: ethical/practical (variables cannot be manipulated) or can show the strength of the relationship; 1 mark: linked to nurses.

practice.stem: A psychologist wants to investigate whether there is a relationship between how much people exercise and how happy they feel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this study could be conducted as a correlation. Include how each co-variable would be measured, the sample and how the results would be presented.
parts.answer: A possible plan: volunteer or opportunity sample of 60 adults aged 18–60 attending a gym and a community centre in Karachi; co-variable 1 – self-reported average daily minutes of exercise over the last month (or a fitness tracker's daily step count over one week); co-variable 2 – score on a happiness/wellbeing rating questionnaire (e.g. ten items rated 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree, total 10–50); standardised instructions, informed consent, confidentiality; scores plotted on a scatter graph with exercise on the x-axis and wellbeing score on the y-axis; look for a positive correlation; directional hypothesis stated; ethics – right to withdraw, debrief.
parts.working: Mark points: both co-variables operationalised; measurement tools with example items; sampling technique and size; procedure/standardisation; hypothesis; scatter graph with axes; direction of expected correlation; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of your plan and one reason why it could not show that exercise causes happiness.
parts.answer: Strength: measuring exercise with a fitness tracker gives objective data, so it is not affected by people overestimating how much they exercise. Causation: happier people may simply be more motivated to exercise, or a third variable such as free time or income could increase both, so the direction of cause is unknown.
parts.working: 2 marks: strength identified and explained with reference to the plan; 2 marks: causation problem explained with reverse causality or a third variable.

practice.stem: In a hypothetical experiment in a university laboratory in Lahore, 20 students chewed gum while learning and recalling a list of 25 words and another 20 students did not chew gum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this experiment.
parts.answer: IV: whether the students chewed gum or not during the test. DV: the number of words correctly recalled.
parts.working: 1 mark each; DV must be operationalised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the type of experiment used.
parts.answer: A laboratory experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark: laboratory experiment (controlled setting, IV manipulated).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one strength of this type of experiment.
parts.answer: Extraneous variables such as noise and test time can be controlled, so differences in recall are more likely to be caused by chewing gum (cause and effect).
parts.working: 1 mark: control of variables; 1 mark: allows a causal conclusion in context.

practice.stem: A researcher compared the general knowledge of children in a village in Gilgit-Baltistan that had recently received internet access with children in a similar village that had not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is a natural experiment.
parts.answer: The researcher did not manipulate the IV (whether the village had internet access or not); the difference already existed naturally and she only measured its effect.
parts.working: 1 mark: IV not manipulated by the researcher; 1 mark: occurs naturally, linked to internet access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of a natural experiment in this study.
parts.answer: Participants cannot be randomly allocated to conditions, so the two villages may differ in other ways (e.g. wealth, schooling), which could explain differences in children's general knowledge.
parts.working: 1 mark: no random allocation/confounding variables/no control; 1 mark: example linked to the villages.

practice.stem: A researcher wants to find out whether offering free food samples increases sales of a new product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this field experiment could be conducted. Include the IV, the DV, the design, and controls.
parts.answer: A possible plan: field experiment in a large Islamabad supermarket; IV – whether a free-sample stall for a new biscuit is present at the end of an aisle (condition A) or absent (condition B), alternating on matched weekdays over four weeks; DV – number of packets of the biscuit sold per hour from the store's sales records (or the proportion of shoppers passing who pick up a packet, observed by two researchers); independent measures (different shoppers each day); controls – same price, same shelf position, same times (5–8 p.m.), same days of the week, same stall assistant with a standard script; shoppers unaware (covert); ethics – public place, no identification of individuals, debrief not possible so no personal data kept.
parts.working: Mark points: field setting; IV operationalised with two conditions; DV operationalised; design (independent/repeated) with justification; controls (time, day, price, script); sampling of participants; procedure; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan and how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Weakness: other factors that change from day to day, such as weather or special offers in another aisle, could affect sales and cannot be fully controlled in a field setting, reducing internal validity. Improvement: run the study over more days, alternating conditions randomly, and note any special events so those days can be excluded.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify; 1 mark: explain in context; 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how it helps.

practice.stem: A researcher wants to investigate whether rickshaw drivers in Lahore are more stressed during rush hour than at quieter times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two physiological measures the researcher could use to measure stress in the drivers.
parts.answer: Heart rate and cortisol level in saliva (accept blood pressure, skin conductance/galvanic skin response).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid physiological measures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using physiological measures rather than self-report to measure stress.
parts.answer: Physiological measures are objective: a driver cannot easily fake their heart rate, so the data are not affected by social desirability (e.g. not wanting to admit being stressed).
parts.working: 1 mark: objective / not affected by demand characteristics or social desirability; 1 mark: linked to drivers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what an fMRI scan measures.
parts.answer: It measures changes in blood flow (oxygenated blood) in the brain, which shows which areas are more active while a person performs a task.
parts.working: 1 mark: blood flow/oxygen use; 1 mark: shows brain activity in specific areas during a task.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using fMRI scans in psychological research.
parts.answer: Participants must lie still inside a noisy, enclosed scanner, so tasks are unlike real life (low ecological validity) and some people find it stressful, which may change brain activity.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (low ecological validity, cost, small samples, only shows correlation, stressful); 1 mark: explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how an MRI scan (structural) differs from an fMRI scan.
parts.answer: A structural MRI shows the physical structure of the brain (e.g. size of regions or grey matter), whereas fMRI shows activity over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: structure vs function/activity.

practice.stem: In a hypothetical study in Dhaka, participants gave a short speech to an audience. Their heart rate was measured with a monitor and they also rated their anxiety from 1 to 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researcher measured the participants' heart rate as well as asking them to rate their anxiety.
parts.answer: The rating is subjective and participants might under- or overstate their anxiety; heart rate gives an objective measure of arousal, so the two can be compared to check validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report subjective/biased; 1 mark: physiological measure objective, allows triangulation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem with using heart rate as a measure of anxiety.
parts.answer: Heart rate can rise for reasons other than anxiety, such as excitement, physical movement or caffeine, so a high heart rate does not definitely mean the participant was anxious.
parts.working: 1 mark: not specific to anxiety; 1 mark: example of another cause.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mean heart rate rose from 72 beats per minute before the speech to 99 beats per minute during it. Calculate the percentage increase. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the materials used in the Revised Eyes Test.
parts.answer: 36 black-and-white photographs of the eye region of different actors' and actresses' faces, taken from magazines. Each photo was surrounded by four words describing mental states: one target word and three foils. A glossary defined every word.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: 36 photographs; eye region only; black and white; from magazines; four words per photo (one target, three foils); foils of the same emotional valence as the target; glossary of word meanings; similar numbers of male and female faces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the four groups of participants in Baron-Cohen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Group 1: 15 adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism; Group 2: 122 adults from the general population; Group 3: 103 students at Cambridge University; Group 4: 14 adults from the general population, matched on IQ with Group 1.
parts.working: 1 mark for each group. Numbers not required but credit them as detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'theory of mind'.
parts.answer: The ability to attribute mental states (beliefs, intentions, emotions) to oneself and to other people, and to understand that others' mental states can differ from one's own.
parts.working: B1 for the ability to understand/attribute mental states to others.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one way the findings of Baron-Cohen et al.'s study could be used in everyday life.
parts.answer: The Eyes Test could be used as part of an assessment to help identify adults who may have subtle difficulties understanding others' feelings, so they can be offered support or social skills training.
parts.working: 1 mark: application. 1 mark: explained, ethical and linked to the study (subtle deficits, adults, eyes).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean Eyes Test scores (out of 36) were: Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism group 21.9, general population 26.2, students 28.0, IQ-matched group 30.9. Calculate the difference between the mean of the Asperger/autism group and the mean of the IQ-matched group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express the Asperger/autism group's mean as a percentage of the maximum score. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what these results suggest about theory of mind in adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism.
parts.answer: They scored lowest of all groups, even below people of the same IQ, which suggests adults with AS/HFA have a specific difficulty in attributing mental states to others from the eyes (a subtle theory of mind deficit), not just lower general intelligence.
parts.working: 1 mark: AS/HFA group lowest, including below IQ-matched group. 1 mark: conclusion – subtle theory of mind deficit that is not explained by IQ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two problems with the original Eyes Test that Baron-Cohen et al. tried to solve in the revised version.
parts.answer: The original had only two answer choices, so participants could score 50% by guessing and many people scored near the top (ceiling effect); the revised test used four choices. The original had only 25 items, giving a narrow range of scores; the revised test had 36. (Also: original foils were often the semantic opposite of the target, making it too easy; some items could be solved by basic emotions or gaze direction; there were more female faces.)
parts.working: 2 marks per problem: 1 for the problem in the original, 1 for how the revision fixed it. Problems: two-choice forced format/guessing; ceiling effect; too few items (25 → 36); foils were opposites (→ same emotional valence); basic emotions/gaze direction cues; unequal male/female faces; no glossary (→ glossary added).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why participants in Baron-Cohen et al.'s study also completed the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) questionnaire.
parts.answer: To measure autistic traits in all participants, so the researchers could test whether scores on the Eyes Test were related (negatively correlated) to the number of autistic traits a person has.
parts.working: 1 mark: AQ measures autistic traits/self-reported characteristics. 1 mark: to test the correlation with Eyes Test scores (prediction of a negative correlation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the correlation found between AQ scores and Eyes Test scores.
parts.answer: Negative – the higher the AQ score, the lower the Eyes Test score.
parts.working: B1: negative correlation (with explanation of meaning).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of the sampling of the Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism group in Baron-Cohen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: All had a clinical diagnosis of AS or HFA, so the researchers could be confident the group really had the condition being studied, which increases the validity of comparisons with the other groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: identified strength (diagnosed by clinicians / matched on IQ with Group 4). 1 mark: explained in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of this group's sample.
parts.answer: There were only 15 participants, all of them men, so the results may not represent all adults with AS/HFA, e.g. women, reducing generalisability.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (small, 15 people; all male; volunteers). 1 mark: consequence for generalisability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two friends are arguing about the validity of the Revised Eyes Test. Bilal says it is a valid measure of theory of mind; Sana says it is not. Explain one argument for each friend.
parts.answer: Bilal: the test was carefully developed – target words were checked by judges, foils had the same emotional valence, a glossary removed vocabulary problems – and people with AS/HFA scored lower, as predicted, so it seems to measure the ability to read mental states. Sana: the photographs are static, black-and-white images of eyes only, whereas in real life we judge mental states from whole faces, voices, movement and context, so the test may not measure everyday theory of mind (low ecological/construct validity).
parts.working: 2 marks for Bilal (point + link to the test's design or results). 2 marks for Sana (point + link, e.g. static images, eyes only, no context, adults only).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Baron-Cohen et al.'s study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about the use of quantitative data.
parts.answer: Strengths: quantitative data (scores out of 36, AQ scores) allowed objective comparison of the four groups and correlation with AQ; standardised procedure (same 36 photos, same instructions, glossary) increased reliability; inclusion of control groups (general population, students, IQ-matched) meant differences could be attributed to AS/HFA rather than IQ. Weaknesses: quantitative scores do not show why a participant chose a word or how they reasoned – no qualitative insight; low ecological validity – static photos of eyes only; small, mainly male AS/HFA group limits generalisability; the student group was not representative of the general population.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed with examples from the study, quantitative data point discussed in detail, balanced. Level 3 (5–7): four points with some explanation including quantitative data, or three detailed points. Level 2 (3–4): limited explanation/links. Level 1 (1–2): brief generic points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the participants in the doodling condition were asked to do in Andrade's study.
parts.answer: While listening to a monotonous 2½-minute mock telephone message about a party, they shaded in printed squares and circles on a sheet of paper. They were told that speed and neatness did not matter. They also had to write down the names of people who would be coming to the party.
