parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline how the children were matched before being placed in the three conditions.
parts.answer: Each child was rated for pre-existing aggressiveness by the experimenter and a nursery teacher who knew the children well; children were then put into groups of three with similar aggression scores and one from each trio was assigned to each condition.
parts.working: 1 mark: rated on prior aggression by the experimenter and a teacher (rating scales for physical, verbal, object aggression and aggression inhibition). 1 mark: children with similar ratings were matched in threes and split across conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the adult model did in the aggressive-model condition of Bandura et al.'s study.
parts.answer: After about a minute of assembling toys, the model turned to the large inflated Bobo doll and attacked it for the rest of the session: laid it on its side and sat on it, punched it on the nose, struck it on the head with a mallet, tossed it in the air and kicked it about the room, while saying things such as 'Sock him in the nose', 'Hit him down', 'Kick him' and 'Pow'.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: model attacks the Bobo doll after about 1 minute; sits on Bobo / punches it on the nose; hits it with a mallet; tosses it in the air / kicks it around the room; repeated the sequence about three times; aggressive verbal comments (e.g. 'Sock him in the nose', 'Pow'); non-aggressive comments ('He keeps coming back for more').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the model did in the non-aggressive condition.
parts.answer: The model quietly assembled the tinker toys for the whole session and ignored the Bobo doll.
parts.working: 1 mark: played quietly with tinker toys / ignored Bobo.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the children were mildly frustrated (Stage 2) before being observed in Bandura et al.'s study.
parts.answer: The researchers wanted all children to be in a similar state of mild arousal so that any aggression could be expressed; without this, children who had seen the non-aggressive model might be inhibited, and the frustration also ensured the control group had an equal chance to show aggression, so that differences were due to the model.
parts.working: 1 mark: to raise the chance of aggression being shown / arouse all children equally. 1 mark: so that differences in aggression could be attributed to the model condition (or so that the non-aggressive group's behaviour was not just due to inhibition).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline how this mild aggression arousal was produced.
parts.answer: Each child was taken to a room containing very attractive toys (e.g. a fire engine, a jet fighter, a doll set). After about two minutes of play the experimenter said these were her very best toys and she had decided to keep them for other children.
parts.working: 1 mark: child allowed to play with attractive toys briefly. 1 mark: told the toys were reserved for other children / taken away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two categories of behaviour that were recorded in the test room in Bandura et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Any two of: imitative physical aggression; imitative verbal aggression; imitative non-aggressive verbal responses; partially imitative responses (e.g. mallet aggression on other toys, sitting on Bobo without hitting); non-imitative aggression (e.g. punching Bobo, aggressive gun play).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two named categories.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how inter-rater reliability was checked in this study.
parts.answer: The male model watched every child, and a second observer independently scored half of the children; the two sets of scores were compared and were highly correlated, showing the coding was consistent.
parts.working: 1 mark: a second observer independently scored some children (half). 1 mark: scores compared / correlated and found to agree highly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the final stage of Bandura et al.'s study each child spent 20 minutes in the test room and was observed through a one-way mirror. Behaviour was recorded at 5-second intervals. Calculate the number of response units recorded for each child.
parts.answer: 240 response units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why using a one-way mirror improved the validity of the observation.
parts.answer: The children could not see the observers, so they were less likely to change their behaviour because they knew they were being watched; this reduced demand characteristics, so the aggression recorded was more likely to be the child's natural response to the model.
parts.working: 1 mark: observers hidden / covert observation. 1 mark: reduces participant reactivity / demand characteristics, so behaviour more genuine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one finding from Bandura et al.'s study about the sex of the child.
parts.answer: Boys produced more imitative physical aggression than girls, whereas the difference between boys and girls in imitative verbal aggression was much smaller.
parts.working: 1 mark: boys showed more (imitative) physical aggression than girls. 1 mark: comparison/detail, e.g. girls and boys similar in verbal aggression, or boys more influenced by the male model.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason, based on social learning, why children may be more likely to imitate a same-sex model.
parts.answer: Children identify more with models who are similar to them, and they may expect the same consequences (vicarious reinforcement) for behaviour shown by someone like themselves; also some behaviour is seen as sex-appropriate, e.g. physical aggression as 'masculine'.
parts.working: 1 mark: identification with a similar model. 1 mark: expansion – sex-typed behaviour seen as appropriate / expectation of similar consequences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hamza's parents notice that their 6-year-old son copies the wrestling moves he sees on television on his younger cousin. Using Bandura et al.'s study, suggest two pieces of advice for Hamza's parents.
parts.answer: 1. Limit his viewing of aggressive role models, or watch with him, because Bandura found children who saw an aggressive adult copied specific aggressive acts, whereas those who saw a non-aggressive model did not. 2. Provide non-aggressive same-sex models (e.g. his father or older brother playing calmly and resolving conflict without force), because children in Bandura's study imitated the behaviour of the model they watched, and boys were especially influenced by male models.
parts.working: For each piece of advice: 1 mark for a suitable, ethical suggestion; 1 mark for a link to Bandura's findings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bandura et al.'s study is often said to be high in standardisation but low in ecological validity. Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: High standardisation: every child experienced the same room layout, same toys, same 10-minute modelling period, same frustration procedure and the same 20-minute test, and models followed a set script of aggressive acts and phrases, so the study could be replicated and differences attributed to the IV. Low ecological validity: the child watched a stranger attack an inflatable doll that is designed to bounce back, alone in an unfamiliar room, for only a short time; hitting a Bobo doll is not the same as hurting a real person, so it may not reflect aggression in everyday life. However, it was set in a familiar nursery school with real toys, which partly supports validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: standardisation with example (same script/acts, timings, toys). 1 mark: benefit – replicable/reliable/control. 1 mark: low ecological validity with example (Bobo designed to be hit, stranger model, short exposure). 1 mark: balanced judgement or counterpoint (school setting, toys familiar).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue raised by Bandura et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Protection from harm: young children were deliberately frustrated and exposed to an aggressive adult, which may have caused distress and taught them aggressive behaviour that could persist after the study.
parts.working: 1 mark: named issue (protection from harm / consent of children / right to withdraw). 1 mark: linked to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Bandura et al.'s study of the imitation of aggression in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about generalisability.
parts.answer: Strengths, e.g. (1) controlled lab setting with standardised procedure – same toys, timings, scripted model behaviour, so cause and effect between the model condition and imitation can be established; (2) quantitative data from time sampling every 5 s gave objective comparisons between groups, and inter-rater reliability was high; (3) matched-participants design on prior aggression controlled participant variables. Weaknesses, e.g. (1) generalisability – all children came from one university nursery (Stanford) and were aged about 3 to 5 years, so results may not apply to older children or other cultures; (2) low ecological validity – a Bobo doll is designed to be hit and the model was a stranger; (3) ethics – children were frustrated and exposed to aggression; (4) only short-term effects were measured.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed with study detail, generalisability point clearly explained, well organised. Level 3 (6–8): four points, some lack detail or generalisability is brief. Level 2 (3–5): fewer points or mostly undeveloped/generic. Level 1 (1–2): one or two basic points. Generalisability must be included for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one similarity and one difference between Bandura et al.'s study and Fagen et al.'s study of elephant learning.
parts.answer: Similarity: both studies investigate learning from the learning approach and produced quantitative data – Bandura recorded counts of imitative acts in 5-second intervals, Fagen recorded whether elephants performed each step of the trunk wash. Difference: Bandura investigated social learning (observational learning without direct reinforcement) in human children in a laboratory experiment with three conditions, whereas Fagen investigated operant conditioning using direct positive reinforcement (food) to shape behaviour in young Asian elephants in Nepal in a natural working setting with no control group.
parts.working: For each of similarity and difference: 1 mark identification, 1–2 marks explanation, 1 mark examples from each study (up to 4 marks each). Accept other valid similarities (e.g. both use non-adult participants; both standardised procedures) and differences (humans vs animals; lab vs field; social learning vs operant conditioning; experiment vs field study).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the research method used by Saavedra and Silverman.
parts.answer: A case study (of one child).
parts.working: 1 mark: case study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the participant in Saavedra and Silverman's study, including how his phobia began.
parts.answer: A 9-year-old Hispanic-American boy with a phobia of buttons. It began when he was about 5 years old: in his kindergarten class he was reaching for buttons in a large bowl for an art activity, the bowl tipped and the buttons fell on him, which was very distressing.
parts.working: 1 mark: 9-year-old boy. 1 mark: button phobia. 1 mark: origin – buttons fell on him from a bowl at school when he was about 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how the boy's fear hierarchy was arranged in Saavedra and Silverman's study.
parts.answer: Button-related stimuli were ranked from least to most distressing: large denim jeans buttons were least distressing, and small plastic buttons were the most distressing.
parts.working: 1 mark: ranked list from least to most distressing. 1 mark: correct examples (large denim buttons low; small plastic buttons high).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the boy was asked to rate his distress on a 'feelings thermometer' throughout the therapy.
parts.answer: It gave a quick numerical measure of his distress for each step, so the therapist could check whether distress fell with exposure and decide when to move to the next item in the hierarchy.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantitative / self-rated measure of distress. 1 mark: to track change and guide progress up the hierarchy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Saavedra and Silverman followed up the boy after treatment. State when the follow-ups took place and explain why follow-up is useful.
parts.answer: At 6 months and 12 months after treatment. Follow-up shows whether the improvement lasted rather than being a short-term effect, so the therapy can be judged effective in the long term.
parts.working: 1 mark: 6 months and 12 months. 1 mark: shows whether improvement is long-lasting. 1 mark: e.g. rules out short-term demand effects / relapse check.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the boy's button phobia could have been acquired through classical conditioning.
parts.answer: Before the incident buttons were a neutral stimulus. In kindergarten the buttons fell on him (unconditioned stimulus), causing distress and disgust (unconditioned response). Because buttons were paired with this experience, they became a conditioned stimulus that on their own produced fear/disgust (conditioned response), which then generalised to buttons on clothing.
parts.working: 1 mark: buttons as neutral → conditioned stimulus. 1 mark: the falling incident as UCS producing distress (UCR). 1 mark: association means buttons alone trigger fear/disgust (CR), with link to the case.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how positive reinforcement was used in the treatment.
parts.answer: The boy was rewarded (e.g. with praise and small agreed rewards) each time he completed a step of in-vivo exposure to buttons, which encouraged him to keep engaging with the feared items.
parts.working: 1 mark: rewards/praise given. 1 mark: contingent on successfully completing exposure steps (contingency management).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the disgust imagery exposure used with the boy.
parts.answer: The therapist guided the boy to imagine buttons in unpleasant, disgust-related ways, for example imagining buttons falling on him or touching his body, and thinking about how they look, feel and smell. He stayed with these images while his disgust was rated and was encouraged to see that the disgusting thoughts were not dangerous, so the disgust reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark: imagined (not real) button scenarios. 1 mark: focus on disgust-related sensations (touching, smell, feel). 1 mark: repeated / rated until disgust reduced, linked to cognitive change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the researchers concluded that targeting disgust was important for this child.
parts.answer: The boy's main reaction to buttons was disgust rather than fear, and behavioural exposure alone did not reduce it much; when the imagery focused on disgust his distress ratings fell and the gains lasted at follow-up.
parts.working: 1 mark: disgust was the dominant emotion. 1 mark: imagery that targeted disgust produced greater/lasting improvement than exposure with reinforcement alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha, aged 10, is terrified of cotton wool after a bad experience at a clinic. Using Saavedra and Silverman's study, suggest how a therapist could help her.
parts.answer: Build a hierarchy of cotton-wool situations from least to most distressing (e.g. a picture of cotton wool, a closed bag, touching a ball, rubbing it on her arm). Expose her gradually to each step, asking her to rate her distress on a feelings thermometer and moving on only when ratings fall. Reward each completed step with praise or small prizes. If she reports disgust, add imagery exercises where she imagines touching cotton wool, as disgust imagery helped the boy in the study.
parts.working: 1 mark: hierarchy with relevant examples. 1 mark: gradual exposure. 1 mark: rating scale / positive reinforcement. 1 mark: disgust imagery, linked to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two friends are discussing Saavedra and Silverman's study. Nadia says the findings are useful for treating other children with phobias. Bilal says nothing can be generalised from a single case. Explain who you agree with.
parts.answer: Bilal is partly right: it was one 9-year-old boy with a rare phobia in which disgust was the main emotion, so other children (different ages, cultures or phobias) may not respond the same way. However, Nadia also has a point: the study gives detailed, in-depth evidence that adding disgust-focused imagery helped where exposure alone did not, which therapists can test with other children whose phobias involve disgust. Conclusion: the case is useful for generating ideas but needs replication before generalising.
parts.working: 1 mark: Bilal's point explained with study detail (one boy, unusual phobia). 1 mark: Nadia's point explained (in-depth data; practical application). 1 mark: link to disgust imagery/exposure. 1 mark: reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Saavedra and Silverman's study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about the use of qualitative and quantitative data.
parts.answer: Strengths, e.g. (1) both quantitative data (feelings thermometer distress ratings at each step) and qualitative data (the boy's descriptions of feelings, parent interview data from the ADIS) were collected, giving a detailed and measurable picture; (2) case study gives in-depth insight into a rare phobia and the role of disgust; (3) useful application – disgust imagery added to exposure; (4) follow-ups at 6 and 12 months show lasting change. Weaknesses, e.g. (1) self-report ratings by a child may be affected by demand characteristics or limited understanding of the scale; (2) one participant limits generalisability; (3) therapist was also researcher – possible bias; (4) the cause of the original phobia was reconstructed from memory.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed with study detail; named issue (qualitative/quantitative data) explicitly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): four points, some lack detail. Level 2 (3–5): limited or generic points. Level 1 (1–2): basic points only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of learning used to train the elephants in Fagen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Operant conditioning (positive reinforcement training).
parts.working: 1 mark: operant conditioning / positive reinforcement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how positive reinforcement and a bridging stimulus were used in the training.
parts.answer: Each time an elephant performed the target behaviour (or a step of it) it was given a food reward, which made that behaviour more likely to be repeated (positive reinforcement). A bridging stimulus (a signal such as a word or sound) was given at the exact moment the correct behaviour occurred, so the elephant could link that precise behaviour with the reward that followed a moment later.
parts.working: 1 mark: food reward given for the correct behaviour/step. 1 mark: reward increases the likelihood of the behaviour being repeated. 1 mark: bridging stimulus marks the exact moment of the correct behaviour / bridges the delay before the food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it was useful to train the elephants to perform a trunk wash.
parts.answer: A trunk wash collects a sample of fluid from the elephant's trunk that can be tested for tuberculosis (TB). TB is a serious disease in captive elephants and can pass between elephants and people, so being able to test elephants safely helps protect both elephant and human health.
parts.working: 1 mark: trunk wash gives a sample to test for TB. 1 mark: elaboration – TB is a serious risk to elephants / can spread between elephants and humans, so screening protects health.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline why Fagen et al. wanted to show that positive reinforcement could replace traditional elephant-training methods.
parts.answer: Traditional training of working elephants often relies on punishment, dominance and fear (negative reinforcement), which harms welfare and can make elephants dangerous to handle. Showing that elephants can learn new behaviour with rewards alone offers a more humane and safer alternative.
parts.working: 1 mark: traditional methods use punishment/dominance/fear. 1 mark: positive reinforcement is more humane / better welfare / safer for handlers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Fagen et al.'s study supports one assumption of the learning approach.
parts.answer: The learning approach assumes that behaviour is learned from the environment, for example through the consequences of behaviour (operant conditioning). The trunk wash is not a natural behaviour for elephants, but it was acquired because each step was followed by a food reward and the steps were shaped into the full sequence, showing that a completely new behaviour can be learned through reinforcement.
parts.working: 1 mark: states an assumption (behaviour learned through experience/consequences). 1 mark: the trunk wash is a new, not innate, behaviour. 1 mark: it was acquired through reinforcement/shaping.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the aim of Fagen et al.'s study of elephant learning.
parts.answer: To find out whether young (juvenile) Asian elephants could be trained, using operant conditioning with positive reinforcement only, to perform a trunk wash – the behaviour needed to collect a sample to test for tuberculosis – showing a humane alternative to traditional training methods.
parts.working: 1 mark: train elephants to perform the trunk wash (for TB testing). 1 mark: using positive reinforcement / operant conditioning.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the participants in Fagen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Five juvenile (young) Asian elephants living at an elephant facility in Nepal, cared for by their mahouts (handlers).
parts.working: 1 mark: five juvenile elephants. 1 mark: Asian elephants in Nepal / handled by mahouts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Fagen et al.'s study could be considered ethical in terms of the guidelines for research with animals.
parts.answer: 1. No pain, punishment or distress was used: the elephants were trained only with food rewards, so the procedure was humane and caused no harm. 2. The research had clear benefits for the animals themselves – it allowed safe testing for tuberculosis and showed a kinder alternative to traditional training – so any small cost (e.g. time spent in training sessions) was outweighed by the benefits.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identification (no harm/punishment – rewards only; benefits to elephants' health and welfare outweigh costs; elephants kept in their normal environment with familiar handlers), 1 mark explanation linked to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how shaping was used to train the elephants in Fagen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: The trunk wash was broken down into smaller steps – raising the trunk, keeping saline solution in the trunk, and lowering the trunk into a collection bag. Each step was reinforced with food as soon as it was performed, using a bridging signal to mark the exact moment of the correct behaviour. Once a step was reliable, rewards were given only for closer approximations, until the elephant performed the whole sequence on cue.
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour broken into steps. 1 mark: named steps (trunk up, hold saline, trunk down into bag). 1 mark: immediate positive reinforcement with food / bridging stimulus. 1 mark: successive approximations combined into the full behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Fagen et al.'s study of elephant learning in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about the use of animals in research.
parts.answer: Strengths, e.g. (1) animals in research: the study used only food rewards and no punishment, and it directly benefited the elephants (TB testing, a humane alternative to traditional training), so it meets ethical guidelines; (2) practical application – it shows handlers how to train useful health behaviours humanely; (3) carried out in the elephants' normal working environment, so it is high in ecological validity; (4) behaviour was broken into clearly defined steps, so progress could be recorded objectively. Weaknesses, e.g. (1) small sample of five juvenile elephants from one place in Nepal, so the findings may not generalise to adult elephants or other settings; (2) no control group (e.g. elephants trained traditionally), so it cannot show that positive reinforcement is better than other methods; (3) animals in research: findings from elephants may not generalise to human learning, and captive working elephants may differ from wild ones; (4) a field setting gives less control over extraneous variables (e.g. distractions, the elephants' daily workload).
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed with study detail; animal issue clearly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): four points, some undeveloped. Level 2 (3–5): limited/generic. Level 1 (1–2): basic only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one similarity and one difference between Fagen et al.'s study and Saavedra and Silverman's study.
parts.answer: Similarity: both used positive reinforcement and broke the target behaviour into graded steps – the elephants were given food for each step of the trunk wash (shaping), while the boy was rewarded for completing each step of his fear hierarchy during exposure. Difference: Saavedra and Silverman carried out a case study of one 9-year-old boy to remove a learned phobia, using exposure with reinforcement and disgust imagery, whereas Fagen et al. trained five juvenile elephants in Nepal to acquire a completely new behaviour (the trunk wash) for health testing.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for the similarity and 4 for the difference: identification (1), explanation (1–2), examples from both studies (1). Accept other valid points (e.g. both have practical applications; human vs animal participants; one participant vs five; removing behaviour vs acquiring behaviour; self-report ratings vs observation of steps).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether the elephants' learning in Fagen et al.'s study is better explained by individual or situational factors.
parts.answer: Situational: the learning was produced by the environment – the reinforcement schedule, the food rewards and the training sessions – which supports the learning approach's view that behaviour is shaped by consequences. Individual: the elephants did not all progress through the steps at the same speed, suggesting individual differences such as temperament, age or previous experiences with handlers also mattered. Conclusion: the situation (training) caused learning but individual characteristics affected how well it worked.
parts.working: 1 mark: defines individual vs situational. 1 mark: situational explanation linked to reinforcement in the study. 1 mark: individual explanation linked to differences between elephants. 1 mark: reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two assumptions of the learning approach.
parts.answer: 1. Behaviour is learned through experience and interaction with the environment (nurture), rather than being innate. 2. Learning occurs through classical conditioning (association), operant conditioning (consequences such as reinforcement and punishment) and social learning (observing and imitating models).
parts.working: For each assumption: 1 mark identification, 1 mark expansion/example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Saavedra and Silverman's study supports one assumption of the learning approach.
parts.answer: The assumption that behaviour is learned through experience: the boy's phobia developed after a single distressing experience with buttons (classical conditioning), and it was reduced by new learning – exposure with positive reinforcement – showing that a learned behaviour can be unlearned.
parts.working: 1 mark: states assumption. 1 mark: acquisition of phobia through association with the button incident. 1 mark: treatment through reinforcement/exposure as evidence of learning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the learning approach, explain whether the nature or nurture side of the debate is more strongly supported. Refer to two studies from the approach.
parts.answer: The learning approach is on the nurture side. Bandura et al. showed that children who watched an aggressive adult reproduced specific acts and phrases they would not otherwise have shown, so aggression was learned by observation. Fagen et al. showed that elephants could acquire a completely new behaviour (the trunk wash) through shaping with food rewards. Saavedra and Silverman showed a phobia acquired through a frightening experience. However, nature also plays a part: boys in Bandura's study showed more physical aggression than girls, which may partly be biological, and individual animals differ in how quickly they learn. Conclusion: the studies strongly support nurture, but innate factors influence what is learned and how easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: defines nature/nurture. 2 marks: first study linked to nurture. 2 marks: second study linked. 1 mark: counterpoint for nature and conclusion.

practice.stem:
A hypothetical study in a Lahore college tested whether background music affects revision. Students learned a list of 30 words either with pop music playing or in silence and then recalled as many words as possible.
Condition | Mean number of words recalled
Music | 14.2
Silence | 17.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of graph that should be used to display the results in the table. Give one reason for your choice.
parts.answer: A bar chart, because the IV (music or silence) is made of separate categories, and the bars show the mean for each condition.
parts.working: 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: reason – discrete/categorical conditions (bars do not touch) / comparing two means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable title, a label for the x-axis and a label for the y-axis for this graph.
parts.answer: Title: 'Mean number of words recalled when revising with music and in silence'. x-axis: 'Condition (music or silence)'. y-axis: 'Mean number of words recalled (out of 30)'.
parts.working: 1 mark each: title mentioning both variables; x-axis = conditions of the IV; y-axis = mean words recalled (must say 'mean').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the two means.
parts.answer: 3.4 words

practice.stem:
A hypothetical time-sampling observation of children's play at break time in an Islamabad primary school recorded the following behaviour categories.
Behaviour | Frequency
Running | 18
Chasing | 12
Sitting and talking | 24
Ball games | 30
Playing alone | 6
Give percentages correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of observations recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of observations that were ball games.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how these data should be displayed as a graph.
parts.answer: A bar chart with the five behaviour categories along the x-axis, with gaps between bars, and the frequency (number of observations) on the y-axis starting from zero; with a title such as 'Frequency of play behaviours observed during break time'.
parts.working: 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: categories on x-axis with separated bars; 1 mark: frequency on labelled y-axis from 0 / suitable title.

practice.stem:
In a hypothetical experiment, each participant chose one of two brands of juice, X or Y. In the 'with friends' condition, the participant shopped with two friends who (as secretly instructed) chose brand X first. In the 'alone' condition, the participant shopped alone but saw a sign saying that most shoppers chose brand X.
Condition | Chose brand X | Chose brand Y
With friends | 22 | 8
Alone | 12 | 18
Give percentages correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how many participants took part in the study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of participants in the 'with friends' condition who chose the same brand as their friends.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the data, state one conclusion from this study.
parts.answer: People are more likely to choose the same brand as others when they shop with friends who choose it (73.3 %) than when they shop alone and only see others' choices (40.0 %), suggesting friends exert stronger social influence on choices.
parts.working: 1 mark: conclusion about social influence/conformity; 1 mark: supported with comparative data (73.3 % vs 40 %).

practice.stem:
A hypothetical correlational study recorded the average daily screen time and average nightly sleep of eight teenagers in Islamabad.
Teenager | Screen time (hours) | Sleep (hours)
A | 1 | 8.5
B | 2 | 8.0
C | 3 | 7.6
D | 4 | 7.4
E | 5 | 6.8
F | 6 | 6.9
G | 7 | 6.1
H | 8 | 5.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of graph that should be used to display these data.
parts.answer: A scatter graph (scattergram).
parts.working: 1 mark: scatter graph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features your graph should have.
parts.answer: Daily screen time (hours) on one axis and sleep duration (hours) on the other, both labelled with units; each teenager plotted as a single point (no lines joining the points); a title stating both co-variables.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: both axes labelled with co-variables and units; points plotted not joined; suitable title; sensible scales starting from a stated value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of correlation shown by the data and explain what it means here.
parts.answer: A (strong) negative correlation: the more hours of screen time a teenager has, the fewer hours they sleep.
parts.working: 1 mark: negative (strong); 1 mark: interpretation in context.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why these data do not show that screen time causes less sleep.
parts.answer: A correlation only shows that two variables change together. A third variable, such as exam stress or a late bedtime routine, might increase screen use and reduce sleep, or poor sleep could lead to more screen use.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation ≠ causation / no manipulation of variables; 1 mark: example of a third variable or reverse direction.

practice.stem:
Reaction times (in milliseconds) of drivers in a hypothetical simulator study were grouped as follows.
Reaction time (ms) | Frequency
200–249 | 3
250–299 | 7
300–349 | 12
350–399 | 9
400–449 | 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one difference between a bar chart and a histogram.
parts.answer: A bar chart shows separate categories (or means of conditions), so the bars have gaps between them; a histogram shows continuous data split into class intervals, so the bars touch and the x-axis is a continuous scale.
parts.working: 1 mark: bar chart = discrete categories, gaps; 1 mark: histogram = continuous data, bars touch / frequency on y-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which type of graph is suitable for the reaction-time data in the table.
parts.answer: A histogram.
parts.working: 1 mark: histogram (data are continuous and grouped into intervals).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the modal class.
parts.working: 1 mark: 300–349 ms (frequency 12).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the number of participants in the study.
parts.answer: 35 participants

practice.stem:
In a hypothetical study, patients attending a support group in Peshawar rated their anxiety each week on a scale from 0 (no anxiety) to 10 (extreme anxiety).
Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Mean rating | 7.5 | 6.1 | 5.3 | 4.7 | 4.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a type of graph that could show the change in anxiety ratings across the five weeks.
parts.answer: A line graph (accept a bar chart of the weekly means).
parts.working: 1 mark: line graph (time on x-axis); accept bar chart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend shown in the data.
parts.answer: Mean anxiety fell each week, from 7.5 in week 1 to 4.2 in week 5, with the biggest drop between weeks 1 and 2 (1.4 points) and smaller drops later.
parts.working: 1 mark: anxiety decreased across weeks; 1 mark: use of data (start/end values or largest fall early).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean anxiety rating from week 1 to week 5. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

practice.stem:
In a hypothetical repeated-measures study of memory in Multan, six participants learned shapes and recalled them after no nap and after a 20-minute nap.
No nap: 12, 15, 9, 14, 11, 17
Nap: 18, 20, 16, 21, 19, 15
Give means to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the range for each condition.
parts.answer: No nap: mean = 13.0, range = 8; Nap: mean = 18.2, range = 6
parts.working: M1 mean method; A1 both means correct (13.0 and 18.2 to 1 d.p.); M1 range = highest − lowest; A1 both ranges (8 and 6).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a summary table of these results should be organised.
parts.answer: Rows for the two conditions (no nap / nap) and columns for the mean and range of the number of shapes remembered, with a title naming the IV and DV.
parts.working: 1 mark: conditions as rows (or columns) with mean and range headings; 1 mark: title/units (number of shapes recalled).

practice.stem:
Two observers watched the same 10-minute video of children in a playground and tallied aggressive behaviours (hypothetical data).
Category | Observer 1 | Observer 2
Hitting | 5 | 5
Grabbing toys | 8 | 7
Pushing | 3 | 3
Verbal threat | 6 | 6
Excluding others | 4 | 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: For how many of the categories did the two observers record exactly the same tally?
parts.working: Same tally for hitting (5), pushing (3) and verbal threat (6): 3 categories.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of behaviours recorded by each observer.
parts.answer: Observer 1: 26; Observer 2: 26
parts.working: B1 each: 26 and 26.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what these data suggest about the inter-rater reliability of the observation, and suggest how it could be improved.
parts.answer: The totals are identical and three of five categories match exactly, with the other two differing by 1, so inter-rater reliability appears high. It could be improved by giving the observers more practice with the operationalised categories (e.g. clearer definitions of 'grabbing' versus 'pushing') before the study, and by video-recording so tallies can be checked.
parts.working: 1 mark: reliability is high/good with reference to data; 1 mark: identifies the discrepancies (grabbing toys and excluding others each differ by 1); 1 mark: improvement (clearer operational definitions, training, recording).

practice.stem: In a hypothetical field experiment in a Karachi shopping mall, a confederate dropped a pile of papers near 80 passers-by. For 50 passers-by the confederate was smartly dressed and for 30 scruffily dressed. 35 people helped the smartly dressed confederate and 12 helped the scruffily dressed confederate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of people who helped in each condition.
parts.answer: Smartly dressed: 70 %; scruffily dressed: 40 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a results table to summarise these findings. Your table should show the number and percentage of people who helped and did not help in each condition (describe the rows and columns in words).
parts.answer: Rows: smartly dressed; scruffily dressed. Columns: number who helped | number who did not help | % who helped. Smart: 35 | 15 | 70 %. Scruffy: 12 | 18 | 40 %. Title: 'Number and percentage of passers-by who helped a person who dropped papers, by how the person was dressed'.
parts.working: 1 mark: rows/columns correctly organised by condition; 1 mark: helped and not-helped numbers correct (35/15, 12/18); 1 mark: percentages correct; 1 mark: informative title / headings with units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why percentages are more useful than raw numbers for comparing the two conditions in this study.
parts.answer: The conditions had different numbers of passers-by (50 and 30), so raw numbers of helpers cannot be compared directly; percentages put both on the same base (out of 100), so the comparison is fair.
parts.working: 1 mark: common base / standardised; 1 mark: allows fair comparison between unequal groups.

practice.stem: Sana drew a bar chart of the mean test scores (out of 100) of students who revised on paper (mean 52) or on a tablet (mean 56). Her y-axis begins at 40 and has no label. The two bars touch each other and the graph has no title.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three problems with Sana's graph.
parts.answer: 1) The y-axis starts at 40, not 0, so the difference between the two conditions looks far larger than it is. 2) The y-axis has no label, so it is not clear that it shows mean scores out of 100. 3) The bars touch, which wrongly suggests continuous data, and there is no title.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: truncated y-axis exaggerates the difference; missing y-axis label/units; bars touching for categorical data; no title; x-axis categories not named.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the problem with the y-axis could mislead a reader.
parts.answer: The means of 52 and 56 differ by only 4 marks, but starting the axis at 40 makes one bar look about 1.3 times taller in relation to the axis (12 vs 16 units above 40), so a reader may think the effect of the IV is large.
parts.working: 1 mark: exaggerates a small difference; 1 mark: use of the data (only 4 points apart / bar heights from 40 are 12 and 16).

practice.stem: A hypothetical study of 20 university students in Kuala Lumpur plotted hours of sport played per week (x-axis, 0–14) against a self-rated mood score (y-axis, 1–10). Most points rise from the bottom left to the top right of the graph. One student who played 12 hours of sport per week had a mood score of 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the two variables shown by the scatter graph.
parts.answer: There is a positive correlation: students who reported more hours of sport per week generally reported higher mood scores, though the points are moderately spread, so it is not perfect.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive; 1 mark: interpretation in context, with strength (moderate/not perfect).

parts.label: b
parts.text: One student (12 hours of sport, mood 3) does not fit the pattern. Suggest two reasons why a researcher might find a point like this.
parts.answer: The student may have had a personal problem (e.g. a family illness) that lowered mood that week; or they may have misread the rating scale or recorded their answer wrongly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two plausible reasons: individual circumstances / other variables; recording or self-report error; misunderstanding the scale; social desirability.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the researcher should not simply remove this point from the data.
parts.answer: Removing data that do not fit the hypothesis is researcher bias; it would make the correlation look stronger than it really is and reduce the validity of the conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: bias / dishonest reporting; 1 mark: the correlation would be misrepresented.

practice.stem: A researcher is investigating how working night shifts affects nurses at a hospital in Rawalpindi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'quantitative data'.
parts.answer: Numerical data, such as scores, counts or ratings.
parts.working: 1 mark: data in the form of numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'qualitative data'.
parts.answer: Descriptive data in words (or pictures), such as detailed answers about thoughts and feelings.
parts.working: 1 mark: data in the form of words/descriptions, not numbers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of each type of data that the researcher in this study could collect.
parts.answer: Quantitative: the number of hours per day each nurse sleeps, or a rating of tiredness from 1 to 10. Qualitative: each nurse's description of how night shifts affect family life.
parts.working: 1 mark each; must be linked to the nurses / shift-work context.

practice.stem:
A questionnaire for gym members in Dubai contains four items:
1 How many times did you exercise last week? ____
2 Describe what motivates you to come to the gym.
3 Rate your fitness: 1 (very poor) to 7 (excellent).
4 Do you prefer exercising alone or with others? (tick one)

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, state whether it collects quantitative or qualitative data.
parts.answer: 1 – quantitative; 2 – qualitative; 3 – quantitative; 4 – quantitative (it gives a frequency/category count).
parts.working: 1 mark each. Item 4 is a closed question giving nominal (count) data, so quantitative.

practice.stem:
Students in Hyderabad were asked an open question: 'Describe how you felt before your last exam.' Seven answers were:
1 I was too nervous to eat
2 My mind went blank
3 I prayed and felt calmer
4 My hands were shaking
5 I could not sleep the night before
6 I talked to my friends and felt better
7 My heart was racing

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sort the seven answers into two categories: 'physical symptoms' and 'coping strategies' (any answer that is neither should be identified).
parts.answer: Physical symptoms: too nervous to eat; hands shaking; could not sleep; heart racing (4). Coping strategies: prayed and felt calmer; talked to friends (2). Neither (cognitive symptom): my mind went blank (1).
parts.working: 1 mark: physical symptoms correct (4 answers; accept 'could not sleep' or 'too nervous to eat' in either a physical or 'other' category); 1 mark: coping strategies correct (2); 1 mark: 'mind went blank' identified as a cognitive symptom/neither.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how sorting answers into categories changes the type of data collected.
parts.answer: Counting how many answers fall into each category turns qualitative data (words) into quantitative data (frequencies), which can be compared and graphed but loses some detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: converts qualitative to quantitative (frequencies); 1 mark: consequence – easier comparison/analysis but loss of depth/meaning.

practice.stem: A hypothetical study interviewed 30 elderly people living in Faisalabad about their experiences of loneliness, recording their answers in full.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of collecting qualitative data in this study.
parts.answer: Unstructured answers let the elderly participants explain in their own words why they feel lonely (e.g. children moving abroad), giving detailed insight that fixed questions might miss, which increases validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: depth / detail / participant's own words; 1 mark: linked to loneliness context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of collecting qualitative data in this study.
parts.answer: It is difficult to compare participants or summarise 30 long interviews objectively; the researcher's interpretation of what counts as loneliness may be biased.
parts.working: 1 mark: hard to analyse/compare or subjective interpretation; 1 mark: linked to the study.

practice.stem: A researcher wrote detailed notes describing how children in two nurseries in Quetta behaved when there were not enough toys for everyone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two behavioural categories the researcher could use to turn her notes into quantitative data. Make sure each is operationalised.
parts.answer: 'Sharing' – child hands an object to another child without being asked. 'Snatching' – child takes an object out of another child's hands.
parts.working: 1 mark for each clearly operationalised, observable category relevant to sharing/toys.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of turning her notes into quantitative data.
parts.answer: Frequencies of each category can be compared between the two nurseries and checked for inter-rater reliability, which is hard with descriptive notes.
parts.working: 1 mark: advantage (objectivity / comparison / reliability / graphs); 1 mark: linked to the study.

practice.stem: Employees at a bank in Lahore rated 'How satisfied are you with your job?' on a scale from 1 to 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the data from the 1–5 rating scale are quantitative.
parts.answer: Each answer is a number that can be added up or averaged.
parts.working: 1 mark: numerical scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the data are still subjective.
parts.answer: Each employee judges what '4' means for themselves; two people with similar satisfaction might choose different numbers, so the score depends on personal interpretation.
parts.working: 1 mark: based on personal opinion/interpretation; 1 mark: example of different interpretations of the scale points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of making the scale less open to interpretation.
parts.answer: Label every point with a description (e.g. 1 = very dissatisfied, 3 = neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, 5 = very satisfied).
parts.working: 1 mark: anchor/label every point, or give examples for each point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by quantitative data and qualitative data, using any examples.
parts.answer: Quantitative data are numerical: e.g. the number of aggressive acts counted in an observation, reaction times in ms, or scores on a rating scale. They are easy to summarise with means and graphs and to compare objectively, but can lack depth. Qualitative data are descriptive: e.g. interview transcripts about how a patient experiences anxiety, or diary entries. They give rich insight into reasons and meanings but are harder to analyse and may be interpreted subjectively.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for each type: 1 for definition, 1 for a relevant example, 1 for elaboration (feature, strength or weakness). Examples may come from any study (e.g. Milgram's voltage = quantitative, participants' comments = qualitative).

practice.stem: A hypothetical study asked patients recovering from knee surgery in a Toronto hospital to rate their pain each evening from 0 to 10 and also to write a short diary entry about their day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why collecting both quantitative and qualitative data could improve the validity of this study.
parts.answer: The rating scale gives comparable numbers showing whether pain changed over the week, while the diary explains why (e.g. pain worse after physiotherapy). If both show the same pattern, the conclusions are supported by two kinds of evidence (triangulation); the diary can also reveal if numbers were misunderstood.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantitative allows comparison/objectivity; 1 mark: qualitative gives reasons/depth; 1 mark: combining checks one against the other (triangulation) to increase validity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one problem the researcher may have when analysing the diaries.
parts.answer: Diaries will vary greatly in length and detail, and deciding which themes appear requires interpretation, so two researchers might code them differently (low inter-rater reliability).
parts.working: 1 mark: problem (time-consuming, subjective interpretation, differing detail); 1 mark: consequence for the study.

practice.stem: Seven participants in a hypothetical memory study recalled the following number of items: 4, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean, median and mode of the scores. Give the mean to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Mean = 8.14; median = 8; mode = 7
parts.working: B1 mean: 57 ÷ 7 = 8.14; B1 median = 8 (4th of 7 ordered values); B1 mode = 7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of the mean as a measure of central tendency.
parts.answer: It uses every score in the data set, so it is the most sensitive measure and represents all participants' performance.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses all scores; 1 mark: elaboration (most sensitive/representative when there are no extreme scores).

practice.stem:
In a hypothetical independent-measures study in a Lahore school, Group 1 learned a word list and Group 2 learned pictures of the same items. Correct answers:
Group 1: 6, 8, 5, 9, 7
Group 2: 10, 9, 12, 11, 8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of correct answers for each group.
parts.answer: Group 1 (word lists): 7; Group 2 (pictures): 10

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the means suggest about the hypothesis that pictures are remembered better than words.
parts.answer: The picture group had a higher mean (10 vs 7), which supports the hypothesis.
parts.working: 1 mark: supports, with reference to the means.

practice.stem: In a hypothetical study, seven shoppers in a Karachi supermarket were timed (in minutes) from entering the store to reaching the checkout: 15, 18, 17, 16, 19, 20, 95.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the median for these data. Give the mean to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Mean = 28.6 minutes; median = 18 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which measure gives the better summary of these data.
parts.answer: The median, because the extreme value of 95 minutes distorts the mean, making it higher than six of the seven scores; the median is not affected by this outlier.
parts.working: 1 mark: median; 1 mark: reason linked to the outlier of 95 inflating the mean.

practice.stem: Eight customers rated a new tea brand on a scale from 1 (strongly dislike) to 7 (strongly like): 4, 6, 3, 4, 2, 5, 4, 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the median rating.
parts.working: M1: ordered 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6 – median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values; A1: (4 + 4) ÷ 2 = 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the median is more appropriate than the mean for these rating-scale data.
parts.answer: Rating-scale data are ordinal: the gap between 'agree' and 'strongly agree' is not necessarily the same as between other points, so averaging the numbers is not meaningful; the median only uses rank order.
parts.working: 1 mark: data are ordinal / intervals not equal; 1 mark: median uses order only, mean assumes equal intervals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the only appropriate measure of central tendency for the question 'Which is your favourite brand of tea?' and explain why.
parts.answer: The mode, because the answers are categories (nominal data) that cannot be ordered or averaged.
parts.working: 1 mark: mode; 1 mark: nominal/categorical data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean of eight participants' scores is 12.5. Seven of the scores are 10, 14, 12, 11, 15, 13 and 9. Calculate the eighth score.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the median of all eight scores.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mean and median are equal here and what this suggests about the distribution of the scores.
parts.answer: The scores are spread evenly (one at each value from 9 to 16), with no extreme values, so the distribution is symmetrical; in a symmetrical distribution the mean and median are equal.
parts.working: 1 mark: evenly spread / no outliers; 1 mark: symmetrical distribution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of a normal distribution.
parts.answer: It is bell-shaped and symmetrical about the centre; the mean, median and mode are all equal and at the highest point; the tails extend in both directions and get closer to the x-axis without touching it; most scores lie near the middle.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: bell-shaped; symmetrical; mean = median = mode at the peak; tails approach but never touch x-axis; about 68 % of scores within one standard deviation of the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what should be shown on each axis when sketching a normal distribution of reaction times.
parts.answer: x-axis: reaction time (ms), the measured variable/score; y-axis: frequency (number of participants).
parts.working: 1 mark: x-axis = score/variable measured with units; 1 mark: y-axis = frequency.

practice.stem: A hypothetical concentration test was given to a large group of Pakistani secondary-school students. The scores were normally distributed with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Between which two scores would you expect about 68 % of the students to fall?
parts.answer: 42 and 58
parts.working: M1: one standard deviation either side of the mean (50 ± 8); A1: 42 and 58.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Approximately what percentage of students would you expect to score above 66?
parts.answer: About 2.5 % (accept 2–2.5 %)
parts.working: 66 is two standard deviations above the mean; about 95 % lie within ±2 SD, so about 2.5 % lie above (exact 2.3 %).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Out of 400 students, approximately how many would you expect to score between 42 and 58?
parts.answer: About 272 students

practice.stem: In a hypothetical proof-reading task in Singapore, the numbers of errors missed by 50 participants had a mean of 14, a median of 11 and a mode of 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether this distribution is normal, positively skewed or negatively skewed. Explain your answer using the three measures.
parts.answer: Positively skewed. The mean (14) is greater than the median (11), which is greater than the mode (10); a few participants made many errors, pulling the mean towards the long tail on the right.
parts.working: 1 mark: positively skewed; 1 mark: mean > median > mode; 1 mark: explanation – a few high scores create a long tail to the right/pull the mean up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the graph of this distribution would look like.
parts.answer: The peak (highest frequency) is towards the left (at low numbers of errors) and there is a long tail stretching out to the right towards high numbers of errors.
parts.working: 1 mark: peak to the left; 1 mark: long tail to the right.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the distribution of errors might not be normal in this study.
parts.answer: The task may have been easy for most people, so most made few errors (a floor effect), while a few tired or distracted participants made many.
parts.working: 1 mark: plausible reason (floor effect, task too easy, a few outliers, small sample).

practice.stem:
Two groups of trainee drivers in Islamabad completed a hazard-perception test (hypothetical scores).
Group A: 22, 25, 24, 23, 26
Group B: 10, 35, 18, 30, 27

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range for each group.
parts.answer: Group A: 4; Group B: 25

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean for each group.
parts.answer: Both groups have a mean of 24
parts.working: 120 ÷ 5 = 24 for each group.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, explain what the results show about the two groups.
parts.answer: Although both groups have the same mean, Group B's scores are much more spread out (range 25 vs 4), so performance in Group B varied a great deal between individuals while Group A performed consistently.
parts.working: 1 mark: same mean; 1 mark: Group B much more variable/less consistent with data.

practice.stem: In a hypothetical study in Melbourne, workers who did a mindfulness course had a mean stress score of 32 (standard deviation 2.1). A control group also had a mean of 32 (standard deviation 7.8).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'standard deviation'.
parts.answer: A measure of spread showing the average amount by which scores differ from the mean; a larger standard deviation means scores are more spread out.
parts.working: 1 mark: spread/variation around the mean; 1 mark: larger SD = more spread (or calculation idea: based on every score's distance from the mean).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the two groups using the means and standard deviations.
parts.answer: Both groups have the same mean stress score (32), but the mindfulness group has a much smaller standard deviation (2.1 vs 7.8), so their scores were closer together and more consistent; the control group varied more.
parts.working: 1 mark: same mean; 1 mark: mindfulness group less spread/more consistent, quoting SDs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of the standard deviation compared with the range.
parts.answer: It uses every score, so it is not distorted by a single extreme score as the range is.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses all data / less affected by one outlier.

practice.stem: Five participants in a hypothetical study in Cairo rated their sleep quality: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean of the scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation of the scores, using the sample formula s = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second group had the same mean but a standard deviation of 0.71. Explain what this tells you.
parts.answer: The second group's scores were much closer to the mean of 8, so participants in that group were far more similar to each other than in the first group.
parts.working: 1 mark: less spread / more consistent; 1 mark: comparison with 3.16.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'operationalising' a variable.
parts.answer: Defining a variable precisely in terms of how it will be manipulated or measured, so that it can be tested and the study repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark: clear/precise definition; 1 mark: in measurable / testable terms (or example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment at a bus station in Lahore tests whether people are more helpful when the person asking is smiling. Suggest how 'helpfulness' could be operationalised.
parts.answer: Whether the passer-by stops and gives directions to the bus stand within 10 seconds of being asked (recorded as helped / did not help).
parts.working: 1 mark for a measurable behaviour; 1 mark for precise detail (time limit / what counts).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study asks students how anxious they feel before a mathematics test. Write a rating scale question to measure anxiety. Your scale must have labelled anchors.
parts.answer: 'How anxious do you feel right now about the test? Circle one number: 1 = not at all anxious, 2, 3, 4, 5 = extremely anxious.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a question with a numbered scale; 1 mark for labelled anchors at both ends.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one weakness of measuring anxiety in this way.
parts.answer: Students may give socially desirable answers (e.g. boys under-reporting anxiety), so the score may not reflect their real anxiety.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explanation in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical experiment, students in Nairobi either listen to music or work in silence while learning a list of 30 words. Suggest how the dependent variable 'memory' could be operationalised.
parts.answer: The number of words (out of 30) correctly written down in 3 minutes of free recall immediately after the learning period.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of words recalled; 1 mark: detail (out of 30 / time limit / spelling rule).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the independent variable could be operationalised.
parts.answer: Music condition: an instrumental piece played through headphones at the same volume for the 5-minute learning period; silence condition: the same headphones worn with no sound.
parts.working: 1 mark for each condition clearly defined.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study states: 'The dependent variable is how happy people feel after exercising.' Explain why this variable has not been operationalised.
parts.answer: It does not say how happiness will be measured (no scale, score or behaviour), so another researcher could not repeat the measurement in the same way.
parts.working: 1 mark: no measurement stated; 1 mark: consequence (not replicable / subjective).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite the dependent variable so that it is operationalised.
parts.answer: The score from 1 (very unhappy) to 7 (very happy) that each participant circles on a mood scale 5 minutes after finishing a 20-minute walk.
parts.working: 1 mark measure; 1 mark timing / anchors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher plans a hypothetical observation of aggression among children in a school playground in Rawalpindi. Suggest two behavioural categories for 'physical aggression' and two for 'verbal aggression'.
parts.answer: Physical: pushing another child with one or both hands; kicking another child. Verbal: calling another child a rude name; shouting a threat such as 'I'll hit you'.
parts.working: 1 mark for each clearly observable, operationalised category (vague terms such as 'being mean' get 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the categories need to be operationalised before the observation starts.
parts.answer: So that every observer records the same behaviours in the same way, which improves inter-observer reliability and makes the data objective.
parts.working: 1 mark: consistency between observers; 1 mark: reliability / objectivity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigates sleep quality among night-shift nurses in Karachi. Describe one objective and one subjective way of operationalising 'sleep quality'.
parts.answer: Objective: a wrist activity monitor records the number of minutes of sleep and the number of awakenings each night for a week. Subjective: each morning nurses rate 'How well did you sleep?' on a scale from 1 (very badly) to 10 (very well).
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 for the method, 1 for precise measurement detail.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether background traffic noise affects concentration. Each participant proofreads a page of text containing 40 planted spelling errors, once in a quiet room and once with recorded traffic noise. They have 10 minutes for each page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher has operationalised 'concentration'.
parts.answer: Concentration is measured as the number of planted errors (out of 40) correctly found in the 10-minute proofreading task.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of errors found; 1 mark: out of 40 / in 10 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One participant found 34 errors in the quiet condition and 26 in the noisy condition. Calculate the percentage of errors found in each condition.
parts.answer: Quiet: 85%; noisy: 65%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one problem with this way of measuring concentration.
parts.answer: Finding errors also depends on reading and spelling ability, not only concentration, so it may lack validity (or participants may remember error positions if the same passage is reused).
parts.working: 1 mark problem; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study tests whether a breathing exercise reduces stress before a driving test in Dubai. Suggest how stress could be operationalised physiologically and by self-report.
parts.answer: Physiological: heart rate in beats per minute measured with a finger pulse monitor for one minute just before the test. Self-report: 'How stressed do you feel?' on a 0–10 scale where 0 = completely calm and 10 = extremely stressed.
parts.working: 2 marks each: method + unit/scale detail.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using both measures.
parts.answer: If both measures show the same pattern, the researcher can be more confident the result is valid (triangulation); the self-report also shows how the person feels, which heart rate cannot.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Singapore wants to measure how long teenagers spend on social media each day. Describe two ways of operationalising this variable.
parts.answer: 1) Read the phone's screen-time report for social media apps, recorded in minutes per day averaged over 7 days. 2) Ask the teenager: 'On a normal school day, about how many minutes do you spend on social media?' recorded as a number of minutes.
parts.working: 2 marks each: method + unit/time period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which way is more likely to be reliable.
parts.answer: The screen-time report, because it is recorded automatically and the same each time it is checked, whereas teenagers' estimates may change from one occasion to the next and depend on memory.
parts.working: 1 choice; 1 reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical observation at a farm in Punjab investigates play in young goats. Suggest two operationalised behaviour categories for 'play'.
parts.answer: Jumping with all four feet leaving the ground at once; head-butting another kid gently without injury (no chasing away afterwards).
parts.working: 1 mark each clearly observable category.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the researcher could use time sampling to record these behaviours.
parts.answer: Every 30 seconds for 20 minutes, the observer looks at a focal goat and records which category (if any) it is showing at that moment, giving 40 observations per goat.
parts.working: 1 mark: record at fixed intervals; 1 mark: detail of interval and duration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigates whether volunteers at a charity in Manchester have higher empathy than non-volunteers. Describe how 'empathy' could be operationalised in two different ways.
parts.answer: 1) Self-report: a questionnaire of 10 statements (e.g. 'I feel upset when I see someone in pain') each rated 1–5 from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree', giving a total score out of 50. 2) Behavioural/task: the number of correct emotions identified when shown 20 photographs of faces, or whether the participant offers help when a researcher 'accidentally' drops a pile of papers.
parts.working: 2 marks each: method + precise scoring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which of your two ways would give more valid data.
parts.answer: The behavioural measure may be more valid because it records what people actually do and is less affected by social desirability, which is likely to be strong for a quality such as empathy in charity volunteers.
parts.working: 1 mark choice; 1 mark justification (accept the reverse with a good reason).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment tests whether pupils obey a teacher more when the teacher wears a formal suit than casual clothes. The teacher asks each pupil to pick up a piece of litter. Operationalise 'obedience' so that it could be recorded reliably.
parts.answer: Obedience = the pupil picks up the litter and puts it in the bin within 15 seconds of the instruction, without the instruction being repeated. Recorded as obeyed / did not obey.
parts.working: 1 mark: specific behaviour; 1 mark: time limit; 1 mark: clear rule for what does not count (repeated request, partial compliance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way the operationalisation of the IV could be standardised.
parts.answer: The same teacher wears the same dark suit and tie (formal) or the same jeans and T-shirt (casual) on every trial.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether caffeine improves reaction time. The IV is operationalised as either 3 mg of caffeine per kilogram of body mass, dissolved in a fruit drink, or the same fruit drink with no caffeine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the caffeine dose a participant of mass 72 kg would receive.
parts.answer: 216 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: A drink contains 80 mg of caffeine per can. Calculate how many cans' worth of caffeine the 72 kg participant receives. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 2.7 cans

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the researcher operationalised the IV as a dose per kilogram rather than giving everyone the same amount.
parts.answer: The same amount would have a stronger effect on lighter people than heavier people, which would be a participant variable; a dose per kilogram makes the effect more equal across participants, so differences in the DV are more likely due to caffeine itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: body mass affects the effect; 1 mark: controls a participant variable / improves validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'participant variable'.
parts.answer: A characteristic of an individual participant, such as age, intelligence or personality, that could affect the DV.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment compares two methods of teaching reading to children in Hyderabad, using two different groups. Give two participant variables that could affect the results.
parts.answer: Children's existing reading ability; their age / how much English is spoken at home.
parts.working: 1 mark each, must be plausible for reading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical laboratory experiment tests whether noise affects mental arithmetic. Identify two situational variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Room temperature; time of day the test is taken (also accept lighting, instructions, the experimenter).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how one of these could be controlled.
parts.answer: Test all participants in the same room with the air conditioner set to 22 °C so temperature cannot explain differences in arithmetic scores.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each of the following, state whether it is a participant variable or a situational variable:
(i) a participant's handedness
(ii) the brightness of the lighting in the testing room
(iii) the friendliness of the experimenter
(iv) how tired the participant was before arriving
parts.answer: (i) participant (ii) situational (iii) situational (iv) participant
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why participant variables are a particular problem in an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Different people are in each condition, so a difference in the DV could be caused by differences between the groups (e.g. one group being more able) rather than by the IV.
parts.working: 1 mark: different people in each condition; 1 mark: confounds the result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how random allocation could reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Put each participant's name on a slip, mix the slips in a box and draw them out, putting alternate names in condition A and B, so every participant has an equal chance of being in either group and participant variables should be spread evenly.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark how it helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment in a market in Karachi tests whether shoppers are more likely to take a free leaflet from a smiling or a neutral-faced researcher. Explain two situational variables that would be hard to control.
parts.answer: 1) Crowding – on busy days shoppers may hurry past and take fewer leaflets regardless of facial expression. 2) Weather – heat or rain may change how willing shoppers are to stop. These could vary between the conditions and confound the results.
parts.working: 2 marks each: variable + effect in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe participant variables and situational variables, using any examples.
parts.answer: Participant variables are characteristics of the people taking part that might affect the DV, e.g. age, IQ, gender, mood, prior experience. They matter mainly in independent measures designs and are controlled by random allocation, matched pairs or repeated measures. Situational variables are features of the environment or procedure, e.g. noise, temperature, time of day, instructions, experimenter's behaviour. They are controlled by standardisation – keeping these features the same for every participant.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks each: definition (1), example (1), how controlled / why a problem (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical experiment, a male researcher tested participants in the morning and a female researcher tested participants in the afternoon. Explain why this is a problem.
parts.answer: The researcher is a situational variable that changes with the condition/time, so any difference could be caused by the researcher (or the time of day) rather than the IV – it is a confounding variable.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify uncontrolled situational variable; 1 mark: confounding explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how this could be avoided.
parts.answer: Use one researcher for all participants, testing at the same time of day, or have each researcher test equal numbers in each condition and read from the same script.
parts.working: 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical online experiment lets participants in Pakistan and Canada complete a memory task at home at any time. Explain two situational variables that the researcher cannot control.
parts.answer: 1) Time of day – some do it late at night when tired, others in the morning, which affects memory. 2) Distractions – family noise, television or phone notifications may interrupt some participants, lowering their scores.
parts.working: 2 marks each: variable + effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce the effect of one of these variables.
parts.answer: Ask participants to complete the task between 9 am and 12 noon local time, in a quiet room with their phone switched off, and record the time from the website.
parts.working: 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark detail.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment with 40 students in a college in Kuala Lumpur compares two revision techniques (flashcards and re-reading) on a French vocabulary test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a matched pairs design could be used to control participant variables in this study.
parts.answer: Give all 40 students a vocabulary pre-test; rank them by score; pair the top two, the next two and so on; then randomly put one member of each pair into the flashcard group and the other into the re-reading group. The groups then have similar starting ability.
parts.working: 1 mark pre-test on a relevant variable; 1 mark pairing; 1 mark random allocation within pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many participants would be in each condition.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one participant variable that matching on the pre-test would not control.
parts.answer: Motivation to revise / amount of revision done at home.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A hypothetical study compares memory scores of people using a memory-training app with people using a paper workbook. Participants chose which method to use. Their ages (years) were:
App group: 19, 21, 23, 20, 28
Paper group: 35, 41, 30, 38, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean age of each group. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: App group: 22.2 years; paper group: 36.8 years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why the researcher cannot conclude that the app caused better memory scores.
parts.answer: The app group was about 14.6 years younger on average; age is a participant variable that is linked to memory and familiarity with apps, so it is a confounding variable – the younger age, not the app, may explain the better scores.
