parts.working: 1 mark: groups differ in age (with numbers); 1 mark: age could affect memory/app use; 1 mark: confounding variable so cause unclear.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the design could be improved.
parts.answer: Randomly allocate participants to conditions, or match pairs on age.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment tests whether students in Peshawar who sleep for at least 8 hours remember more facts than students who sleep for less than 5 hours. Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: Students who sleep for at least 8 hours will recall more facts (out of 20) the next morning than students who sleep for less than 5 hours.
parts.working: 1 mark: direction stated; 1 mark: both IV levels and operationalised DV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be no difference in the number of facts recalled the next morning by students who sleep at least 8 hours and those who sleep less than 5 hours; any difference will be due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark: no difference; 1 mark: IV and DV included.

practice.stem: A hypothetical field experiment in Cairo records whether drivers stop at a zebra crossing for a pedestrian who is either a child or an elderly person.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be a difference in the number of cars that stop (out of 100) for a pedestrian waiting at the crossing depending on whether the pedestrian is a child or an elderly person.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference without direction; 1 mark: IV and DV clear.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the researcher might choose a non-directional hypothesis.
parts.answer: Previous research does not clearly predict which pedestrian will receive more help – drivers might stop more for a child (seen as vulnerable) or for an elderly person – so the direction cannot be predicted.
parts.working: 1 mark: no clear previous research / contradictory findings; 1 mark: linked to context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an aim and a hypothesis.
parts.answer: An aim is a general statement of what the study intends to investigate; a hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction about the expected result.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigates whether players of fast action video games have quicker reaction times than non-players. Write an aim for this study.
parts.answer: To investigate whether playing fast action video games is related to reaction time.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a directional hypothesis for the same study.
parts.answer: People who play fast action video games for at least 5 hours a week will have faster mean reaction times (in milliseconds, on a computer test) than people who never play.
parts.working: 1 direction; 1 operationalised variables.

practice.stem: A hypothetical study with office workers in Lahore investigates whether longer commuting time is related to lower job satisfaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a directional hypothesis for this correlational study.
parts.answer: There will be a negative correlation between the number of hours per week employees spend commuting and their job satisfaction score (out of 50).
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation and direction; 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised. Do not credit wording about difference or cause.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be no correlation between hours per week spent commuting and job satisfaction score; any relationship found will be due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark: no correlation; 1 mark: co-variables.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the researcher cannot conclude that commuting causes low job satisfaction.
parts.answer: A correlation does not show cause and effect: a third variable (e.g. lower pay meaning people live further away and are also less satisfied) could explain both.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation not causation; 1 mark: example of a third variable or reverse direction.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment in Toronto: one group chews mint gum while learning 25 words; another group does not. Both groups write down as many words as they can remember 10 minutes later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable.
parts.answer: Whether participants chewed gum or not while learning.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the dependent variable.
parts.answer: The number of words (out of 25) recalled after 10 minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark (must be operationalised for credit).

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment in a sports centre in Islamabad allocates participants to sit still, walk slowly or jog, each for 15 minutes. Afterwards each person rates their mood on a scale from 1 (very low) to 10 (very good).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the three levels of the independent variable.
parts.answer: Sitting still for 15 minutes, walking slowly for 15 minutes, jogging for 15 minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark for all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the dependent variable and state how it was measured.
parts.answer: Mood, measured by the score circled on a 1–10 mood scale (1 = very low, 10 = very good) after the activity.
parts.working: 1 mark DV; 1 mark measurement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify one variable that should be controlled and explain why.
parts.answer: Time of day / temperature – it could affect mood independently of the activity, so it must be kept the same for all conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark variable; 1 mark reason.

practice.stem: A hypothetical study collects data from 60 secondary-school pupils in Mumbai on the hours of homework they do per week and their score on the end-of-term science test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two co-variables in this study.
parts.answer: Hours of homework per week; score (%) on the end-of-term science test.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these are called co-variables rather than an independent and dependent variable.
parts.answer: Neither variable is manipulated by the researcher; both are simply measured as they occur, to see whether they change together, so neither can be said to be the cause.
parts.working: 1 mark not manipulated / measured naturally; 1 mark no cause and effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'informed consent'.
parts.answer: Agreement to take part in a study given by a participant who has been told enough about the aims and procedure to make a knowledgeable decision.
parts.working: B1: agreement to participate given with full knowledge of what the study involves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A researcher secretly observes how people queue at a bank in Lahore. Explain why she cannot obtain informed consent in this study.
parts.answer: The observation is covert; if she asked customers for consent they would know they were being watched and might change how they queue, so the behaviour would no longer be natural.
parts.working: 1 mark: covert/naturalistic observation of strangers. 1 mark: asking would cause participant reactivity / demand characteristics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two pieces of information that should be given to participants in a debrief.
parts.answer: Any two of: the true aim of the study; whether any deception was used and why; that their data will be kept confidential; that they may withdraw their data; how to contact the researcher or find out the results; reassurance that their behaviour was normal.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: Dr Malik gives a 20-minute questionnaire about exam stress to 60 Grade 11 students in Faisalabad. Describe how Dr Malik should give the students the right to withdraw.
parts.answer: Before starting she should tell them clearly that they can stop answering at any time, without giving a reason and without any penalty, and that they can ask for their completed questionnaire to be removed and destroyed afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: told before and during they may leave at any time without penalty/reason. 1 mark: can also withdraw their data afterwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the right to withdraw is especially important in this study.
parts.answer: Questions about exam stress may upset some students, and as school pupils they may feel pressure to obey an adult researcher, so they need to know they can stop if they feel uncomfortable.
parts.working: 1 mark: sensitive topic may cause distress. 1 mark: young participants / power imbalance with researcher or teacher.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between confidentiality and privacy as ethical guidelines.
parts.answer: Confidentiality means participants' personal information and results must not be shared or published in a way that identifies them. Privacy means participants should not be observed or asked about things in situations where they would expect not to be watched, unless they have agreed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct explanation of each term.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a psychologist uses a confederate who pretends to drop her shopping in a busy street in Peshawar, and records whether passers-by help. Identify two ethical guidelines that may be broken in this study.
parts.answer: Any two of: informed consent; deception; right to withdraw; debriefing (passers-by usually leave before they can be debriefed).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct guidelines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researcher could reduce one of these ethical problems.
parts.answer: After a passer-by has helped or walked past, a researcher could approach them, explain the true purpose (debrief) and offer them the chance to have their data removed.
parts.working: 1 mark: suggestion. 1 mark: explained as reducing a named problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'protection from harm' in psychological research.
parts.answer: Participants should not be exposed to more physical or psychological risk than they would meet in everyday life, and should leave the study in the same state as they entered it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hypothetical study: participants watch upsetting news clips about a flood before rating their mood. Suggest two ways the researcher could protect participants from harm.
parts.answer: Any two of: warn participants beforehand about the content and get consent; screen out people who have experienced floods; show a cheerful clip afterwards to restore mood; full debrief with contact details for support; remind them they may stop watching at any time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two suitable ways.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'deception' in psychological research.
parts.answer: Misleading participants, or withholding information, about the true aims or procedure of a study.
parts.working: B1: lying to or misleading participants (including withholding information).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why researchers sometimes need to use deception.
parts.answer: If participants knew the real aim they might change their behaviour to fit (demand characteristics), so deception keeps their behaviour natural and the results valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: participants would change their behaviour/demand characteristics. 1 mark: validity of findings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher wants to interview 9-year-old children in a Hyderabad primary school about bullying. Identify who must give consent for the children to take part.
parts.answer: Their parents or legal guardians (as well as permission from the school, and the children's own agreement).
parts.working: B1: parent/guardian consent (accept head teacher as well but not alone).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one other ethical issue the researcher must consider in this study.
parts.answer: Protection from harm: talking about bullying may upset the children, so the researcher should use gentle questions, allow them to stop at any time, and make sure a teacher or counsellor is available afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies an issue (harm, confidentiality vs safeguarding, right to withdraw, debriefing in simple language). 1 mark: explained in this context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the ethical guidelines of confidentiality and debriefing. Use any examples to support your answer.
parts.answer: Confidentiality: personal details and results must be kept secret and published anonymously, e.g. using participant numbers rather than names, storing questionnaires securely. In Baron-Cohen et al.'s study, participants' test scores would not be published with names. Debriefing: at the end of a study participants are told its true aim, any deception is explained, they are reassured and offered the chance to withdraw their data; e.g. Milgram introduced participants to the unharmed learner and explained the shocks were not real.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for each guideline: 1 for a definition, 1 for elaboration (how it is done), 1 for a relevant example (from a study or a suitable hypothetical one). Full marks require both guidelines and examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a psychologist installs cameras in a hospital staff room in Karachi to record how nurses take breaks. The nurses agreed to take part in 'a study of working life' but were not told about the cameras. Explain which two ethical guidelines are most clearly broken.
parts.answer: Privacy: a staff room is a private space where nurses would not expect to be filmed, so recording them there invades their privacy. Informed consent/deception: they agreed to a general study but were not told about the filming, so their consent was not fully informed and they were deceived about the procedure.
parts.working: 2 marks per guideline: 1 for naming it, 1 for explaining why it is broken in this scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: an online questionnaire asks 300 university students in Islamabad about their use of social media late at night. Explain two ways the researcher should maintain confidentiality.
parts.answer: Do not ask for names or student ID numbers – use code numbers so answers cannot be linked to individuals. Store the data on a password-protected computer and only report group results (e.g. averages), so no single student can be identified.
parts.working: 2 marks per way: 1 for the method, 1 for explaining how it protects identity. Accept: anonymous responses, coded IDs, secure storage, delete data after use, report only group data, do not share with university.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'presumptive consent'.
parts.answer: Asking a group of people similar to the participants whether they would find the study acceptable; if they would, it is presumed the real participants would also consent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem with using presumptive consent.
parts.answer: The people asked are not the actual participants, so individual participants may still object to what happened to them; they have not personally agreed to take part.
parts.working: 1 mark: real participants did not agree themselves. 1 mark: they may still feel upset/object once they find out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: participants are paid PKR 2000 for a 2-hour study on reaction times. The researcher tells them they will only be paid if they complete the whole study. Explain why this is unethical.
parts.answer: It undermines the right to withdraw: participants may feel they cannot leave because they would lose the money, so they are pressured to continue even if uncomfortable.
parts.working: 1 mark: right to withdraw. 1 mark: explanation – payment is conditional, so participants feel forced to continue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the researcher could change the payment arrangement to be ethical.
parts.answer: Pay all participants the full amount (or pay for time spent) whether or not they complete the study, and make this clear at the start.
parts.working: 1 mark: payment not dependent on completing. 1 mark: participants told in advance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher interviews adults in Quetta who have recently lost a family member, to investigate coping. Suggest two ethical precautions the researcher should take.
parts.answer: Gain fully informed consent, explaining that the questions will be about their loss, and remind them they may stop at any time. Arrange support: provide contact details of a counsellor and end the interview gently with neutral questions, so participants are not left distressed.
parts.working: 2 marks per precaution: identified (1) + linked to the bereavement scenario (1). Accept: confidentiality of sensitive details, avoid probing questions, pilot the interview, trained interviewer, debrief.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'retrospective consent'.
parts.answer: Asking participants for their consent after they have taken part, usually during the debrief, when they know the true aims.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give an example of a study where retrospective consent would be appropriate, and explain why.
parts.answer: A field experiment on helping in a market, where passers-by cannot be told beforehand without spoiling the study; afterwards they are told what happened and asked whether their data may be used.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable example (field experiment, covert observation, deception study). 1 mark: explanation – prior consent would spoil natural behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of a cost–benefit analysis in deciding whether a study is ethical.
parts.answer: Before approving a study, an ethics committee weighs the possible costs to participants (distress, deception, loss of privacy) against the benefits of the knowledge gained for society; if the benefits clearly outweigh the costs, and harm is minimised, the study may go ahead.
parts.working: 1 mark: weighing costs to participants. 1 mark: against benefits to society/knowledge. 1 mark: decision made by an ethics committee / study approved only if benefits outweigh costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: Dr Khan tells half of a group of students in Lahore that they scored very low on an 'intelligence test' (false feedback) and then measures how long they persist at difficult puzzles. Explain two ethical guidelines broken in this study and describe what the debrief should include.
parts.answer: Deception: students were given false information about their intelligence. Protection from harm: being told they are of low intelligence could lower self-esteem and cause distress beyond everyday life. The debrief should: explain the true aim (effect of feedback on persistence); state clearly that the feedback was false and not their real score; reassure them that their performance was normal; offer the chance to withdraw their data; give contact details for questions or support.
parts.working: 2 marks per guideline (named + explained in context) = 4. 2 marks for the debrief: must include that the feedback was false + one other feature (true aim, reassurance, withdraw data, contact).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two researchers disagree about a planned covert observation of how people use their phones while walking in a shopping mall in Dubai. Researcher A says it is ethical; Researcher B says it is not. Explain one argument for each researcher.
parts.answer: A: the mall is a public place where people expect to be seen by strangers, so observing them does not invade privacy; no names are recorded and no one is harmed, so it is acceptable to observe without consent. B: people have not given consent and cannot withdraw; if the observers note details such as appearance, or record the content of screens or conversations, this could invade privacy, and they cannot be debriefed.
parts.working: 2 marks for each researcher's argument: 1 for the point (public place/privacy; no consent/right to withdraw), 1 for development in the scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the need for valid results can conflict with ethical guidelines. Use one example from a psychological study.
parts.answer: To get valid results, participants often should not know the true aim, because knowing it could create demand characteristics. This conflicts with informed consent and deception guidelines. For example, Milgram told participants the study was about learning and that the shocks were real; if they had known it was about obedience and that no one was harmed, their behaviour would not have shown real obedience. So high validity was gained at an ethical cost (deception, distress).
parts.working: 1 mark: validity needs natural behaviour / avoid demand characteristics. 1 mark: conflicts with consent/deception. 1 mark: example from a study. 1 mark: explanation of the trade-off in that example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a 3-year longitudinal study follows 150 teenagers in Rawalpindi to see how part-time work affects school grades. The researchers need to link each teenager's data across the three years. Explain how they could keep the data confidential while still linking it.
parts.answer: Give each teenager a unique code number at the start, used on all questionnaires and records instead of names; keep a separate key linking names to codes in a locked or password-protected file that only the lead researcher can access; publish results only as group data and destroy the key at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark: code numbers instead of names. 1 mark: separate, secure key linking names and codes with restricted access. 1 mark: report group data only / destroy key / no identifiable details published.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one other ethical issue that is more of a problem in a longitudinal study than in a one-off study.
parts.answer: Consent must be renewed: the teenagers' circumstances change over three years and they may later wish to withdraw, so they should be reminded each year of their right to withdraw and asked to confirm consent (and their own consent sought when they become adults).
parts.working: 1 mark: issue (ongoing consent, withdrawal, long-term data storage, repeated testing stress). 1 mark: explained in a longitudinal context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: patients in a psychiatric ward in Lahore are asked to take part in a study of a new relaxation technique by the doctor who treats them. Explain two ethical problems with this procedure.
parts.answer: Consent: patients with mental health problems may not fully understand the information, so their consent may not be truly informed; extra checks or a guardian's agreement may be needed. Right to withdraw/pressure: because the request comes from their own doctor, patients may feel they must agree or that their treatment will suffer if they refuse or leave the study.
parts.working: 2 marks per problem: 1 for naming it, 1 for linking it to the vulnerable patients and their doctor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the ethical guidelines of deception and the right to withdraw. Use any examples to support your answer.
parts.answer: Deception: participants should not be misled about the aims or procedure unless it is necessary and is not likely to cause distress; any deception must be explained in the debrief. Example: in Andrade's study participants were not told about the surprise memory test, which was necessary so they would not rehearse the information, and was harmless. Right to withdraw: participants must be told they can leave at any time and remove their data, without penalty. Example: in Milgram's study the prods ('you have no other choice, you must go on') made it hard for participants to feel they could leave.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks per guideline: definition (1), elaboration – when allowed / how given (1), example (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: In a Multan university, a lecturer asks the students in her own class to take part in her study on memory. She says it is voluntary but records the names of those who refuse. Evaluate the ethics of this procedure, referring to two guidelines.
parts.answer: Right to withdraw/voluntary participation: students may feel pressured to take part because their lecturer marks their work, and recording names of those who refuse suggests consequences, so participation is not truly voluntary. Confidentiality: recording names links individuals with their decision (and possibly their results), which should be kept anonymous. To be ethical, an independent person should recruit and no names of refusers should be kept.
parts.working: 2 marks per guideline: identified (1) + explained in scenario (1). Allow 1 of the 4 marks for a suitable improvement if one guideline is only weakly explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ethical guidelines that apply to research with animals.
parts.answer: Any two of: replacement; species and strain; number of animals; pain and distress; housing; reward, deprivation and aversive stimuli; anaesthesia, analgesia and euthanasia.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the guideline of 'replacement'.
parts.answer: Researchers should consider whether animals can be replaced with other methods, such as computer simulations, videos or recordings of animals, before using live animals.
parts.working: 1 mark: use alternatives where possible. 1 mark: example of an alternative.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher plans to test maze learning in 60 rats, though a pilot study suggests 20 would give clear results. Explain which animal guideline is relevant.
parts.answer: Number of animals: researchers should use the smallest number of animals needed to get meaningful results, so the researcher should use about 20 rats, not 60.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of animals (reduction). 1 mark: applied – use the minimum needed (fewer rats).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: pigeons are kept at 80% of their normal body weight so that they will work for food rewards in a learning experiment. Explain which ethical guideline this raises and how the researcher could meet it.
parts.answer: Reward, deprivation and aversive stimuli: depriving animals of food can cause distress. The researcher should consider the species' normal feeding pattern, use the minimum deprivation needed, use highly preferred food treats as rewards instead, and monitor the birds' health.
parts.working: 1 mark: names guideline. 1 mark: explains the problem (deprivation causes distress/harm). 1 mark: suitable way to minimise it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: young monkeys are housed alone in small cages during a study of learning. Explain why this breaks the guideline on housing.
parts.answer: Monkeys are social animals; housing them alone in small cages can cause stress and abnormal behaviour, so they should be kept in suitable social groups with enough space and enrichment.
parts.working: 1 mark: social species/needs company or space. 1 mark: isolation/crowding causes distress; suggest appropriate housing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how poor housing could also reduce the validity of the study's results.
parts.answer: Stressed, isolated monkeys may learn or behave differently from normal monkeys, so the learning measured would reflect the effects of stress rather than normal ability.
parts.working: 1 mark: stress changes behaviour. 1 mark: results not representative/confounded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the guideline on 'species and strain' when researchers select animals for a study.
parts.answer: Researchers should choose a species that is suited to the research purpose and that is likely to suffer least, considering the animals' background (e.g. bred for research vs caught in the wild); endangered species should not be used unless the research benefits their conservation.
parts.working: 1 mark: choose species suited to the aim and least likely to suffer. 1 mark: extra detail (wild-caught or endangered species, knowledge of the species' needs).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the animal ethical guidelines of 'pain and distress' and 'anaesthesia, analgesia and euthanasia'. Use any examples to support your answer.
parts.answer: Pain and distress: researchers should avoid or minimise pain, suffering and lasting harm to animals; any procedure causing distress must be justified by the value of the research and requires approval, e.g. a study using mild electric shocks must use the weakest shock that works and monitor the animal. Anaesthesia, analgesia and euthanasia: animals must be given appropriate anaesthetic during painful procedures and painkillers afterwards; if an animal suffers lasting pain it must be humanely killed by a trained person using an approved method, e.g. rats after brain surgery receive pain relief and are monitored.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks per guideline: definition (1), elaboration (1), example (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher studies fear learning in 12 zebrafish, which are bred in the laboratory, live in a large group tank, and are briefly startled by a tap on the tank. Evaluate whether this study meets two animal ethical guidelines.
parts.answer: Housing: met – the fish live in a large group tank, suitable for a social species, which reduces stress. Pain and distress: largely met – the startle is brief and mild rather than painful, though repeated startles could still cause stress, so the number of trials should be kept low. (Also: species – lab-bred fish rather than wild; number – only 12 used.)
parts.working: 2 marks per guideline: 1 for a judgement (met/not met), 1 for justification from the scenario. Accept replacement, species, number, aversive stimuli.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Different participants take part in each condition of the experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment in Quetta compares memory for pictures and memory for words using an independent measures design. Explain one weakness of this design for this study.
parts.answer: Participant variables such as natural memory ability may differ between the picture group and the word group, so differences in recall may be due to the people rather than the type of material.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark linked to context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an 'order effect' in a repeated measures design.
parts.answer: A change in performance caused by the order in which the conditions are done rather than by the IV, e.g. doing better in the second condition through practice, or worse through fatigue or boredom.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 1 mark example (practice / fatigue / boredom).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how counterbalancing could be used in a repeated measures experiment on whether people type faster on a laptop keyboard or a phone screen.
parts.answer: Split participants into two halves: one half types on the laptop first and then the phone; the other half uses the phone first and then the laptop, so order effects are balanced across the conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: two groups in opposite orders; 1 mark: in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could use a matched pairs design in a hypothetical experiment comparing two diets for weight loss among adults in Lagos.
parts.answer: Measure each volunteer's starting weight (and perhaps age and sex); pair people with similar starting weight; randomly allocate one member of each pair to diet A and the other to diet B.
parts.working: 1 mark: pre-measure a relevant variable; 1 mark: form pairs; 1 mark: one of each pair to each condition (randomly).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using a matched pairs design in this study.
parts.answer: It is time-consuming to measure and match people, and if one member of a pair drops out the other's data may be lost (or matching cannot be perfect on all variables).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment with 48 participants in Hong Kong tests whether people compare shop prices faster when the prices are shown as a vertical bar chart or as a horizontal bar chart. Each participant does both conditions; half do vertical first and half do horizontal first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many participants should do the order 'vertical chart first, then horizontal chart'?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the technique the researcher is using and state its purpose.
parts.answer: Counterbalancing (ABBA / two orders); to balance out order effects such as practice and fatigue between the two conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark name; 1 mark purpose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study compares the spatial ability of left-handed and right-handed people. Explain why it must use an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Handedness is a characteristic of the participant that cannot be changed, so each person can only be in one condition (left-handed or right-handed).
parts.working: 1 mark: IV is a participant characteristic / not manipulated; 1 mark: so cannot be in both conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could randomly allocate 30 participants to two conditions.
parts.answer: Give each participant a number from 1 to 30, put the numbers in a hat and draw them out; the first 15 drawn go to condition A and the remaining 15 to condition B (or use a random number generator).
parts.working: 1 mark random method; 1 mark equal groups / how it is used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why random allocation is used.
parts.answer: So that each participant has an equal chance of being in either condition, spreading participant variables evenly and avoiding researcher bias in choosing groups.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe repeated measures design and matched pairs design, using any examples.
parts.answer: Repeated measures: the same participants do every condition, e.g. each person takes a memory test in silence and with music. It removes participant variables between conditions and needs fewer participants, but suffers from order effects (practice, fatigue) and demand characteristics, controlled by counterbalancing. Matched pairs: different participants in each condition but each participant is paired with another who is similar on a key variable (e.g. IQ or age), one of each pair going into each condition. It reduces participant variables without order effects, but matching is time-consuming and never perfect.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks each: description (1), example (1), strength/weakness or control (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Islamabad investigates whether students learn new Urdu poetry better when they study it at 8 am or at 8 pm. Explain which experimental design you would choose and why.
parts.answer: Matched pairs (or independent measures): the same poem cannot be learned twice by the same person, so repeated measures would cause practice effects; matching on a pre-test of memory ability reduces participant variables between the 8 am and 8 pm groups.
parts.working: 1 mark design; 1 mark reason against repeated measures (practice/learning the same material); 1 mark reason for chosen design.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the researcher could use a repeated measures design instead.
parts.answer: Use two different but equally difficult poems (one for each time) and counterbalance which poem is learned at which time.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether visitors find their way through a large hospital in Kuala Lumpur faster using a printed map or a phone map. The measure is the time taken to walk from the entrance to the eye clinic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researcher should not use a repeated measures design.
parts.answer: After the first condition participants would already know the route, so their time in the second condition would be quicker because of learning (a practice effect), not because of the type of map.
parts.working: 1 mark practice/learning effect; 1 mark linked to route.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which design should be used and give one strength of it for this study.
parts.answer: Independent measures: each participant uses only one map, so there are no order effects and they cannot work out the aim by comparing conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark design; 1 mark strength.

practice.stem: In a hypothetical driving-simulator study in Sydney, each participant drives for one hour while talking on a hands-free phone and then for one hour while using a hand-held phone. Reaction time to hazards is measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a fatigue effect could affect the results of this study.
parts.answer: In the second hour participants will be tired and bored, so their reaction times will be slower whatever the condition; since the hand-held phone condition always comes second, it will appear worse than it really is.
parts.working: 1 mark tiredness slows reactions; 1 mark confounds the second condition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of reducing this problem.
parts.answer: Counterbalance the order (half do hands-free first); give a rest break between conditions / shorten each session.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
A hypothetical experiment in an office training centre in Lahore compares a new keyboard layout with a standard layout. Twelve learners took a typing pre-test and were formed into 6 matched pairs; one member of each pair was randomly allocated to each layout. After two weeks of practice, their typing speeds (words per minute) were:
Pair 1: new 42, standard 38
Pair 2: new 35, standard 36
Pair 3: new 50, standard 44
Pair 4: new 28, standard 25
Pair 5: new 46, standard 41
Pair 6: new 31, standard 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean typing speed for each layout. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: New layout: 38.7 words per minute; standard layout: 35.7 words per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State in how many of the pairs the learner using the new layout was faster.
parts.answer: 5 of the 6 pairs (all except pair 2).
parts.working: Pairs 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 = 5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a matched pairs design was used here rather than a repeated measures design.
parts.answer: With repeated measures each learner would practise on both layouts, so skill learned on the first layout would carry over to the second (an order/practice effect, and the layouts could interfere with each other); matched pairs avoids this while still controlling typing ability, because the pairs were matched on the pre-test.
parts.working: 1 mark: order/practice or interference effect with repeated measures, in context; 1 mark: matching on the pre-test still controls the main participant variable.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one problem that would arise if the learner using the new layout in pair 4 left the study before the final test.
parts.answer: The other member of pair 4 has no partner to be compared with, so their data are also lost (or must be excluded), reducing the sample to 5 pairs.
parts.working: 1 mark: partner's data cannot be used / sample reduced.

practice.stem: In a hypothetical independent measures experiment in Doha, 60 adults were randomly allocated to an 8-week group exercise programme or an individual exercise programme (30 in each). Six people dropped out of the group programme and one dropped out of the individual programme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of participants who dropped out of each condition.
parts.answer: Group exercise: 20%; individual exercise: 3.3% (to 1 d.p.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of all participants who completed the study. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the uneven drop-out could affect the validity of comparing the two groups.
parts.answer: The people who stayed in the group-exercise condition may be the most motivated, so the groups are no longer equivalent; any difference in fitness may be due to motivation (a participant variable) rather than the type of exercise.
parts.working: 1 mark groups no longer equal; 1 mark participant variable confounds result.

practice.stem: A hypothetical repeated measures experiment with 36 students in Riyadh tests concentration in three conditions: silence, instrumental music, and speech playing in the background.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of different orders in which the three conditions could be presented.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If each order is used equally, how many participants complete each order?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many participants do the 'speech' condition first?
parts.working: 2 of the 6 orders start with speech: 2 × 6 = 12 (or 36 ÷ 3).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why full counterbalancing of all orders is better than just using a single order for everyone.
parts.answer: With one order, the last condition would always benefit from practice or suffer from fatigue, confounding the results; using every order equally means each condition appears in each position equally often, so order effects cancel out.
parts.working: 1 mark problem with single order; 1 mark how full counterbalancing solves it.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment in schools in Karachi tests whether children aged 8–10 choose a healthy snack more often after watching a cartoon advert for fruit than after watching a cartoon advert for toys.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using an independent measures design rather than a repeated measures design in this study.
parts.answer: Strength: each child sees only one advert, so they cannot compare the adverts and guess the aim (fewer demand characteristics) and there are no order effects such as boredom. Weakness: the two groups may differ in participant variables, e.g. some children may already like sweet snacks more, which could explain any difference in snack choice instead of the advert.
parts.working: 2 marks each: point + context (children, adverts, snack choice).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a laboratory experiment to investigate whether chewing gum improves short-term memory, using a matched pairs design. Your plan should include details of the variables, the matching procedure, controls and how the data will be analysed.
parts.answer: Example plan: IV – chewing sugar-free mint gum vs not chewing; DV – number of digits recalled in the correct order on a digit-span test (strings of increasing length, read out by recording). Sample: 40 university students; pre-test on a digit-span test, rank by score, pair adjacent participants, randomly allocate one of each pair to each condition. Controls: same room, same time of day, same recorded instructions and digit lists, gum given 2 minutes before the test, no other food or drink. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, check for allergies, debrief. Data: compare mean (or median) digit span of the two conditions; bar chart.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): accurate and detailed plan covering IV and operationalised DV, clear matching procedure with random allocation within pairs, several controls, ethics and data analysis; replicable. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan with matching mentioned but vague. Level 1 (1–2): little relevant detail. Max 4 if design is not matched pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan and suggest how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Weakness: matching only on digit span leaves other participant variables, such as anxiety, unmatched. Improvement: also measure anxiety with a short rating scale and match on both, or use repeated measures with two equivalent digit lists and counterbalancing.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explanation; 1 mark improvement; 1 mark why improvement helps.

practice.stem:
A hypothetical repeated measures experiment tests reading comprehension (score out of 25) with phone notifications switched off (condition A) or on (condition B). The order was counterbalanced.
Order 1 (A then B): A scores 18, 16, 19, 17, 20; B scores 14, 13, 15, 12, 16
Order 2 (B then A): B scores 11, 12, 10, 13, 14; A scores 19, 20, 18, 21, 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean score for condition A and for condition B, using all ten participants.
parts.answer: Condition A: 19; condition B: 13.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain whether there is evidence of an order effect.
parts.answer: Yes, a practice effect: condition A mean was 18 when done first and 20 when done second; condition B mean was 12 when done first and 14 when done second, so each condition scored 2 more when done second.
parts.working: 1 mark: A first 18 vs second 20; 1 mark: B first 12 vs second 14; 1 mark: names practice effect / both improve when second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the researcher can still draw a conclusion about the IV.
parts.answer: Because the design was counterbalanced, the practice effect was spread equally over both conditions, so the 6-point difference between A and B is still due to the notifications.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether students in a school in Accra understand a passage better when it is printed on paper or shown on a tablet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the repeated measures and independent measures designs for this study, and explain which you would recommend.
parts.answer: Repeated measures removes differences in reading ability between conditions and needs half as many students, but students would read two passages and could guess the aim or improve with practice; independent measures avoids order effects and guessing, but differences in reading ability between groups could confound the result. Recommendation: repeated measures with two passages of equal difficulty and counterbalancing, because reading ability varies widely between students and is the biggest threat to validity.
parts.working: 1 mark repeated strength; 1 mark repeated weakness; 1 mark independent strength/weakness; 1 mark justified recommendation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'standardisation' in an experiment.
parts.answer: Keeping the procedure, instructions and conditions the same for every participant.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment tests whether colour of ink (red or blue) affects how well students in Multan remember a list of words. Give two ways the procedure could be standardised.
parts.answer: Every participant is given the same list of 20 words printed in the same font size; every participant gets exactly 2 minutes to study the list (also: same instructions, same room).
parts.working: 1 mark each, linked to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a control condition in an experiment.
parts.answer: It provides a baseline in which the IV is absent, so the experimental condition can be compared with it to see whether the IV had an effect.
parts.working: 1 mark baseline/no IV; 1 mark for comparison.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical study tests whether a 10-minute meditation app reduces exam anxiety in Karachi students. Suggest a suitable control condition.
parts.answer: Students listen to a 10-minute recording of neutral information (e.g. a weather report) through the same app at the same time.
parts.working: 1 mark (same length / same setting, no meditation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical memory experiment, all participants see the same 20 pictures. Explain why the researcher presents the pictures in a different random order to each participant.
parts.answer: Pictures near the start and end of a list are usually remembered better; randomising the order stops particular pictures always benefiting from their position, so position does not bias the results.
parts.working: 1 mark position effects; 1 mark randomising spreads them out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical study, the same researcher read the same script to every participant in a calm, neutral voice. Explain why.
parts.answer: To standardise the procedure: different researchers or tones of voice could affect participants' behaviour (experimenter effect), which would be an extraneous variable.
parts.working: 1 mark standardisation; 1 mark avoids experimenter effects.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment in Ankara tests whether a cup of coffee increases alertness in the afternoon. Alertness is measured by a reaction-time test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researcher should include a placebo condition.
parts.answer: Participants who know they have had caffeine may expect to feel more alert and try harder; a placebo (decaffeinated coffee that looks and tastes the same) controls for these expectations, so any difference is due to caffeine itself.
parts.working: 1 mark expectations / demand characteristics; 1 mark placebo isolates effect of caffeine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a double-blind procedure could be used in this study.
parts.answer: A colleague prepares coded cups so that neither the participants nor the researcher who gives the drinks and measures alertness knows which cups contain caffeine until all the data are collected.
parts.working: 1 mark participants unaware; 1 mark researcher unaware (with method).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a set of standardised instructions for participants in a hypothetical experiment in which they solve anagrams under time pressure.
parts.answer: 'You will be shown 15 jumbled words, one at a time, on the screen. Rearrange the letters to make a real English word and type it in the box. You have 20 seconds for each word. If you cannot solve one, press Next. Please work alone and do not use your phone. You may stop at any time. Press Start when ready.'
parts.working: 1 mark task explained; 1 mark time limit/what to do if stuck; 1 mark clear, neutral, includes right to withdraw; must not reveal the hypothesis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why standardised instructions are important.
parts.answer: So all participants receive the same information and differences in the DV are not caused by differences in what they were told.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe controls and standardisation, using any examples.
parts.answer: Controls are ways of keeping extraneous variables from affecting the DV, so that only the IV changes, e.g. keeping room temperature, noise and time of day the same, using a control group or placebo, random allocation, counterbalancing. Standardisation is a type of control in which the procedure is identical for everyone, e.g. the same instructions read from a script, the same materials and timing. Both increase validity (the effect is due to the IV) and reliability (the study can be repeated).
parts.working: Up to 3 marks each: description (1), example (1), why it matters (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is harder to control variables in a field experiment than in a laboratory experiment.
parts.answer: In a natural setting the researcher cannot control things like noise, crowds or weather, which may vary between conditions, whereas a lab lets these be kept the same.
parts.working: 1 mark: real setting variables vary; 1 mark: contrast with lab.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment in a park in Lahore tests whether a dog increases the number of people who smile at a walker. Suggest two controls the researcher could use.
parts.answer: The same walker, wearing the same clothes, walks the same 200 m path at the same time of day in both conditions; trials are done only on dry days.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment in Dhaka tests whether children who learn spelling with tablets do better than children who learn with books. The researcher believes tablets are better and personally tests every child.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher's expectations could affect the results.
parts.answer: The researcher may unconsciously give more encouragement or extra time to the children with tablets, making their scores higher because of the researcher's behaviour rather than the tablets.
parts.working: 1 mark unconscious bias / cues; 1 mark effect on scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two controls that would reduce this experimenter effect.
parts.answer: Give instructions by a recording; have the tests marked by someone who does not know which group each child was in (blind marking).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A hypothetical study at a bird sanctuary in Sindh records how often parrots interact with two types of enrichment toy (a puzzle feeder or a hanging rope).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two controls the researcher should use when observing the parrots.
parts.answer: Observe at the same time each day (e.g. 30 minutes after the morning feed); use the same observer standing at the same distance behind a screen so the birds are not disturbed.
parts.working: 1 mark each, in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why controlling the time of observation is important.
parts.answer: Birds are more active at certain times (e.g. early morning, before feeding), so observing at different times in different conditions could change the number of toy interactions regardless of the toy type.
parts.working: 1 mark activity varies with time; 1 mark confound.

practice.stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether a radio advert for a juice drink is more persuasive when it uses a famous singer's voice or an unknown person's voice. Participants rate how much they want to buy the drink from 1 to 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two variables, other than the IV, that should be kept the same in the two conditions.
parts.answer: The length and content of the advert / the volume at which it is played; the room and time of day (also: the same products shown on the rating sheet).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the researcher should allocate participants to the conditions randomly.
parts.answer: So that participant variables such as age or liking for the product are spread equally between the conditions, and the researcher does not unconsciously put certain people in one group.
parts.working: 1 mark spread participant variables; 1 mark avoid researcher bias.

practice.stem: A hypothetical laboratory experiment in Singapore tests whether people change their answers to match others in an online group chat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher could use a cover story to reduce demand characteristics.
parts.answer: Tell participants the study is about which colours people prefer for a new website, so they do not know conformity is being measured and behave naturally when they hear others' answers.
parts.working: 1 mark cover story example; 1 mark explanation of how it reduces demand characteristics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical problem with using a cover story and how it could be dealt with.
parts.answer: It is deception, so participants cannot give fully informed consent; they should be debriefed fully afterwards, told the real aim and offered the chance to withdraw their data.
parts.working: 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of strict controls in laboratory experiments. Refer to one strength and one weakness.
parts.answer: Strength: strict controls (same room, time, instructions) remove extraneous variables, so the researcher can be confident that the IV caused the change in the DV (high internal validity) and the study can be replicated. Weakness: the more controlled the situation, the more artificial it becomes, so participants may behave differently from real life (low ecological validity) and may respond to demand characteristics.
parts.working: 2 marks each: point + explanation (example credited).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'validity' in psychological research.
parts.answer: Validity is the extent to which a study or measure tests or measures what it claims to test or measure.
parts.working: 1 mark: measures what it intends to measure (accept 'accuracy of the findings / conclusions').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'ecological validity'.
parts.answer: The extent to which the findings of a study can be generalised to real-life settings and everyday behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark: findings apply to real-world situations / everyday life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study tested memory by asking university students in Lahore to learn lists of 30 unrelated nonsense syllables in a quiet laboratory. Explain one reason why this study may be low in ecological validity.
parts.answer: Learning nonsense syllables in silence is not like everyday memory tasks, such as remembering a shopping list or a conversation in a noisy setting, so the results may not reflect how people remember in real life.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies artificial task/setting. 1 mark: explains why it differs from everyday memory, linked to the scenario.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one change that would increase the ecological validity of this study.
parts.answer: Ask participants to remember a realistic list, e.g. items to buy at a bazaar, while background market noise is played (or test them in a real shop).
parts.working: 1 mark: realistic task or setting. 1 mark: detail showing how it is more like everyday life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'demand characteristics'.
parts.answer: Cues in a study that tell participants what the aim is, so they change their behaviour – for example to help the researcher (or to spoil the results) – rather than acting naturally.
parts.working: 1 mark: features/cues revealing the aim. 1 mark: participants change behaviour, reducing validity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a hypothetical experiment in Islamabad, participants drink either a caffeinated or a decaffeinated cola and then complete a reaction-time task. Suggest one way of reducing demand characteristics in this experiment.
parts.answer: Use a single-blind procedure: both drinks look and taste the same and participants are not told which one they received or that the study is about caffeine (e.g. say it is about 'drink preference and attention').
parts.working: 1 mark: single-blind / deception about aim / identical drinks. 1 mark: linked to the caffeine study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by 'social desirability bias' and suggest why it may affect a questionnaire about how often teenagers in Karachi help with household chores.
parts.answer: Social desirability bias is when participants give answers that make them look good rather than truthful ones. Teenagers may over-report how often they help at home because helping parents is seen as respectful and expected, so the results would overestimate helping.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition – answering to present oneself favourably. 1 mark: application – over-report chores. 1 mark: reason – helping is valued / expected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researcher could reduce this bias.
parts.answer: Make the questionnaire anonymous (no names, sealed collection box).
parts.working: 1 mark: anonymity / confidentiality / filler questions / compare with parent reports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a single-blind and a double-blind procedure.
parts.answer: In a single-blind procedure the participants do not know which condition they are in (or the aim). In a double-blind procedure neither the participants nor the researcher who collects the data know which condition each participant is in.
parts.working: 1 mark: single-blind – participants unaware. 1 mark: double-blind – participants and data collector both unaware.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a double-blind procedure would improve the validity of a hypothetical trial testing whether a herbal tea improves sleep quality.
parts.answer: If the researcher rating sleep quality does not know who drank the herbal tea, their expectations cannot bias their ratings (researcher bias), and participants cannot react to knowing they received the 'real' tea (placebo/demand effects), so any difference is more likely due to the tea.
parts.working: 1 mark: removes researcher bias / expectations. 1 mark: removes participant expectation effects; difference due to IV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an extraneous variable and a confounding variable.
parts.answer: An extraneous variable is any variable other than the IV that might affect the DV. A confounding variable is an extraneous variable that has actually varied systematically with the IV, so it is impossible to tell whether the IV or the confound caused the change in the DV.
parts.working: 1 mark: extraneous – any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV. 1 mark: confounding – varies with the IV/conditions, so effect cannot be attributed to the IV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a hypothetical study, Class A in a Lahore school is taught spelling with a phone app in the morning, and Class B is taught with workbooks in the afternoon. Identify one confounding variable and explain how it reduces validity.
parts.answer: Time of day: pupils may be more alert in the morning, so if Class A scores higher it could be due to alertness rather than the app, so the study may not be measuring the effect of the teaching method.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies confound (time of day / different class / different teacher). 1 mark: explains why the DV difference cannot be attributed to the method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist designs a new 'exam stress' questionnaire for O Level students in Rawalpindi. Explain what is meant by 'face validity' and suggest how it could be checked for this questionnaire.
parts.answer: Face validity is whether a measure looks, on the surface, as if it measures what it claims to measure. It could be checked by asking experts (e.g. school counsellors or psychologists) and some students to read the questions and judge whether they appear to be about exam stress.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition – appears to measure what it should. 1 mark: method – experts/others judge items. 1 mark: application to exam stress questionnaire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using a placebo condition can improve the validity of a drug trial.
parts.answer: Participants in both conditions believe they may be receiving the drug, so any improvement due simply to expecting to get better (the placebo effect) occurs in both groups; a greater improvement in the drug group can therefore be attributed to the drug itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: controls for expectation/placebo effect. 1 mark: difference can then be attributed to the drug.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to measure 'aggression' in children in a school playground in Peshawar. Explain why it is important to operationalise this variable, and give two examples of operationalised behaviours.
parts.answer: Operationalising means defining the variable in terms of specific, observable behaviours so it can be measured precisely; this means observers record the same thing, improving validity and reliability. Examples: pushing another child with both hands; hitting another child with a closed fist; shouting an insult at another child; kicking.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of operationalisation. 1 mark: why – precise/measurable, so the measure is valid/consistent. 1 mark each for two observable behaviours (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new 10-item self-esteem questionnaire is given to 50 adults in Dubai, who also complete a well-established self-esteem scale. 46 of the 50 adults are placed in the same category (high or low self-esteem) by both measures. Calculate the percentage of adults placed in the same category.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name this way of checking validity and explain what the result suggests.
parts.answer: Concurrent validity (comparing a new measure with an established one taken at the same time). The high level of agreement (92 %) suggests the new questionnaire measures self-esteem in much the same way as the established scale, so it appears to be valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: concurrent validity. 1 mark: explanation of method – compare with an established measure. 1 mark: interpretation – high agreement supports validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a laboratory experiment usually has high internal validity but may have low ecological validity. Use an example of a laboratory experiment in your answer.
parts.answer: In a lab the researcher controls extraneous variables (e.g. noise, lighting, instructions), so changes in the DV can be confidently linked to the IV – high internal validity. But the setting and tasks are often artificial, so behaviour may differ from real life – low ecological validity. Example: a lab study of distraction where participants solve puzzles while a recording of a phone ringing is played, which controls noise exactly but is unlike being distracted in a busy office.
parts.working: 1 mark: control of extraneous variables. 1 mark: cause and effect / internal validity. 1 mark: artificial setting/task reduces ecological validity. 1 mark: suitable example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe researcher bias and explain how it could affect a hypothetical observation of whether boys or girls share more toys at a nursery in Multan.
parts.answer: Researcher bias is when the researcher's expectations influence how they collect or interpret data. If the observer expects girls to share more, they may record ambiguous behaviour (e.g. a girl passing a toy) as sharing but code the same behaviour by a boy differently, so the data would be biased towards the hypothesis.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition. 1 mark: application – observer's expectation about girls/boys. 1 mark: effect – biased coding of ambiguous acts, findings invalid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing researcher bias in this observation.
parts.answer: Use observers who do not know the hypothesis (blind observers), or two observers with clear behaviour categories.
parts.working: 1 mark: blind observers / operationalised categories / inter-rater checks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by standardisation and explain why it improves validity. Use any examples.
parts.answer: Standardisation means keeping procedures, instructions and materials the same for every participant (e.g. the same written instructions, the same timing and the same room). This means differences in the DV are not caused by differences in how participants were treated, so the IV is more likely to be the cause; for example, if one group were given clearer instructions, their better scores might be due to the instructions rather than the IV.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition. 1 mark: example. 1 mark: reduces extraneous/situational variables. 1 mark: conclusions about the IV more valid (with example).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Nairobi asked shoppers to rate a new advertisement while a researcher stood beside them holding a clipboard with the company logo. Explain two threats to validity in this procedure.
parts.answer: 1. Demand characteristics / social desirability: shoppers can see the company logo and the researcher watching, so they may give more positive ratings to please the researcher. 2. Researcher (investigator) effects: the researcher's presence, tone or body language may influence how shoppers answer, so ratings may not reflect their true opinions.
parts.working: For each threat: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher measured 'helpfulness' in a hypothetical study by counting how many times participants said they would help a stranger in a questionnaire. Explain one reason why this measure may lack validity, and suggest a more valid measure.
parts.answer: What people say they would do is not necessarily what they actually do: they may overestimate their helpfulness because of social desirability, so the questionnaire may measure self-image rather than helping. A more valid measure would be to observe real helping, e.g. a confederate drops a bag of oranges in a shopping centre and the observer records whether passers-by help pick them up within 10 seconds.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report vs actual behaviour. 1 mark: social desirability explanation. 1 mark: suggests behavioural measure. 1 mark: operationalised detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two researchers disagree. Sana says a field experiment is always more valid than a laboratory experiment. Haris says a laboratory experiment is more valid. Explain who you agree with.
parts.answer: Both are partly right because validity has different types. Sana: field experiments take place in natural settings, so participants behave more naturally and findings have higher ecological validity, and participants may not know they are in a study, reducing demand characteristics. Haris: laboratory experiments control extraneous variables more tightly, so they have higher internal validity – we can be more confident that the IV caused the DV. Conclusion: neither is 'always' more valid; the best choice depends on whether control or realism matters more for the research question.
parts.working: 1 mark: Sana's point explained. 1 mark: Haris's point explained. 1 mark: distinguishes internal vs ecological validity. 1 mark: reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigated whether a mindfulness app reduces stress in nurses at a hospital in Karachi. Nurses chose whether to use the app (20 did) or not (20 did not). After four weeks, all nurses rated their stress on a scale of 1 to 10. Explain three reasons why the conclusion 'the app reduces stress' may not be valid.
parts.answer: 1. Self-selection/participant variables: nurses who chose the app may already have been more motivated or less stressed, so differences may not be due to the app. 2. Demand characteristics / placebo: app users knew they were using a stress-reduction tool and may have rated themselves lower to fit expectations. 3. No baseline: stress was only measured afterwards, so we cannot tell whether stress actually changed. Also: other uncontrolled variables (e.g. different shifts or wards) may have affected stress.
parts.working: For each of three reasons: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the nurses/app study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by 'ecological validity' and 'demand characteristics', using any examples.
parts.answer: Ecological validity: how far findings can be applied to real-life settings; it depends on the setting, task and materials being realistic, e.g. a study of road-crossing decisions using a virtual-reality street is lower in ecological validity than observing pedestrians at a real crossing. Demand characteristics: cues that reveal the aim of the study so participants change their behaviour, e.g. if participants are asked about their mood before and after watching a comedy, they may guess the aim and report feeling happier. Both affect whether results reflect genuine behaviour.
parts.working: 3 marks for each concept: 1 mark definition, 1 mark elaboration, 1 mark example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could conduct a laboratory experiment to investigate whether background music affects reading comprehension, so that the study is as valid as possible. Include the IV and DV, the design, controls and how validity is protected.
parts.answer: IV: background music (instrumental music at a set volume vs silence). DV: reading comprehension score – number correct out of 20 multiple-choice questions on a 600-word passage. Design: independent measures (to avoid practice effects with the same passage), random allocation from a sample of e.g. 40 sixth-form students. Controls: same passage and questions, same 10-minute reading time, same room, lighting, time of day, headphones at same volume; standardised written instructions. Validity: single-blind cover story ('a study of reading speed') to reduce demand characteristics; the person marking answers does not know the condition (double-blind marking); exclude participants who are not fluent in the language of the passage; pilot study to check the questions measure comprehension (face validity). Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, debrief.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): IV and DV operationalised; appropriate design with allocation; several specific controls; at least two explicit validity measures; procedure replicable. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, little detail on validity. Level 1 (1–2): vague.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'reliability'.
parts.answer: Reliability is the consistency of a measure or procedure: whether it gives the same results if it is repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark: consistency / same results on repetition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline how the test-retest method could be used to check the reliability of a questionnaire on screen-time habits.
parts.answer: Give the same questionnaire to the same participants twice, a suitable time apart (e.g. two weeks), and compare (correlate) the two sets of scores; a strong positive correlation shows the questionnaire is reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: same people, same test, two occasions with time gap. 1 mark: compare/correlate scores – high agreement = reliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two observers recorded the number of times a toddler at a day-care centre in Islamabad made eye contact with a carer during 20 one-minute periods. They agreed on 18 of the 20 periods. Calculate the percentage agreement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this result shows about the observation.
parts.answer: It shows high inter-rater (inter-observer) reliability: the two observers recorded the behaviour in a consistent way, so the behaviour categories were clear and the data are not just the opinion of one observer.
parts.working: 1 mark: inter-rater reliability is high. 1 mark: explanation – observers consistent / categories clear.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between reliability and validity, using an example of a bathroom scale.
parts.answer: Reliability is consistency, validity is accuracy. A scale that shows 2 kg too heavy every time is reliable (it gives the same reading each time) but not valid (the reading is not the true weight). A valid scale must also be reliable, but a reliable scale is not necessarily valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: reliability = consistency. 1 mark: validity = measures what it should / accuracy. 1 mark: example showing reliable but not valid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways of improving the inter-rater reliability of an observation of customer behaviour in a shopping mall.
parts.answer: 1. Operationalise the behaviour categories clearly (e.g. 'picks up a product and reads the label for at least 3 seconds'), so both observers know exactly what to record. 2. Train the observers together with practice recordings (e.g. video clips of shoppers) and compare scores until they agree highly before the real observation.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the mall context. Accept also: time sampling with fixed intervals; use of a coding sheet; video recording for later checking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical memory test was given to 140 students in Lahore and repeated three weeks later. 112 students were placed in the same score band (low, medium or high) both times. Calculate the percentage of students placed in the same band.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why some students may have been placed in a different band on the second occasion, even if the test is reliable.
parts.answer: 1. Practice effect: students may remember some items from the first test and score higher the second time. 2. Situational/participant changes: on one occasion a student may have been tired, ill or anxious (or the room was noisy), which changed their performance. Also: genuine change in memory over three weeks (e.g. learning).
parts.working: For each: 1 mark reason, 1 mark explanation linked to the test-retest situation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe 'test-retest reliability' and 'inter-rater reliability', using any examples.
parts.answer: Test-retest reliability: the same participants complete the same test on two occasions, separated by enough time to avoid remembering answers but not so long that the trait changes; scores are correlated and a strong positive correlation indicates consistency, e.g. an anxiety questionnaire taken two weeks apart. Inter-rater reliability: two or more observers or raters independently record or score the same behaviour; their scores are compared (correlation or % agreement), e.g. two observers coding aggressive acts in a playground. High agreement means the scoring is consistent and not based on one person's interpretation.
parts.working: 3 marks each: 1 mark definition, 1 mark how it is assessed, 1 mark example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'generalisability'.
parts.answer: The extent to which findings from a sample can be applied to the wider target population (and other settings).
parts.working: 1 mark: findings apply beyond the sample to the population/other people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical study of sleep habits used 25 male medical students from one university in Peshawar. Explain one reason why the findings may not be generalisable.
parts.answer: The sample is all male, from one university and one course; medical students may have unusual sleep patterns because of long study hours and night shifts, so results may not apply to women, older adults or people in other jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a sample bias (one gender/one institution/one course/small). 1 mark: explains why the wider population may differ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the sampling technique and sample size affect the generalisability of a study. Use examples.
parts.answer: A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection, so the sample is more representative, e.g. randomly selecting pupils from the register of every school in a district. An opportunity or volunteer sample may over-represent certain types of people, e.g. volunteers who are more confident. A larger sample reduces the effect of unusual individuals, so findings are more likely to apply to the population; a very small sample may be biased by chance.
parts.working: 1 mark: representative techniques explained. 1 mark: biased techniques explained. 1 mark: sample size effect. 1 mark: relevant examples.

parts.label: a
